## Mission background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-126&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Mission background")]

The mission marks:[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-ql-4)

*   155th NASA crewed space flight
*   124th Space Shuttle mission since [STS-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-1 "STS-1")
*   99th post-_[Challenger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Challenger "Space Shuttle Challenger")_ mission
*   11th post-_[Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia")_ mission
*   22nd flight of _Endeavour_
*   27th shuttle mission to the ISS
*   31st night launch[[NASA 19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-night-32)

## Shuttle processing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-126&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Shuttle processing")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b9/STS-126.JPG/250px-STS-126.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS-126.JPG)

_[Endeavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour")_ at [launch pad 39B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center_Launch_Complex_39B "Kennedy Space Center Launch Complex 39B") prior to moving to [pad 39A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center_Launch_Complex_39A "Kennedy Space Center Launch Complex 39A").

Space Shuttle _Endeavour_ was moved from the [Orbiter Processing Facility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbiter_Processing_Facility "Orbiter Processing Facility") (OPF-2) at Kennedy Space Center to the [Vehicle Assembly Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vehicle_Assembly_Building "Vehicle Assembly Building") (VAB) on 11 September 2008. Rollout to [launch pad 39B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center_Launch_Complex_39B "Kennedy Space Center Launch Complex 39B") took place overnight on 18 September 2008 and was completed at 12:00 UTC on 19 September 2008.

_Endeavour_ was originally moved to launch pad 39B ahead of the normal schedule to be on standby as the [Launch on Need](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-401 "STS-401") (LON) flight for [STS-125](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-125 "STS-125"). In the event that something happened to _[Atlantis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Atlantis "Space Shuttle Atlantis")_ during its flight to service the [Hubble Space Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_Space_Telescope "Hubble Space Telescope"), a rescue flight could be performed with _Endeavour_. With both _Atlantis_ and _Endeavour_ on the pads, it was the 18th time that two flight-ready orbiters were in position at both launch pads at the same time.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-pads-33)

On 29 September 2008, NASA announced that due to a problem with the Hubble telescope, they would be revising the manifest to postpone [STS-125](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-125 "STS-125") until 2009, so a solution to the issue with the telescope could be integrated into the flight plan.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-nyt1-34)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-delay1-35) This moved STS-126 to the next flight, so on 23 October 2008 _Endeavour_ was moved from launch pad 39B to 39A.

The payload for STS-126, including the MPLM _Leonardo_, arrived at launch pad 39A early on 22 October 2008.

## Mission timeline

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-126&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Mission timeline")]

### Launch preparations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-126&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Launch preparations")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/79/STS-126_Launch.jpg/250px-STS-126_Launch.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS-126_Launch.jpg)

[Space Shuttle _Endeavour_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour") as it lifted off to begin the STS-126 mission to the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station").

The countdown to launch began on 11 November 2008 and the crew flew in from [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyndon_B._Johnson_Space_Center "Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center") (JSC) to the Kennedy Space Center to prepare for the launch. On 12 November 2008, Mission Management Team (MMT) Chairman [LeRoy E. Cain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LeRoy_E._Cain "LeRoy E. Cain") announced that the MMT gave the official "go" for _Endeavour_'s launch on 13 November 2008 and Ferguson and Boe practiced landings in the [Shuttle Training Aircraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle_Training_Aircraft "Shuttle Training Aircraft") (STA).[[NASA 20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-rss-36) Weather reports on 13 November 2008 gave a 70% chance of acceptable weather conditions for launch.[[NASA 20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-rss-36)

### 14 November (Flight day 1, Launch)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-126&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: 14 November (Flight day 1, Launch)")]

Filling of the external tank with [liquid hydrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid_hydrogen "Liquid hydrogen") and [liquid oxygen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid_oxygen "Liquid oxygen")[propellants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Propellant "Propellant") started at 15:30 UTC on 14 November 2008.[[NASA 20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-rss-36) After suiting up into the launch and entry suits, the crew left the [Operations and Checkout Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operations_and_Checkout_Building "Operations and Checkout Building") (O&C) in the [Astrovan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut_transfer_van "Astronaut transfer van") and arrived at the launch pad at 21:22 UTC.[[NASA 5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-lb-8) At 21:30 UTC, the crew began ingress into the orbiter, and by 22:25 UTC, all crewmembers were in their seats and performed communications checks with the ground control personnel.[[NASA 5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-lb-8) At 23:00 UTC, the closeout crew closed and locked _Endeavour_'s hatch, and the orbiter's cabin was pressurized in preparation for launch.[[NASA 5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-lb-8) Despite a last minute issue with the [white room](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Service_structure "Service structure") closeout door not being fully secured, NASA Launch Director [Michael D. Leinbach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_D._Leinbach "Michael D. Leinbach") polled the team, determined the door did not pose a hazard to the orbiter or crew, and told the crew "Good luck, Godspeed and have a happy Thanksgiving in orbit".[[NASA 5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-lb-8)_Endeavour_ lifted off on time at 00:55:39 UTC.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-launch1-37)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-launch2-7)[[NASA 5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-lb-8) External tank separation occurred at 01:03 UTC.[[NASA 5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-lb-8)

After reaching orbit, the crew began working through the post-insertion timeline, which included opening the orbiter's payload bay doors, deploying the [Ku-band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ku_band "Ku band") antenna, powering up and activating the shuttle robotic arm ([Canadarm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadarm "Canadarm")), and performing a burn of the [Orbital Maneuvering System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbital_Maneuvering_System "Orbital Maneuvering System") (OMS).[[NASA 21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-flightplan2-38)

### 15 November (Flight day 2)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-126&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: 15 November (Flight day 2)")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b9/STS-126_Kimbrough.jpg/250px-STS-126_Kimbrough.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS-126_Kimbrough.jpg)

On 15 November 2008, Kimbrough stops for a photo while working on the aft flight deck of _Endeavour_.

The second day in space for the crew was devoted to completing the initial inspection of _Endeavour_'s heat shield. Using the shuttle's robotic arm (Canadarm) and the [Orbiter Boom Sensor System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbiter_Boom_Sensor_System "Orbiter Boom Sensor System") (OBSS), the crew took detailed images of the exterior of the orbiter for the image analysis team to review.[[NASA 22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-SR3-39) The crew also continued to prepare for docking with the station on 16 November 2008, by extending the docking ring, installing the centerline camera, and organizing the tools needed for rendezvous with the station.[[NASA 23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-SR2-40)[[NASA 24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-rss2-41) The crew also performed a checkout of the [spacesuits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_suit "Space suit") that will be used for the [spacewalks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extravehicular_activity "Extravehicular activity") during the mission.[[NASA 23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-SR2-40)

During the Mission Management Team briefing, LeRoy E. Cain noted that upon initial review of the ascent imagery, a small piece of [thermal blanket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermal_blanket "Thermal blanket") appeared to come loose under the left Orbital Maneuvering System (OMS) pod, but explained that the area is not in an area of concern, as it does not experience high heat during reentry.[[NASA 22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-SR3-39)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-day2a-42) During the Mission Status briefing, lead Flight Director Mike Sarafin said that after having the crew focus the camera on the left OMS pod, it did not appear that there was any damage, but the image analysis team would take a closer look at the area.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-wp1-43)

Two issues with the orbiter's [Ku-band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ku_band "Ku band") antenna were noted by Cain, although he stated they would not impact the mission. The antenna was not handing over from Ku to [S-band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S_band "S band") automatically as it should, which meant that teams on the ground had to manually switch the antenna from Ku- to S-Band and back again.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-day2a-42) Sarafin noted that this was likely a software issue, and would not affect the crew on board, or the mission. The other issue had to do with the antenna's failure to "lock on" to satellite targets after being given the pointing data. Instead, the antenna was drifting, which meant that the teams on the ground would have to use an alternate method of pointing the antenna.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-day2a-42)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-wp1-43) There was a possibility that the shuttle crew would need to use a backup procedure during rendezvous with the station, but it was not a concern, and would not change the timeline, Cain noted.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-day2a-42)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-wp1-43)

### 16 November (Flight day 3)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-126&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: 16 November (Flight day 3)")]

After waking up, the crew set to work preparing for the rendezvous and docking with the station. The orbiter performed a final burn of the engines at 19:27 UTC to refine the approach, and by 21:00 UTC, the shuttle was in position below the station to allow the station crew to photograph the underside of the orbiter. Ferguson guided the shuttle manually through the [Rendezvous pitch maneuver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rendezvous_pitch_maneuver "Rendezvous pitch maneuver") (RPM) while station crew used 400 mm (16 in) and 800 mm (31 in) cameras to take high-resolution images of the thermal tiles on _Endeavour_.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-dock2-44) The images were downlinked to NASA's image analysis team to assist in the evaluation of the thermal protection system of the orbiter.[[NASA 25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-dock-45) After the RPM was complete, Ferguson guided the orbiter into a safe docking at 22:01 UTC, and the hatches were opened at 00:16 UTC.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-dock2-44)[[NASA 25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-dock-45)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-dock3-46) Upon entering the station, Ferguson joked "Hey, we figured we'd go for a 10-year anniversary party for the space station, so that's what we showed up for".[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-dock3-46) Ferguson was referring to the 20 November 1998 launch of [Zarya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zarya_(ISS_module) "Zarya (ISS module)"), the first component of the International Space Station.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-dock3-46)

After the two crews exchanged greetings, they performed a safety briefing, and then set right to work, beginning transfers and preparing for robotic operations. At 02:50 UTC, Chamitoff and Magnus officially switched positions, with the swap of their Soyuz seatliners. Chamitoff joined the STS-126 crew as a mission specialist, and Magnus officially became the flight engineer 2 for Expedition 18.[[NASA 25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-dock-45)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-dock3-46)

During the mission status briefing, LeRoy E. Cain stated that the image analysis team was still evaluating the ascent imagery, but that the vehicle looked very clean, and the only event that was seen on launch, the area under the left OMS pod, appeared to have been ice.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-dock3-46) The images taken during the flight day two survey showed that all of the thermal blankets in that area were intact, as were the tiles.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-dock3-46) Cain stated that the item did not strike the orbiter, it was the only event that the Mission Management Team was still evaluating, and that the orbiter was in good shape.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-dock3-46) Sarafin confirmed that the Ku-band antenna performed properly in radar mode, and docking was carried out without any problems with the antenna.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-dock3-46)

### 17 November (Flight day 4)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-126&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: 17 November (Flight day 4)")]

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c8/STS-126_FD3a.jpg/250px-STS-126_FD3a.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS-126_FD3a.jpg)

Following the docking of _Endeavour_, [Expedition 18](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_18 "Expedition 18") crewmembers welcome the shuttle crew into the station.

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/12/STS-126_EVA1_Stefanyshyn-Piper01.jpg/250px-STS-126_EVA1_Stefanyshyn-Piper01.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS-126_EVA1_Stefanyshyn-Piper01.jpg)

Mission Specialist Stefanyshyn-Piper handles the Nitrogen Tank Assembly during EVA 1.

Following the wake-up call, the two crews began the procedures to move the _Leonardo_ MPLM out of the orbiter's payload bay to install it on the Earth-facing port of the _Harmony_ module.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-tank-47) Using the station's [Canadarm2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobile_Servicing_System "Mobile Servicing System"), Pettit and Kimbrough began maneuvering the 12,247 kg (27,000 lb) container around 16:45 UTC, and by at 18:04 UTC it was locked in place.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-moving-48)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-cargo-49)[[NASA 26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-SR7-50) After performing leak checks, the hatch was opened at 23:43 UTC.[[NASA 26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-SR7-50) The crews took air samples and examined the container for any signs of condensation or shifting of the contents during launch. The container had no issues, and transfer of cargo between the container and the station began shortly after the hatch was opened.[[NASA 26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-SR7-50) The team also worked on experiments that were flown with _Endeavour_, including one that involves observing [spiders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spider "Spider") and [butterflies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Butterfly "Butterfly") in space.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-spider-51)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-spider2-52) The experiment from [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"), [Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas "Texas") and [Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado "Colorado") schoolchildren is being conducted to compare spider webs created in [microgravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micro-g_environment "Micro-g environment") with those on [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-latimes-18) The insects will be returned to Earth with the shuttle for additional study.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-spider-51)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-spider2-52)

Later in the day, the crew members reviewed spacewalk procedures to prepare for the first of the four planned EVAs. [Piper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heidemarie_Stefanyshyn-Piper "Heidemarie Stefanyshyn-Piper") and Bowen began the protocol known as the "[campout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extravehicular_activity "Extravehicular activity")" prior to their sleep period.[[NASA 26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-SR7-50) Camping out consists of spending the night in the _[Quest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quest\_Joint\_Airlock "Quest Joint Airlock")_ joint airlock at lower air pressure (70.33 [kPa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pascal_(unit) "Pascal (unit)") (10.2 [psi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pound_per_square_inch "Pound per square inch"))) to lessen the time needed to acclimate to the environment in the spacesuits.[[NASA 26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-SR7-50)

During the Mission Management Team briefing, Cain confirmed that the orbiter's wing leading edge had been cleared, and that no focused inspection would be required.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-FI1-53) The time that was scheduled for that inspection on day six would instead be spent working on the station's new water reclamation unit.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-moving-48)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-FI1-53) While the image analysis team was still reviewing the imagery from the day two inspection and RPM, Cain said the orbiter was "doing extremely well", and expected the image analysis team to clear it for re-entry within a day.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-FI1-53) Cain noted that the imagery from the external tank showed it to be extremely clean, with only three small areas of foam loss noted.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-tank-47)

During the Mission Status briefing, ISS Deputy Program Manager Kirk Shireman noted the upcoming ten-year anniversary of the International Space Station. Shireman reviewed the progress and advancements that have come from the project, and reviewed some of the major milestones. Thirty [Progress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progress_(spacecraft) "Progress (spacecraft)") vehicles have visited the station, seventeen [Soyuz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_(spacecraft) "Soyuz (spacecraft)") vehicles, twenty-seven space shuttles, and one [Automated Transfer Vehicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automated_Transfer_Vehicle "Automated Transfer Vehicle") (ATV). One hundred sixty-four people had visited the station from fourteen nations prior to STS-126, (167 once STS-126 docked) and on 20 November 2008, the tenth anniversary, Shireman said the station will have orbited the Earth 57,509 times, for a total distance of over 2,100,000,000 km (1.3×10 9 mi).[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-orbits-54)

### 18 November (Flight day 5)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-126&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: 18 November (Flight day 5)")]

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/80/Bye_tool_bag.jpg/250px-Bye_tool_bag.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bye_tool_bag.jpg)

The crew lock bag holding tools floats away from the space station during EVA 1.

Following their post-sleep period, the crews set to work preparing for the first spacewalk of the mission. Stefanyshyn-Piper and Bowen were suited up and in the airlock ahead of schedule, and the EVA started at 18:09 UTC, with Piper becoming the first female Lead Spacewalker.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-bloom-55)[[NASA 27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-rsseva1-56)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-toolbag-57)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-bag1-58) While Piper was preparing to begin work on the SARJ, she noticed a significant amount of grease in her tool bag, "I think we had a grease gun explode in the large bag, because there's grease in the bag", Piper reported to Kimbrough, who was working inside the shuttle to help coordinate the EVA.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-toolbag-57) Mission Control managers instructed Piper to clean up the grease using a dry wipe, and while she was doing the cleanup, one of the crew lock bags floated away. "I guess one of my crew lock bags was not transferred and it's loose", Piper told Kimbrough.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-toolbag-57) The bag floated aft and starboard of the station, and did not pose a risk to the station or orbiter.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-kerrick-59) After taking an inventory of the items inside the lost bag, managers on the ground determined that Bowen had all those items in his bag, and the two could share equipment.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-toolbag-57) While it extended the EVA duration slightly, the major objectives were not changed, and all EVA tasks were accomplished.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-toolbag-57)[[NASA 28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-SR9-60) The estimated value of the lost tool bag was US$100,000.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-latimes-18)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-bloom-55) An amateur astronomer later observed the tool bag as it orbited the Earth prior to re-entering.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-universetoday-20081123-61) It was not the first time that equipment had gotten away from spacewalkers, items lost in the past include tools, nuts and bolts, glue guns, cameras, cloths, and even a robotic arm.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-debris-62) The [United States Space Surveillance Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Space_Surveillance_Network "United States Space Surveillance Network") constantly monitors over 12,500 items in orbit around the Earth.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-debris-62)

During the Mission Status briefing, lead ISS Flight Director Ginger Kerrick noted that there was no way to know what caused the bag to come loose.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-kerrick-59) "We don't know that this incident occurred because they forgot to tether something. We don't know if perhaps the hook just came loose inside the bag", Kerrick said. "You've got to remember, we are working with humans here and we are prone to human error. We do the best we can, and we learn from our mistakes".[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-kerrick-59) Kerrick noted that the team would be taking extra precautions to avoid any further problems with the grease guns, by attaching them to the outside of the bags instead of inside to prevent the plungers from being inadvertently activated.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-kerrick-59)

### 19 November (Flight day 6)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-126&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: 19 November (Flight day 6)")]

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/06/STS-126_CrewRack.jpg/250px-STS-126_CrewRack.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS-126_CrewRack.jpg)

Chamitoff and Magnus transfer one of the two new crew quarters racks. Visible on the back of the rack are the signatures of the members of the ground team that worked on the new equipment.

Flight day six was devoted to transfer operations, and the two crews worked through the morning to complete all the rack transfers.[[NASA 29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-SR11-63) Magnus and Chamitoff successfully installed the two crew quarters racks into the _Harmony_ node, and installed a rack with equipment to be returned to Earth into the MPLM.[[NASA 29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-SR11-63) During the Mission Status briefing, Lead ISS Flight Director Ginger Kerrick noted that all the racks were now on station, and about 25% of the cargo transfers had been completed, which was slightly ahead of schedule.[[NASA 29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-SR11-63)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-water1-64) The two crews also began working on activating the Water Recovery System, so that samples of water from two areas could be taken and returned to Earth with _Endeavour_.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-day6-65) The system's initial checkout was initiated, and water samples would be taken after several days of operation.[[NASA 29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-SR11-63)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-water1-64) Later in the day, the two crews reviewed procedures for the mission's second EVA, and Stefanyshyn-Piper and Kimbrough would sleep in the station's airlock as part of the pre-EVA campout procedure.[[NASA 29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-SR11-63)

### 20 November (Flight day 7)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-126&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: 20 November (Flight day 7)")]

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c1/STS-126_ISS_and_Endeavour_crews_02.jpg/250px-STS-126_ISS_and_Endeavour_crews_02.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS-126_ISS_and_Endeavour_crews_02.jpg)

Following the traditional joint crew news conference, shuttle and station crews posed for a group photo.

On the tenth anniversary of the International Space Station, Stefanyshyn-Piper and Kimbrough successfully conducted the mission's second spacewalk.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-eva2a-66)[[NASA 30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-SR13-67) The EVA was 6 hours and 45 minutes in duration, and all tasks were accomplished without complications.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-latimes-18) Two crew equipment carts were relocated in preparation for the arrival of the final set of solar arrays, the station's robotic arm was lubricated, and the work on the starboard SARJ continued.[[NASA 30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-SR13-67)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-birthday-68) Inside the station, crewmembers continued to transfer cargo from _Leonardo_ to the station, items to be returned to Earth into the MPLM, and continued the activation of the Water Recovery System.[[NASA 30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-SR13-67)

### 21 November (Flight day 8)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-126&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: 21 November (Flight day 8)")]

Following the crew wake up call, the two crews set to work on the day's planned activities. Fincke and Magnus tested latches on the Exposed Facility Berthing Mechanism for the Japanese Kibo laboratory.[[NASA 31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-SR15-69) Magnus continued with the installation of the [Total Organic Carbon Analyzer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_organic_carbon "Total organic carbon") (TOCA), while engineers on the ground worked through troubleshooting of the Urine Processor Assembly (UPA).[[NASA 31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-SR15-69) The component initially ran on the evening of 20 November 2008, but shut itself down during that initial test, and shut down again the following morning after two hours of operations.[[NASA 31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-SR15-69)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-motor-70) Engineers were considering if the issue was a problem with the sensors, or with the centrifuge motor.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-motor-70) At 17:10 UTC, Ferguson and Boe used the shuttle's engines to reboost the station's altitude, raising it by about 1.9 km (1.2 mi) to prepare for the next Progress arrival.[[NASA 32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-SR14-71)

The two crews also participated in the traditional Joint Crew News Conference, answering questions from reporters around the world, and took the traditional crew photo.[[NASA 31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-SR15-69) Cargo transfers continued between the vehicles, and the crew was about 75% complete with all transfers to and from the MPLM.[[NASA 33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-fd9ep-72) After a bit of off-duty time, the two crews participated in an EVA review, in preparation for the mission's third spacewalk. Piper and Bowen spent the night in the _Quest_ airlock for the campout prior to the next day's spacewalk.[[NASA 31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-SR15-69)

### 22 November (Flight day 9)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-126&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: 22 November (Flight day 9)")]

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/00/STS-126_EVA4_Bowen.jpg/250px-STS-126_EVA4_Bowen.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS-126_EVA4_Bowen.jpg)

Bowen works on the SARJ during the mission's third spacewalk.

After awakening, the two crews prepared for the mission's third EVA, which began at 18:01 UTC.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-eva3b-73) The entire spacewalk was devoted to completing the cleaning, lubrication, removal and replacement of the trundle bearings assemblies in the starboard SARJ.[[NASA 34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-SR16-74)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-eva3a-75) The final trundle bearing assembly installation was deferred to the fourth EVA, but all other tasks scheduled were accomplished without any issues.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-eva3b-73) Stefanyshyn-Piper's fifth EVA moved her to the twenty-fifth spot in [cumulative EVA time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cumulative_spacewalk_records "List of cumulative spacewalk records") with thirty-three hours, forty-two minutes.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-eva3a-75)

On the station, the crews continued to work on transfer operations, and continued work on the water reclamation system. During the Mission Status briefing, lead ISS Flight Director Ginger Kerrick noted that a sample was taken from the Water Processor Assembly that contained 10% urine and 90% condensate, and would be returned to the ground with the shuttle.[[NASA 35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-SR17-76) Kerrick noted that if activation of the system continued on schedule, a sample from the potable water dispenser would be taken on flight day eleven (24 November 2008). The ground crew continued to troubleshoot the Urine Processor Assembly, looking at whether there is a sensor touching part of the system's centrifuge as it rotates, which might be causing it to slow down.[[NASA 35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-SR17-76)

### 23 November (Flight day 10)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-126&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: 23 November (Flight day 10)")]

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0c/STS-126_EVA4_Bowen03.jpg/250px-STS-126_EVA4_Bowen03.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS-126_EVA4_Bowen03.jpg)

Mission Specialist Stephen Bowen during the mission's final spacewalk

The two crews continued transfer operations, and Finke and Pettit worked together to reconfigure the Urine Processing Assembly (UPA) to try to dampen any vibration that may be contributing to the unit's shutting down prematurely.[[NASA 36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-SR19-77) The unit has continued to operate sporadically, shutting itself down after two to three hours of operations, and the engineers on the ground are still evaluating the possible causes and solutions.[[NASA 36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-SR19-77)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-h2oa-78) Managers on the ground would make a decision on 24 November 2008 on whether to extend _Endeavour_'s mission by one docked day, to help with the troubleshooting of the Water Recovery System (WRS).[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-h2oa-78) The _Endeavour_ crew had several hours of off-duty time, and participated in media interviews.[[NASA 36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-SR19-77)

### 24 November (Flight day 11)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-126&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: 24 November (Flight day 11)")]

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3c/FD13_Boe_patch.jpg/250px-FD13_Boe_patch.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:FD13_Boe_patch.jpg)

Continuing a long-standing tradition, pilot Eric Boe places the STS-126 patch onto a wall in the _[Unity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unity\_(ISS\_module) "Unity (ISS module)")_ node of the International Space Station.

Following the wake-up call, the two crews got to work preparing for the mission's final spacewalk. Bowen and Kimbrough officially began the EVA at 18:24 UTC.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-EVA4-17) Shortly before the spacewalk began, managers on the ground radioed up to the crew that the Mission Management Team had approved an extra docked day of operations for the crews, extending the mission to sixteen days.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-EVA4-17) The extra time was being given to allow the crews more time to resolve the issues with the Urine Processing Assembly.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-EVA4-17) The spacewalk successfully concluded after 6 hours and 7 minutes, bringing the total time spent in EVA activities for the mission to 26 hours, 41 minutes.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-EVA4ends-79)

### 25 November (Flight day 12)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-126&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: 25 November (Flight day 12)")]

The crews dedicated most of the day to completing the transfer of supplies from the space station to _Endeavour_ and _Leonardo_.[[NASA 37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-SR22-80) The starboard Solar Alpha Rotary Joint was automatically tracking the [Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun "Sun") for the first time in more than a year during a three-hour, two-orbit test that was initiated at 10:55 UTC.[[NASA 37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-SR22-80) The Urine Processor Assembly completed its second full five-hour run.[[NASA 37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-SR22-80)

During the Mission Status briefing, International Space Station Program Manager Mike Suffredini noted that the water recycling system appeared to be functioning normally after the modifications performed by the crew on orbit.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-Nov25a-81) Additional water samples were taken, and the crew would be bringing home approximately six liters of sample water for extensive testing.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-Nov25a-81) The crew on the station would not be drinking any of the water until the engineers and scientists on the ground had a chance to thoroughly analyze the samples taken.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-Nov25a-81) Suffredini also noted that while the goal of the EVA activities to perform maintenance on the starboard SARJ was to allow it to operate "periodically", the initial test showed encouraging results, and the lubrication and other work done by the spacewalkers may allow for more routine operations than originally expected.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-Nov25a-81) It should be weeks before a more complete assessment could be given, the joint should need to be put through more testing, as well as analysis of the results from engineers on the ground, but Suffredini was encouraged by the initial results.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-Nov25a-81)

### 26 November (Flight day 13)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-126&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: 26 November (Flight day 13)")]

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e8/STS-126_FD14_Ferguson_Zarya.jpg/250px-STS-126_FD14_Ferguson_Zarya.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS-126_FD14_Ferguson_Zarya.jpg)

Commander Chris Ferguson continued the long-standing tradition of placing the cloth patch for STS-126 crew in the _[Zvezda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zvezda\_(ISS\_module) "Zvezda (ISS module)")_ module.

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e3/Sts-126-fd15_flyaround06.jpg/250px-Sts-126-fd15_flyaround06.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sts-126-fd15_flyaround06.jpg)

A frame taken from [an animation](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Sts-126-fd15-flyaround.png) of [slow scan TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slow_scan_TV "Slow scan TV") images taken on a flyaround inspection of the station by the shuttle.

Pettit and Kimbrough used the station's Canadarm2 to move _Leonardo_ from the _Harmony_ module and placed in the shuttle's cargo bay at 21:52 UTC. Stefanyshyn-Piper packed up equipment and supplies used for the four spacewalks and moved them to _Endeavour_ for return, while Magnus continued work on the station's new regenerative life support system. She drained a condensate collection tank to create the optimum ratio of condensate and distillate from the Urine Processor Assembly (UPA), and gathered additional water samples for testing.[[NASA 38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-SR25-82)

### 27 November (Flight day 14)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-126&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: 27 November (Flight day 14)")]

In their final day of joint operations, the two crews had some off-duty time, spoke to reporters, and shared a Thanksgiving Day meal together.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-thanksgiving2-83)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-thanksgiving-84) Following the meal, the crews worked on last minute transfers, and gathered in the _Harmony_ node to bid farewell.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-farewell-85) The hatches between the two vehicles were closed 23:31 UTC, with the crew of _Endeavour_ reviewing the procedures and tools they would use the next day for undocking, scheduled for 14:47 UTC.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-farewell-85)[[NASA 39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-SR27-86)

### 28 November (Flight day 15)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-126&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: 28 November (Flight day 15)")]

_Endeavour_ undocked from the International Space Station at 14:47 UTC.[[NASA 7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-SR29-10) The total docked time was 11 days, 16 hours, and 46 minutes, making it the second-longest docked shuttle mission to the station, after [STS-123](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123 "STS-123")'s 11 days, 20 hours and 36 minutes.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-second-87)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-first-88)[[NASA 40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-STS123-89) Pilot Eric Boe maneuvered the shuttle through a flyaround inspection of the complex, but the final separation burn was delayed to avoid bringing the shuttle near the remains of a Russian Cosmos satellite that broke apart in March 2008.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-cosmos-90)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-junk1-91)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-sfn-20081129-92) While the burn would have only brought them about 11 km (6.8 mi) from the debris, Flight Director Mike Sarafin noted during the Mission Status briefing that "Per the flight rules, it was the safe course of action to not perform that burn".[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-cosmos-90) The burn was instead completed at 23:23 UTC.[[NASA 7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-SR29-10) After separating from the station, the crew of _Endeavour_ conducted an inspection of the shuttle's heat shield with the robotic arm, Canadarm.[[NASA 7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-SR29-10)

### 29 November (Flight day 16)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-126&action=edit&section=27 "Edit section: 29 November (Flight day 16)")]

Following the late inspection of _Endeavour_'s heat shield, the Mission Management Team officially cleared the orbiter for re-entry.[[NASA 41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-SR31-93) The crew spent the day preparing for landing, performing inspections and checkout of the shuttle's flight control surfaces and reaction control system thrusters.[[NASA 41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-SR31-93) Near the end of the crew's day, a [Department of Defense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Defense "United States Department of Defense") satellite, [Picosat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Small_satellite "Small satellite"), was deployed.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-picosat-94) The satellite tested two new types of [photovoltaic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photovoltaics "Photovoltaics")[solar cells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_cell "Solar cell"), to determine their effectiveness for generating power.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-picosat-94)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-picosat2-95)

Due to a less than favorable forecast for Kennedy Space Center on 30 November 2008 that was not expected to improve by 1 December 2008, mission managers decided to call up Edwards Air Force Base for the first day of landing opportunities.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-picosat2-95)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-landing2-96) There were two KSC opportunities, with two more opportunities for Edwards later in the day.[[NASA 41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-SR31-93)[[NASA 42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-landing-97) If the first two opportunities at KSC were called off due to weather, [Bryan Lunney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryan_Lunney "Bryan Lunney"), Entry Flight Director stated during the Mission Status Briefing that they would take the Edwards opportunities; the weather was not likely to improve, so there would be no reason to delay landing for a day.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-landing2-96) The forecast at KSC called for thunderstorms within 48 km (30 mi) of the landing site, as well as high crosswinds, both conditions that would violate the weather constraints for landing.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-landing2-96)[[NASA 43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-landing3-98)[[NASA 44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-landing4-99)

### 30 November (Flight day 17, Landing)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-126&action=edit&section=28 "Edit section: 30 November (Flight day 17, Landing)")]

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1a/STS-126_Endeavour_landing.jpg/250px-STS-126_Endeavour_landing.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS-126_Endeavour_landing.jpg)

Space shuttle _Endeavour_ and the STS-126 crew land at Edwards Air Force Base, [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California") after completing a mission to the International Space Station.

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/45/STS-126_Shuttle_Carrier_Aircraft.jpg/250px-STS-126_Shuttle_Carrier_Aircraft.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS-126_Shuttle_Carrier_Aircraft.jpg)

_Endeavour_ lands back at Kennedy Space Center atop the 747 [Shuttle Carrier Aircraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle_Carrier_Aircraft "Shuttle Carrier Aircraft").

After awakening, the crew of _Endeavour_ got to work preparing for reentry. While working through the deorbit timeline, Entry Flight Director Bryan Lunney, after reviewing the weather, waved off the first KSC landing opportunity due to excessive crosswinds on the runway.[[NASA 8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-landingblog-11)[[NASA 45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-rss3-100) After evaluating the weather, the second KSC landing opportunity was also waved off, as the weather was "no go" and forecasted "no go" per the landing weather requirements.[[NASA 45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-rss3-100) Lunney continued to watch the weather for possible changes in Monday's weather forecast prior to making the decision whether to land at Edwards, or wait one day to get a Kennedy landing, but following further analysis of the projected weather in Florida for Monday, Lunney decided to take the first Edwards Air Force Base landing opportunity.[[NASA 45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-rss3-100) The deorbit burn was initiated at 20:19 UTC, and the orbiter landed at Edwards Air Force Base at 21:25 UTC.[[NASA 45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-rss3-100)

STS-126 was the only mission to land on the temporary runway 04 at Edwards Air Force Base, as the main runway was completing refurbishment.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-nsf-20081130-101) The use of the temporary runway required new braking and rollout techniques that have never been used before, as the runway is 910 m (2,990 ft) shorter than the normal runway.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-runway22-102) This was the last landing at Edwards for _Endeavour_.

_Endeavour_ was returned to Florida on top of one of NASA's [Shuttle Carrier Aircraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle_Carrier_Aircraft "Shuttle Carrier Aircraft"), arriving back at the Kennedy Space Center on 12 December 2008 after a three-day cross-country trip.

## Contingency mission

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-126&action=edit&section=31 "Edit section: Contingency mission")]

The [Contingency Shuttle Crew Support](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contingency_Shuttle_Crew_Support "Contingency Shuttle Crew Support") mission which would have been launched in the event that _[Endeavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour")_ became disabled during STS-126 would have been performed by _[Discovery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Discovery "Space Shuttle Discovery")_.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-LON2-104)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-cscs-105) It would have been a modified version of the [STS-119](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-119 "STS-119") mission of _[Discovery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Discovery "Space Shuttle Discovery")_,[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-LON2-104) which would have involved the launch date being brought forward, but the goal would have been to carry STS-119's full payload and complete the mission as planned, in addition to rescuing the crew of STS-126.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-conting1-106)

**STS-126** was the one hundred and twenty-fourth [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")[Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") mission, and twenty-second orbital flight of the _[Space Shuttle Endeavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour")_ (OV-105) to the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station") (ISS).[[NASA 3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-presskit-5) The purpose of the mission, referred to as **ULF2** by the ISS program, was to deliver equipment and supplies to the station, to service the [Solar Alpha Rotary Joints](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integrated_Truss_Structure "Integrated Truss Structure") (SARJ), and repair the problem in the starboard SARJ that had limited its use since [STS-120](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-120 "STS-120").[[NASA 3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-presskit-5)[[NASA 4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-overview-6) STS-126 launched on 15 November 2008 at 00:55:39 UTC from [Launch Pad 39A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center_Launch_Complex_39A "Kennedy Space Center Launch Complex 39A") (LC-39A) at NASA's [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center") (KSC) with no delays or issues.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-launch2-7)[[NASA 5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-lb-8)_Endeavour_ successfully docked with the station on 16 November 2008.[[NASA 6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-stat05-9) After spending 15 days, 20 hours, 30 minutes, and 30 seconds docked to the station, during which the crew performed four [spacewalks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extravehicular_activity "Extravehicular activity"), and transferred cargo, the orbiter undocked on 28 November 2008.[[NASA 7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-SR29-10) Due to poor weather at Kennedy Space Center, _Endeavour_ landed at [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base") on 30 November 2008 at 21:25:09 UTC.[[NASA 8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-landingblog-11)

## Mission payloads

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-126&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Mission payloads")]

STS-126 was scheduled to be a sixteen-day mission with four [spacewalks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extravehicular_activity "Extravehicular activity") (EVA), largely dedicated to servicing and repair of the Solar Alpha Rotary Joints (SARJ).[[NASA 3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-presskit-5)[[NASA 12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-overview3-16) An additional docked day was added to the flight plan to give the crew more time to complete their tasks.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-EVA4-17) The starboard SARJ had shown anomalous behavior since August 2007, and its use has been minimized pending diagnosis and repair.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-latimes-18)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-sarj1-19) Both the [port and starboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_and_starboard "Port and starboard") SARJs were serviced.[[NASA 13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-overview2-20)[[NASA 14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-summary2-21) In addition to lubricating both [bearings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bearing_(mechanical) "Bearing (mechanical)"), the remaining 11 trundle bearings in the starboard SARJ were replaced.[[NASA 4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-overview-6)[[NASA 13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-overview2-20) Trundle bearing assembly No. 5, one of the 12 assemblies, was removed during an [Expedition 16](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_16 "Expedition 16") EVA for further examination in December 2007.[[NASA 15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-bearing-22)

STS-126 included the _Leonardo_[Multi-Purpose Logistics Module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-Purpose_Logistics_Module "Multi-Purpose Logistics Module") (MPLM) on its fifth spaceflight.[[NASA 3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-presskit-5)_Leonardo_ held over 6,400 kg (14,100 lb) of supplies and equipment. Among the items packed into the MPLM were two new crew quarters racks, a second galley (kitchen) for the _[Destiny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Destiny\_(ISS\_module) "Destiny (ISS module)")_ laboratory, a second Waste and Hygiene Compartment (WHC) rack (lavatory), the [advanced Resistive Exercise Device](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advanced_Resistive_Exercise_Device "Advanced Resistive Exercise Device") (aRED), two water reclamation racks, spare hardware, and new experiments.[[NASA 3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-presskit-5)[[NASA 16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-water-23)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-aRED-24) Also included in _Leonardo_ was the [General Laboratory Active Cryogenic ISS Experiment Refrigerator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minus_Eighty_Degree_Laboratory_Freezer_for_ISS "Minus Eighty Degree Laboratory Freezer for ISS"), or GLACIER, a double locker cryogenic freezer for transporting and preserving science experiments.[[NASA 3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-presskit-5) The shuttle also carried irradiated turkey, [candied yams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candied_yams "Candied yams"), stuffing and dessert for a special [Thanksgiving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thanksgiving_(United_States) "Thanksgiving (United States)") meal at the station, as well as an Official Flight Kit with mementos for those who supported the astronauts and helped them complete their mission successfully.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-lm-25)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-ofk-26) Also carried was a Lightweight MPESS Carrier (LMC) carrying a Flex Hose Rotary Coupler (FHRC) and returning a Nitrogen Assembly Tank from _Quest_ for refurbishment.

### Educational outreach

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-126&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Educational outreach")]

STS-126 carried the signatures of over 500,000 students that participated in the 2008 Student Signatures in Space program, jointly sponsored by NASA and [Lockheed Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_Martin "Lockheed Martin").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-spaceday.org-27) In celebration of Space Day last May 2008, students from over 500 schools signed giant posters, their signatures were scanned onto a disk, and the disk was flown on the STS-126 mission.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-spaceday.org-27) The Student Signatures in Space project has been active since 1997, and has flown student signatures on seven other shuttle flights, starting with [STS-86](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-86 "STS-86").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-spaceday.org-27)

### Agricultural camera (AgCam)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-126&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Agricultural camera (AgCam)")]

Also aboard STS-126 was the [Agricultural Camera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AgCam "AgCam") (AgCam) which was installed in the _Destiny_ module and is used to assist farmers and provide educational opportunities for students around the country.[[NASA 17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-AgCam-28)[[NASA 18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-AgCam2-29) Students and faculty at the [University of North Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_North_Dakota "University of North Dakota") built the Agricultural Camera (AgCam), that was to be delivered and installed on the International Space Station.[[NASA 17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-AgCam-28) The students will operate the camera from their campus and work with NASA engineers and station astronauts to take visible and [infrared light images](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infrared "Infrared") of growing crops, grasslands, forests and wetlands in the [Great Plains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Plains "Great Plains") and [Rocky Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocky_Mountains "Rocky Mountains") regions.[[NASA 17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-AgCam-28)[[NASA 18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-AgCam2-29)

The information from AgCam provided data to agricultural producers in [North Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Dakota "North Dakota") and neighboring states, benefiting farmers and ranchers and providing ways for them to protect the environment. AgCam imagery also may assist in disaster management, such as flood monitoring and wild fire mapping.[[NASA 17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-AgCam-28)

### Cow embryos and pig cells in space

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-126&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Cow embryos and pig cells in space")]

STS-126 also flew the first bovine [embryos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embryo "Embryo") as well as porcine embryonic stem cells on an American spacecraft for an experiment to evaluate effects of the environment of space on embryonic development. The project was a joint project of ZeroGravity Inc., [University of Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Florida "University of Florida") and [USDA ARS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agricultural_Research_Service "Agricultural Research Service").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-embryos-30)

## Mission background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-126&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Mission background")]

The mission marks:[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-ql-4)

*   155th NASA crewed space flight
*   124th Space Shuttle mission since [STS-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-1 "STS-1")
*   99th post-_[Challenger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Challenger "Space Shuttle Challenger")_ mission
*   11th post-_[Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia")_ mission
*   22nd flight of _Endeavour_
*   27th shuttle mission to the ISS
*   31st night launch[[NASA 19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-night-32)

## Shuttle processing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-126&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Shuttle processing")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b9/STS-126.JPG/250px-STS-126.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS-126.JPG)

_[Endeavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour")_ at [launch pad 39B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center_Launch_Complex_39B "Kennedy Space Center Launch Complex 39B") prior to moving to [pad 39A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center_Launch_Complex_39A "Kennedy Space Center Launch Complex 39A").

Space Shuttle _Endeavour_ was moved from the [Orbiter Processing Facility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbiter_Processing_Facility "Orbiter Processing Facility") (OPF-2) at Kennedy Space Center to the [Vehicle Assembly Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vehicle_Assembly_Building "Vehicle Assembly Building") (VAB) on 11 September 2008. Rollout to [launch pad 39B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center_Launch_Complex_39B "Kennedy Space Center Launch Complex 39B") took place overnight on 18 September 2008 and was completed at 12:00 UTC on 19 September 2008.

_Endeavour_ was originally moved to launch pad 39B ahead of the normal schedule to be on standby as the [Launch on Need](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-401 "STS-401") (LON) flight for [STS-125](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-125 "STS-125"). In the event that something happened to _[Atlantis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Atlantis "Space Shuttle Atlantis")_ during its flight to service the [Hubble Space Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_Space_Telescope "Hubble Space Telescope"), a rescue flight could be performed with _Endeavour_. With both _Atlantis_ and _Endeavour_ on the pads, it was the 18th time that two flight-ready orbiters were in position at both launch pads at the same time.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-pads-33)

On 29 September 2008, NASA announced that due to a problem with the Hubble telescope, they would be revising the manifest to postpone [STS-125](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-125 "STS-125") until 2009, so a solution to the issue with the telescope could be integrated into the flight plan.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-nyt1-34)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-126#cite_note-delay1-35) This moved STS-126 to the next flight, so on 23 October 2008 _Endeavour_ was moved from launch pad 39B to 39A.

The payload for STS-126, including the MPLM _Leonardo_, arrived at launch pad 39A early on 22 October 2008.
