## Mission background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-123&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Mission background")]

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c5/STS-123_Thunderbirds_Flypast.jpg/250px-STS-123_Thunderbirds_Flypast.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS-123_Thunderbirds_Flypast.jpg)

The [USAF Thunderbirds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USAF_Thunderbirds "USAF Thunderbirds") display team performs a [flypast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flypast "Flypast") of the STS-123 stack, in commemoration of NASA's 50th anniversary.

The mission marked:

*   Longest shuttle mission to the ISS to date
*   153rd NASA crewed spaceflight
*   122nd Space Shuttle flight since [STS-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-1 "STS-1")
*   97th post-_Challenger_ mission
*   9th post-_Columbia_ mission
*   30th Night Launch
*   16th [KSC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center") Shuttle Night Landing, 22nd Shuttle Night Landing Overall
*   21st launch of _Endeavour_
*   2nd mission of _Endeavour_ since [Return to Flight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-114 "STS-114")[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-sts123ql-9)

## Mission timeline

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-123&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Mission timeline")]

Flight days are based on the days as experienced by the astronauts, who are generally in a day-and-night pattern that is not equal to that of the launch site. The first flight day is the day of launch for the astronauts. That day started at the launch site on March 10, 2008 (local time), with the actual launch in the early hours of the 11th and the astronauts going to bed several hours after launch. March 10, 2008, is called flight day 1 by NASA, even though the actual mission launched on March 11.

### March 11 (Flight day 1, Launch)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-123&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: March 11 (Flight day 1, Launch)")]

[![Image 21: Wikinews logo](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/24/Wikinews-logo.svg/40px-Wikinews-logo.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wikinews-logo.svg)

Wikinews has related news: 

*   [Space Shuttle _Endeavour_ launches for mission STS-123](https://en.wikinews.org/wiki/Space%20Shuttle%20''Endeavour''%20launches%20for%20mission%20STS-123 "wikinews:Space Shuttle ''Endeavour'' launches for mission STS-123")

_Endeavour_ launched on time at 02:28:14 [EDT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Time_Zone "Eastern Time Zone") (06:28:14 [UTC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTC "UTC")) early into the night of March 11, 2008, from [Launch Complex 39](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Launch_Complex_39 "Launch Complex 39")A at the [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center").

The Flash Evaporator System switched from its primary controller to the backup controller during launch, and instrumentation for a few left-side control thrusters was lost due to a card failure. These anomalies were not expected to affect the mission.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-sfn-20080327-10)

### March 12 (Flight day 2)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-123&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: March 12 (Flight day 2)")]

The shuttle closed in on the space station. The crew used a 50 ft (15 m) laser-tipped boom to inspect its wings and nose for any sign of launch damage. The inspection has been standard procedure ever since the 2003 [_Columbia_ disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster"). Flight director Mike Moses said a quick look at the images the astronauts beamed down to Earth revealed no signs of trouble.

In addition to performing the inspection, the astronauts also prepared their spacesuits for the five planned [spacewalks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacewalks "Spacewalks") and gathered the tools they would need for the docking.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-cdt-20080312-11)

### March 13 (Flight day 3)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-123&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: March 13 (Flight day 3)")]

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/eb/S123e005945.jpg/250px-S123e005945.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:S123e005945.jpg)

The pallet with Dextre is temporarily docked to the Mobile Base Station.

Endeavour's commander, Dominic Gorie, guided the shuttle through a 360-degree backflip, known as the [rendezvous pitch maneuver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rendezvous_pitch_maneuver "Rendezvous pitch maneuver"), to allow for full photographic surveillance of the thermal tiles on the Space Shuttle's underside before docking with the space station.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-cnn-20080313-12) Docking occurred at 03:49 UTC and the hatches between the two spacecraft were opened at 05:36 UTC on.[[NASA 4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-STS-123-05-13) After docking the pallet carrying Dextre was moved to the Payload ORU Accommodation (POA) of the [Mobile Base Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadarm2#Mobile_Base_Station "Canadarm2") (MBS) by [Canadarm2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadarm2 "Canadarm2").

### March 14 (Flight day 4)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-123&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: March 14 (Flight day 4)")]

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/84/Iss016e032708.jpg/250px-Iss016e032708.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Iss016e032708.jpg)

Astronaut Linnehan "flies" towards Reisman during the first EVA

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7f/Kibo_ELM-PS_on_ISS.jpg/250px-Kibo_ELM-PS_on_ISS.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kibo_ELM-PS_on_ISS.jpg)

The _Kibō_ ELM-PS as installed on _Harmony_

Spacewalkers Richard Linnehan and Garrett Reisman worked on installing Dextre. However, the Spacelab pallet carrying the SPDM would not power up.[[NASA 5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-STS-123-06-14) Engineers on the ground tried a software patch, though later suspected a design flaw in Dextre's temporary power cable caused the issue.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-spacecom-20080314-15)

Crew members on board _Endeavour_ used a robotic arm to remove the Japanese Logistics Module – Pressurized Section (JLP) from _Endeavour_'s cargo bay and attach it to the space station. The JLP was attached to its interim location on the _[Harmony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmony\_(ISS\_module) "Harmony (ISS module)")_ module at 08:06 UTC.[[NASA 6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-STS-123-07-16)

### March 15 (Flight day 5)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-123&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: March 15 (Flight day 5)")]

The crew spent time outfitting the Japanese Logistics Module, transferring supplies and equipment into it from Space Shuttle _Endeavour_. The station's arm operators grappled the Canadian-built Dextre Friday at 01:59 UTC. Canadarm2 successfully powered up Dextre 11 minutes later. Mission Specialists Rick Linnehan and Mike Foreman spent the night in the station's Quest Airlock in preparation for the second spacewalk of the mission.[[NASA 7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-STS-123-09-17)

### March 16 (Flight day 6)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-123&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: March 16 (Flight day 6)")]

Dextre was put together today during the second spacewalk of STS-123. Mission Specialists Richard Linnehan and Mike Foreman completed their 7-hour, 8-minute orbital stroll Sunday at 06:57 UTC. The spacewalkers encountered some difficulty removing two bolts that secured the robot arm during transport, and had to resort to using a prybar to remove them.

Throughout the day, the station and shuttle crew members continued outfitting the Japanese Logistics Module – Pressurized Section.[[NASA 8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-STS-123-11-18)

### March 17 (Flight day 7)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-123&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: March 17 (Flight day 7)")]

The crews continued outfitting the Japanese Logistics Module – Pressurized Section, transferring supplies and equipment into it from Endeavour, as well as configuring racks inside the module. The crews tested the brakes in the robotic system's arms. One of the joints in the arm seemed to be operating right on the required margin. Engineers expressed confidence that this issue would be resolved

Rick Linnehan and Robert Behnken ended their day by "camping out" in the station's Quest Airlock.[[NASA 9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-STS-123-13-19)

### March 18 (Flight day 8)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-123&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: March 18 (Flight day 8)")]

Linnehan and Behnken began the third EVA at 22:51 UTC. The excursion lasted six hours and 53 minutes. Linnehan and Behnken installed a spare parts platform, cameras, and tool handling assembly for Dextre. Among other tasks, they also checked out and calibrated Dextre's end effector and attached critical spare parts to an [External Stowage Platform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/External_Stowage_Platform "External Stowage Platform").

They were unable to attach a materials science experiment to the [_Columbus_ module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_module "Columbus module") due to issues with the attachment fitting, but anticipated another opportunity later in the mission.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-cnn-20080318-20)

### March 19 (Flight day 9)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-123&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: March 19 (Flight day 9)")]

In a day highlighted by robotics activity, Dextre was attached to a power and data grapple fixture located on the U.S. laboratory _[Destiny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Destiny\_(ISS\_module) "Destiny (ISS module)")_. [Canadarm2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadarm2 "Canadarm2") grabbed the pallet that secured Dextre during its journey to the orbital outpost and returned the pallet to Space Shuttle _Endeavour_'s payload bay for the trip back to Earth.

The station and shuttle crews also prepared hardware to be used in a shuttle tile repair test on the next spacewalk, and got some much needed off duty time.[[NASA 10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-STS-123-16-21)

### March 20 (Flight day 10)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-123&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: March 20 (Flight day 10)")]

The crews of Space Shuttle _Endeavour_ and the International Space Station got some off-duty time at the beginning of their 10th day in orbit. They also spoke to Japanese Prime Minister [Yasuo Fukuda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yasuo_Fukuda "Yasuo Fukuda") and participated in interviews with U.S. media.

The astronauts spent the remainder of their day configuring tools for the fourth STS-123 spacewalk and reviewing spacewalk procedures. Before going to sleep, Mission Specialists Robert L. Behnken and Mike Foreman entered the station's _Quest_ airlock for the standard "camp out".[[NASA 11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-STS-123-19-22)

### March 21 (Flight day 11)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-123&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: March 21 (Flight day 11)")]

Mission Specialists Robert L. Behnken and Mike Foreman completed the fourth STS-123 spacewalk at 04:28 UTC, spending six hours and 24 minutes on the excursion. The two shuttle crew members replaced a failed Remote Power Control Module — essentially a circuit breaker — on the station's truss. However, there were difficulties removing a power connector from the Z1 [truss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integrated_Truss_Structure "Integrated Truss Structure").

With Mission Specialist Rick Linnehan coordinating their activities from inside the orbiting complex, the spacewalkers also tested a repair method for damaged heat resistant tiles on the Space Shuttle. This technique used a caulk-gun-like tool named the Tile Repair Ablator Dispenser to dispense a material called Shuttle Tile Ablator-54 into purposely damaged heat shield tiles. The sample tiles will be returned to Earth to undergo extensive testing on the ground.[[NASA 12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-STS-123-21-23)

### March 22 (Flight day 12)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-123&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: March 22 (Flight day 12)")]

The STS-123 crew performed the final inspection of Space Shuttle _Endeavour_'s heat shield using the shuttle's robot arm and the Orbiter Boom Sensor System ([OBSS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbiter_Boom_Sensor_System "Orbiter Boom Sensor System")). Gorie, Johnson, and Doi surveyed the orbiter's wings and nose cap to ensure that no damage had occurred to the tiles that protect Endeavour from the heat of reentry.

The crews spent the remainder of their day configuring tools and reviewing procedures for the flight's final spacewalk. This included the standard "camp out" in the station's _Quest_ airlock for Behnken and Foreman.[[NASA 13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-STS-123-23-24)

### March 23 (Flight day 13)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-123&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: March 23 (Flight day 13)")]

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/94/S123_EVA5_Foreman.jpg/250px-S123_EVA5_Foreman.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:S123_EVA5_Foreman.jpg)

Foreman helps tie down the OBSS

Michael Foreman and Robert Behnken completed their six-hour EVA at 02:36 (UTC), attaching a 50 ft (15 m) inspection pole to the International Space Station and completing other chores. Foreman and Behnken hooked an extra-long power cord to the inspection pole, to keep its lasers and cameras warm for the next two months, then secured the boom to the outside of the space station.

After finishing that task, Foreman inspected a jammed rotating joint that has restricted the use of a set of solar wings for months. NASA hopes to have a plan for dealing with the jammed joint by the end of the month, space station flight director [Dana Weigel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dana_Weigel "Dana Weigel") said.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-yahoo-20080323-25)

### March 24 (Flight day 14)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-123&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: March 24 (Flight day 14)")]

The crews of Space Shuttle _Endeavour_ and the International Space Station completed their last full day together.

Much of the astronauts' morning was off-duty time. Afterward, the crews wrapped up transfers of equipment and supplies between _Endeavour_ and the station, and out the tools needed for undocking and subsequent activities.

The STS-123 and Expedition 16 crews also held a joint crew news conference, answering questions from members of the media on Earth.[[NASA 14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-STS-123-27-26)

### March 25 (Flight day 15)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-123&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: March 25 (Flight day 15)")]

[![Image 26](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4a/ISS_after_STS-123_in_March_2008_cropped.jpg/250px-ISS_after_STS-123_in_March_2008_cropped.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ISS_after_STS-123_in_March_2008_cropped.jpg)

ISS as seen from the departing Space Shuttle

The hatches between _Endeavour_ and the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station") closed around 21:49 UTC, ending a 12-day stay at the [ISS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISS "ISS"), with a scheduled undocking of 23:57 UTC. Because of problems with a command sent to solar arrays in the [ISS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISS "ISS"), the undocking was delayed 28 minutes and occurred at 00:25 UTC.

### March 26 (Flight day 16)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-123&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: March 26 (Flight day 16)")]

The crew of Space Shuttle _Endeavour_ spent Tuesday getting ready for its journey home and the end of the STS-123 mission. Early in their day, the crew members performed a test of the thrusters that will be used to position the orbiter for re-entry and the control surfaces for its flight through the atmosphere.

The STS-123 astronauts also set up the recumbent seat for Mission Specialist Léopold Eyharts, who joined the crew of _Endeavour_ on the International Space Station. The recumbent seat is a special seat designed to reduce the stress of gravity on those who have spent long periods of time in the weightless environment of space.[[NASA 15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-nasa-123prepares-27)

### March 27 (Flight day 17, landing)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-123&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: March 27 (Flight day 17, landing)")]

[![Image 27](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f0/STS-123_Landing.jpg/250px-STS-123_Landing.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS-123_Landing.jpg)

_Endeavour_ rolls out after touchdown. The yellow flame is from the shuttle's [APUs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auxiliary_power_unit "Auxiliary power unit") and is clearly visible in the pitch black night. Space Shuttles did not have [anti collision lights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strobe_light "Strobe light"), [navigation lights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navigation_light "Navigation light"), or [landing lights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft_landing_lights "Aircraft landing lights")

Flight controllers gave a no-go on de-orbit for the first landing opportunity at 23:05 UTC (19:05 EDT), due to unfavorable weather conditions at the [Shuttle Landing Facility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle_Landing_Facility "Shuttle Landing Facility") at [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center").[[NASA 16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-sts123landingblog-28)

Weather conditions were acceptable for the second landing opportunity, planned for 00:39 UTC March 27, 2008 (20:39 EDT March 26, 2008). The landing occurred at the Shuttle Landing Facility, and was the sixteenth night landing of the [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") at [KSC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center"), 22nd Shuttle night landing overall. Coincidentally, this mission also began with a night launch.

The second landing opportunity was a complete success with main gear touchdown occurring at 20:39:08 EDT (00:39:08 UTC March 27, 2008), nose gear touchdown at 20:39:17 EDT (00:39:17 UTC March 27, 2008), and wheels stop at 20:40:41 EDT (00:40:41 UTC March 27, 2008), completing the STS-123 crew's 16 days, 14 hours, 12 minutes, 27 seconds space voyage.

The exhaust produced by the Hydrazine Gas Generator [APUs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auxiliary_power_unit "Auxiliary power unit") on either side of _Endeavour_'s tail fin created concern among some observers that something was amiss, as it appeared more pronounced than usual in NASA's visual light cameras.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-sfn-20080326-29) However, this exhaust is normal and expected. The three Hydrazine Gas Generator APUs are activated five minutes before the deorbit burn and are running for five minutes after wheels stop. The mono-propellant hydrazine changes phase due to a catalyst and reaches 1,700°F (927°C).[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-pattersonswink-1983-30) The hydraulic power is needed for the shuttle's [rudder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudder "Rudder")/[speed brake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speed_brake "Speed brake"), [elevons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevon "Elevon"), body flap and [landing gear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landing_gear "Landing gear") during descent, and for the main engine nozzles' [gimballing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gimbal "Gimbal") during ascent. Each of the [Solid Rocket Boosters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solid_Rocket_Booster "Solid Rocket Booster") have two similar Hydrazine Gas Generators for their nozzle gimballing.

## Contingency mission

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-123&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Contingency mission")]

[STS-324](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-3xx "STS-3xx") was the designation given to the [Contingency Shuttle Crew Support](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contingency_Shuttle_Crew_Support "Contingency Shuttle Crew Support") mission which would have been launched in the event [Space Shuttle _Endeavour_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour") became disabled during STS-123.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-rescue-34) It would have been a modified version of the [STS-124](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-124 "STS-124") mission and would have involved the launch date being brought forward. The crew for this mission would have been a four-person subset of the full STS-124 crew.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-rescue-34)

**STS-123** was a [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") mission to the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station") (ISS) which was flown by [Space Shuttle _Endeavour_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour"). STS-123 was the 1J/A [ISS assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assembly_of_the_International_Space_Station "Assembly of the International Space Station") mission. The original launch target date was February 14, 2008, but after the delay of [STS-122](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-122 "STS-122"), the shuttle was launched on March 11, 2008. It was the twenty-fifth shuttle mission to visit the ISS, and delivered the first module of the Japanese laboratory, [Japanese Experiment Module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kib%C5%8D_(ISS_module) "Kibō (ISS module)") (_Kibō_), and the Canadian [Special Purpose Dexterous Manipulator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_Purpose_Dexterous_Manipulator "Special Purpose Dexterous Manipulator"), (SPDM) Dextre robotics system to the station. The mission duration was 15 days and 18 hours, and it was the first mission to fully utilize the [Station-to-Shuttle Power Transfer System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrical_system_of_the_International_Space_Station "Electrical system of the International Space Station") (SSPTS), allowing space station power to augment the shuttle power systems. The mission set a record for a shuttle's longest stay at the ISS.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-first-2)

## Shuttle processing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-123&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Shuttle processing")]

In August 2007, STS-123 crew members participated in [crew equipment interface tests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crew_equipment_interface_test "Crew equipment interface test") for the ELM-PS at [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-jaxa-20070817-3) Processing continued on schedule for _Endeavour'_ s launch in early 2008. NASA engineers applied the same ECO sensor modifications used on STS-122's external tank, to _Endeavour's_ tank. In January, a HEPA filter contamination issue was discovered, but was resolved and with no impact to the mission.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-rollover-4)

On February 11, 2008, _Endeavour_ was "rolled over" to the [Vehicle Assembly Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vehicle_Assembly_Building "Vehicle Assembly Building") in preparation for mating with the [external tank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_external_tank "Space Shuttle external tank") and [solid rocket boosters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solid_rocket_booster "Solid rocket booster").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-rollover-4) On February 13, 2008, _Endeavour_ was successfully mated with its external tank and solid rocket boosters, and was rolled out to [Launch Pad 39A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center_Launch_Complex_39 "Kennedy Space Center Launch Complex 39") in the early hours of February 18, 2008, for its planned launch on March 11, 2008.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-aviationweek-5)[[NASA 2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-pad-6) The [Terminal Countdown Demonstration Test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terminal_Countdown_Demonstration_Test "Terminal Countdown Demonstration Test"), a full dress rehearsal for launch with the crew, took place February 23–25, 2008.[[NASA 3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-rehearsal-7)

## Mission background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-123&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Mission background")]

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c5/STS-123_Thunderbirds_Flypast.jpg/250px-STS-123_Thunderbirds_Flypast.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS-123_Thunderbirds_Flypast.jpg)

The [USAF Thunderbirds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USAF_Thunderbirds "USAF Thunderbirds") display team performs a [flypast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flypast "Flypast") of the STS-123 stack, in commemoration of NASA's 50th anniversary.

The mission marked:

*   Longest shuttle mission to the ISS to date
*   153rd NASA crewed spaceflight
*   122nd Space Shuttle flight since [STS-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-1 "STS-1")
*   97th post-_Challenger_ mission
*   9th post-_Columbia_ mission
*   30th Night Launch
*   16th [KSC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center") Shuttle Night Landing, 22nd Shuttle Night Landing Overall
*   21st launch of _Endeavour_
*   2nd mission of _Endeavour_ since [Return to Flight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-114 "STS-114")[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-sts123ql-9)

## Mission timeline

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-123&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Mission timeline")]

Flight days are based on the days as experienced by the astronauts, who are generally in a day-and-night pattern that is not equal to that of the launch site. The first flight day is the day of launch for the astronauts. That day started at the launch site on March 10, 2008 (local time), with the actual launch in the early hours of the 11th and the astronauts going to bed several hours after launch. March 10, 2008, is called flight day 1 by NASA, even though the actual mission launched on March 11.

### March 11 (Flight day 1, Launch)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-123&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: March 11 (Flight day 1, Launch)")]

[![Image 21: Wikinews logo](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/24/Wikinews-logo.svg/40px-Wikinews-logo.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wikinews-logo.svg)

Wikinews has related news: 

*   [Space Shuttle _Endeavour_ launches for mission STS-123](https://en.wikinews.org/wiki/Space%20Shuttle%20''Endeavour''%20launches%20for%20mission%20STS-123 "wikinews:Space Shuttle ''Endeavour'' launches for mission STS-123")

_Endeavour_ launched on time at 02:28:14 [EDT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Time_Zone "Eastern Time Zone") (06:28:14 [UTC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTC "UTC")) early into the night of March 11, 2008, from [Launch Complex 39](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Launch_Complex_39 "Launch Complex 39")A at the [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center").

The Flash Evaporator System switched from its primary controller to the backup controller during launch, and instrumentation for a few left-side control thrusters was lost due to a card failure. These anomalies were not expected to affect the mission.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-sfn-20080327-10)

### March 12 (Flight day 2)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-123&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: March 12 (Flight day 2)")]

The shuttle closed in on the space station. The crew used a 50 ft (15 m) laser-tipped boom to inspect its wings and nose for any sign of launch damage. The inspection has been standard procedure ever since the 2003 [_Columbia_ disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster"). Flight director Mike Moses said a quick look at the images the astronauts beamed down to Earth revealed no signs of trouble.

In addition to performing the inspection, the astronauts also prepared their spacesuits for the five planned [spacewalks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacewalks "Spacewalks") and gathered the tools they would need for the docking.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-cdt-20080312-11)

### March 13 (Flight day 3)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-123&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: March 13 (Flight day 3)")]

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/eb/S123e005945.jpg/250px-S123e005945.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:S123e005945.jpg)

The pallet with Dextre is temporarily docked to the Mobile Base Station.

Endeavour's commander, Dominic Gorie, guided the shuttle through a 360-degree backflip, known as the [rendezvous pitch maneuver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rendezvous_pitch_maneuver "Rendezvous pitch maneuver"), to allow for full photographic surveillance of the thermal tiles on the Space Shuttle's underside before docking with the space station.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-cnn-20080313-12) Docking occurred at 03:49 UTC and the hatches between the two spacecraft were opened at 05:36 UTC on.[[NASA 4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-STS-123-05-13) After docking the pallet carrying Dextre was moved to the Payload ORU Accommodation (POA) of the [Mobile Base Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadarm2#Mobile_Base_Station "Canadarm2") (MBS) by [Canadarm2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadarm2 "Canadarm2").

### March 14 (Flight day 4)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-123&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: March 14 (Flight day 4)")]

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/84/Iss016e032708.jpg/250px-Iss016e032708.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Iss016e032708.jpg)

Astronaut Linnehan "flies" towards Reisman during the first EVA

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7f/Kibo_ELM-PS_on_ISS.jpg/250px-Kibo_ELM-PS_on_ISS.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kibo_ELM-PS_on_ISS.jpg)

The _Kibō_ ELM-PS as installed on _Harmony_

Spacewalkers Richard Linnehan and Garrett Reisman worked on installing Dextre. However, the Spacelab pallet carrying the SPDM would not power up.[[NASA 5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-STS-123-06-14) Engineers on the ground tried a software patch, though later suspected a design flaw in Dextre's temporary power cable caused the issue.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-spacecom-20080314-15)

Crew members on board _Endeavour_ used a robotic arm to remove the Japanese Logistics Module – Pressurized Section (JLP) from _Endeavour_'s cargo bay and attach it to the space station. The JLP was attached to its interim location on the _[Harmony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmony\_(ISS\_module) "Harmony (ISS module)")_ module at 08:06 UTC.[[NASA 6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-STS-123-07-16)

### March 15 (Flight day 5)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-123&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: March 15 (Flight day 5)")]

The crew spent time outfitting the Japanese Logistics Module, transferring supplies and equipment into it from Space Shuttle _Endeavour_. The station's arm operators grappled the Canadian-built Dextre Friday at 01:59 UTC. Canadarm2 successfully powered up Dextre 11 minutes later. Mission Specialists Rick Linnehan and Mike Foreman spent the night in the station's Quest Airlock in preparation for the second spacewalk of the mission.[[NASA 7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-STS-123-09-17)

### March 16 (Flight day 6)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-123&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: March 16 (Flight day 6)")]

Dextre was put together today during the second spacewalk of STS-123. Mission Specialists Richard Linnehan and Mike Foreman completed their 7-hour, 8-minute orbital stroll Sunday at 06:57 UTC. The spacewalkers encountered some difficulty removing two bolts that secured the robot arm during transport, and had to resort to using a prybar to remove them.

Throughout the day, the station and shuttle crew members continued outfitting the Japanese Logistics Module – Pressurized Section.[[NASA 8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-STS-123-11-18)

### March 17 (Flight day 7)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-123&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: March 17 (Flight day 7)")]

The crews continued outfitting the Japanese Logistics Module – Pressurized Section, transferring supplies and equipment into it from Endeavour, as well as configuring racks inside the module. The crews tested the brakes in the robotic system's arms. One of the joints in the arm seemed to be operating right on the required margin. Engineers expressed confidence that this issue would be resolved

Rick Linnehan and Robert Behnken ended their day by "camping out" in the station's Quest Airlock.[[NASA 9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-STS-123-13-19)

### March 18 (Flight day 8)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-123&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: March 18 (Flight day 8)")]

Linnehan and Behnken began the third EVA at 22:51 UTC. The excursion lasted six hours and 53 minutes. Linnehan and Behnken installed a spare parts platform, cameras, and tool handling assembly for Dextre. Among other tasks, they also checked out and calibrated Dextre's end effector and attached critical spare parts to an [External Stowage Platform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/External_Stowage_Platform "External Stowage Platform").

They were unable to attach a materials science experiment to the [_Columbus_ module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_module "Columbus module") due to issues with the attachment fitting, but anticipated another opportunity later in the mission.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-cnn-20080318-20)

### March 19 (Flight day 9)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-123&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: March 19 (Flight day 9)")]

In a day highlighted by robotics activity, Dextre was attached to a power and data grapple fixture located on the U.S. laboratory _[Destiny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Destiny\_(ISS\_module) "Destiny (ISS module)")_. [Canadarm2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadarm2 "Canadarm2") grabbed the pallet that secured Dextre during its journey to the orbital outpost and returned the pallet to Space Shuttle _Endeavour_'s payload bay for the trip back to Earth.

The station and shuttle crews also prepared hardware to be used in a shuttle tile repair test on the next spacewalk, and got some much needed off duty time.[[NASA 10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-STS-123-16-21)

### March 20 (Flight day 10)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-123&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: March 20 (Flight day 10)")]

The crews of Space Shuttle _Endeavour_ and the International Space Station got some off-duty time at the beginning of their 10th day in orbit. They also spoke to Japanese Prime Minister [Yasuo Fukuda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yasuo_Fukuda "Yasuo Fukuda") and participated in interviews with U.S. media.

The astronauts spent the remainder of their day configuring tools for the fourth STS-123 spacewalk and reviewing spacewalk procedures. Before going to sleep, Mission Specialists Robert L. Behnken and Mike Foreman entered the station's _Quest_ airlock for the standard "camp out".[[NASA 11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-STS-123-19-22)

### March 21 (Flight day 11)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-123&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: March 21 (Flight day 11)")]

Mission Specialists Robert L. Behnken and Mike Foreman completed the fourth STS-123 spacewalk at 04:28 UTC, spending six hours and 24 minutes on the excursion. The two shuttle crew members replaced a failed Remote Power Control Module — essentially a circuit breaker — on the station's truss. However, there were difficulties removing a power connector from the Z1 [truss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integrated_Truss_Structure "Integrated Truss Structure").

With Mission Specialist Rick Linnehan coordinating their activities from inside the orbiting complex, the spacewalkers also tested a repair method for damaged heat resistant tiles on the Space Shuttle. This technique used a caulk-gun-like tool named the Tile Repair Ablator Dispenser to dispense a material called Shuttle Tile Ablator-54 into purposely damaged heat shield tiles. The sample tiles will be returned to Earth to undergo extensive testing on the ground.[[NASA 12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-STS-123-21-23)

### March 22 (Flight day 12)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-123&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: March 22 (Flight day 12)")]

The STS-123 crew performed the final inspection of Space Shuttle _Endeavour_'s heat shield using the shuttle's robot arm and the Orbiter Boom Sensor System ([OBSS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbiter_Boom_Sensor_System "Orbiter Boom Sensor System")). Gorie, Johnson, and Doi surveyed the orbiter's wings and nose cap to ensure that no damage had occurred to the tiles that protect Endeavour from the heat of reentry.

The crews spent the remainder of their day configuring tools and reviewing procedures for the flight's final spacewalk. This included the standard "camp out" in the station's _Quest_ airlock for Behnken and Foreman.[[NASA 13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-STS-123-23-24)

### March 23 (Flight day 13)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-123&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: March 23 (Flight day 13)")]

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/94/S123_EVA5_Foreman.jpg/250px-S123_EVA5_Foreman.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:S123_EVA5_Foreman.jpg)

Foreman helps tie down the OBSS

Michael Foreman and Robert Behnken completed their six-hour EVA at 02:36 (UTC), attaching a 50 ft (15 m) inspection pole to the International Space Station and completing other chores. Foreman and Behnken hooked an extra-long power cord to the inspection pole, to keep its lasers and cameras warm for the next two months, then secured the boom to the outside of the space station.

After finishing that task, Foreman inspected a jammed rotating joint that has restricted the use of a set of solar wings for months. NASA hopes to have a plan for dealing with the jammed joint by the end of the month, space station flight director [Dana Weigel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dana_Weigel "Dana Weigel") said.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-yahoo-20080323-25)

### March 24 (Flight day 14)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-123&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: March 24 (Flight day 14)")]

The crews of Space Shuttle _Endeavour_ and the International Space Station completed their last full day together.

Much of the astronauts' morning was off-duty time. Afterward, the crews wrapped up transfers of equipment and supplies between _Endeavour_ and the station, and out the tools needed for undocking and subsequent activities.

The STS-123 and Expedition 16 crews also held a joint crew news conference, answering questions from members of the media on Earth.[[NASA 14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-STS-123-27-26)

### March 25 (Flight day 15)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-123&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: March 25 (Flight day 15)")]

[![Image 26](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4a/ISS_after_STS-123_in_March_2008_cropped.jpg/250px-ISS_after_STS-123_in_March_2008_cropped.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ISS_after_STS-123_in_March_2008_cropped.jpg)

ISS as seen from the departing Space Shuttle

The hatches between _Endeavour_ and the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station") closed around 21:49 UTC, ending a 12-day stay at the [ISS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISS "ISS"), with a scheduled undocking of 23:57 UTC. Because of problems with a command sent to solar arrays in the [ISS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISS "ISS"), the undocking was delayed 28 minutes and occurred at 00:25 UTC.

### March 26 (Flight day 16)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-123&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: March 26 (Flight day 16)")]

The crew of Space Shuttle _Endeavour_ spent Tuesday getting ready for its journey home and the end of the STS-123 mission. Early in their day, the crew members performed a test of the thrusters that will be used to position the orbiter for re-entry and the control surfaces for its flight through the atmosphere.

The STS-123 astronauts also set up the recumbent seat for Mission Specialist Léopold Eyharts, who joined the crew of _Endeavour_ on the International Space Station. The recumbent seat is a special seat designed to reduce the stress of gravity on those who have spent long periods of time in the weightless environment of space.[[NASA 15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-nasa-123prepares-27)

### March 27 (Flight day 17, landing)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-123&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: March 27 (Flight day 17, landing)")]

[![Image 27](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f0/STS-123_Landing.jpg/250px-STS-123_Landing.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS-123_Landing.jpg)

_Endeavour_ rolls out after touchdown. The yellow flame is from the shuttle's [APUs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auxiliary_power_unit "Auxiliary power unit") and is clearly visible in the pitch black night. Space Shuttles did not have [anti collision lights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strobe_light "Strobe light"), [navigation lights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navigation_light "Navigation light"), or [landing lights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft_landing_lights "Aircraft landing lights")

Flight controllers gave a no-go on de-orbit for the first landing opportunity at 23:05 UTC (19:05 EDT), due to unfavorable weather conditions at the [Shuttle Landing Facility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle_Landing_Facility "Shuttle Landing Facility") at [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center").[[NASA 16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-sts123landingblog-28)

Weather conditions were acceptable for the second landing opportunity, planned for 00:39 UTC March 27, 2008 (20:39 EDT March 26, 2008). The landing occurred at the Shuttle Landing Facility, and was the sixteenth night landing of the [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") at [KSC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center"), 22nd Shuttle night landing overall. Coincidentally, this mission also began with a night launch.

The second landing opportunity was a complete success with main gear touchdown occurring at 20:39:08 EDT (00:39:08 UTC March 27, 2008), nose gear touchdown at 20:39:17 EDT (00:39:17 UTC March 27, 2008), and wheels stop at 20:40:41 EDT (00:40:41 UTC March 27, 2008), completing the STS-123 crew's 16 days, 14 hours, 12 minutes, 27 seconds space voyage.

The exhaust produced by the Hydrazine Gas Generator [APUs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auxiliary_power_unit "Auxiliary power unit") on either side of _Endeavour_'s tail fin created concern among some observers that something was amiss, as it appeared more pronounced than usual in NASA's visual light cameras.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-sfn-20080326-29) However, this exhaust is normal and expected. The three Hydrazine Gas Generator APUs are activated five minutes before the deorbit burn and are running for five minutes after wheels stop. The mono-propellant hydrazine changes phase due to a catalyst and reaches 1,700°F (927°C).[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-pattersonswink-1983-30) The hydraulic power is needed for the shuttle's [rudder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudder "Rudder")/[speed brake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speed_brake "Speed brake"), [elevons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevon "Elevon"), body flap and [landing gear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landing_gear "Landing gear") during descent, and for the main engine nozzles' [gimballing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gimbal "Gimbal") during ascent. Each of the [Solid Rocket Boosters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solid_Rocket_Booster "Solid Rocket Booster") have two similar Hydrazine Gas Generators for their nozzle gimballing.

## Contingency mission

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-123&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Contingency mission")]

[STS-324](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-3xx "STS-3xx") was the designation given to the [Contingency Shuttle Crew Support](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contingency_Shuttle_Crew_Support "Contingency Shuttle Crew Support") mission which would have been launched in the event [Space Shuttle _Endeavour_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour") became disabled during STS-123.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-rescue-34) It would have been a modified version of the [STS-124](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-124 "STS-124") mission and would have involved the launch date being brought forward. The crew for this mission would have been a four-person subset of the full STS-124 crew.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123#cite_note-rescue-34)

**STS-120** was a [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") mission to the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station") (ISS) that launched on October 23, 2007, from the [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center"), Florida.[[NASA 4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-120#cite_note-main-6) The mission is also referred to as **ISS-10A** by the ISS program. STS-120 delivered the _[Harmony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmony\_(ISS\_module) "Harmony (ISS module)")_ module and reconfigured a portion of the station in preparation for future assembly missions.[[NASA 2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-120#cite_note-presskit-3) STS-120 was flown by [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle")[_Discovery_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery "Space Shuttle Discovery"), and was the twenty-third Space Shuttle mission to the ISS. It was Discovery's 34th flight.

Two commanders: Melroy and Whitson place the STS-120 mission insignia on the wall of the newly installed _Harmony_ module.

As commander of STS-120, Pamela Melroy became the second woman (after [Eileen Collins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eileen_Collins "Eileen Collins")) to command a Space Shuttle mission.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-120#cite_note-second-7) Additionally, the [Expedition 16](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_16 "Expedition 16") crew that received STS-120 was commanded by [Peggy Whitson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peggy_Whitson "Peggy Whitson"), the first female ISS commander.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-120#cite_note-space2-8)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-120#cite_note-fox2-9) The flight of STS-120 thus became the first time two female mission commanders were in space at the same time.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-120#cite_note-chicks-10)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-120#cite_note-msnbc1-11)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-120#cite_note-history1-12)
