## Astronaut career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paolo_Nespoli&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Astronaut career")]

In July 1998, he was selected as an astronaut for [Italian Space Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_Space_Agency "Italian Space Agency") (ASI) and in August 1998, Nespoli was assigned by the [European Space Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Space_Agency "European Space Agency") to train at NASA's [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center") in [Houston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston "Houston"), [Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas "Texas").

In 2013, Nespoli served as cavenaut into the [ESA CAVES](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESA_CAVES "ESA CAVES")[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paolo_A._Nespoli#cite_note-5) training in [Sardinia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sardinia "Sardinia"), alongside [Jeremy Hansen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Hansen "Jeremy Hansen"), [Michael Barratt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Barratt_(astronaut) "Michael Barratt (astronaut)"), [Jack Fisher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_D._Fischer "Jack D. Fischer"), [Aleksei Ovchinin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aleksey_Ovchinin "Aleksey Ovchinin") and [Satoshi Furukawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satoshi_Furukawa "Satoshi Furukawa").

### STS-120

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paolo_Nespoli&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: STS-120")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4a/S120e006445.jpg/250px-S120e006445.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:S120e006445.jpg)

STS-120 mission specialist Paolo Nespoli in the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station")

On 23 October 2007 Paolo launched on board STS-120 to the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station"); the [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") mission which delivered the _[Harmony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmony\_Module "Harmony Module")_ module (formerly known as Node 2) to the International Space Station. _Harmony_ was built by [Thales Alenia Space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thales_Alenia_Space "Thales Alenia Space") at its facility in [Turin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turin "Turin"), [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy"). He participated as a mission specialist and remained in space for 15 days, 2 hours and 23 minutes. During STS-120, he participated in the Esperia mission for the [European Space Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Space_Agency "European Space Agency").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paolo_A._Nespoli#cite_note-6)

### Expedition 26/27 'MagISStra'

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paolo_Nespoli&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Expedition 26/27 'MagISStra'")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6d/ISS-26_Paolo_Nespoli_with_Robonaut2.jpg/250px-ISS-26_Paolo_Nespoli_with_Robonaut2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ISS-26_Paolo_Nespoli_with_Robonaut2.jpg)

Expedition 26/27 flight engineer Paolo Nespoli poses with [Robonaut 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robonaut_2 "Robonaut 2").

Paolo Nespoli served as first flight engineer for [Expedition 26](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_26 "Expedition 26")/[27](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_27 "Expedition 27"), Europe's third six-month mission to the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station") (ISS).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paolo_A._Nespoli#cite_note-7)

On 15 December 2010 Nespoli flew aboard the [Soyuz TMA-20](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_TMA-20 "Soyuz TMA-20") spacecraft from [Baikonur Cosmodrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baikonur_Cosmodrome "Baikonur Cosmodrome") in [Kazakhstan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazakhstan "Kazakhstan") to the International Space Station with the Russian cosmonaut [Dmitri Kondratyev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dmitri_Kondratyev "Dmitri Kondratyev") and NASA's astronaut [Catherine Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catherine_Coleman "Catherine Coleman"). The three members of the crew returned to Earth on 24 May 2011. This mission, dubbed ‘MagISStra’, is Paolo Nespoli's second flight in space.

From 15 December 2010 to 24 May 2011, Paolo Nespoli's duties[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paolo_A._Nespoli#cite_note-MagISStra-8) aboard the ISS included participating in the docking operations to receive Europe's second [Automated Transfer Vehicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automated_Transfer_Vehicle "Automated Transfer Vehicle") (ATV-2) _Johannes Kepler_, a visiting spacecraft that will deliver essential cargo to the Station.

In early January, Nespoli filmed the majority of the footage for the 2011 documentary film _[First Orbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First\_Orbit "First Orbit")_, and as a result is credited as its [director of photography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinematographer "Cinematographer").

Nespoli took part in the arrival of the second Japanese HII Transfer Vehicle ([HTV-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H-II_Transfer_Vehicle "H-II Transfer Vehicle")), an uncrewed spacecraft used to resupply the ISS. He was the prime operator for berthing the HTV-2 to the ISS after the free-flying vehicle was captured by NASA astronaut Catherine Coleman. In May 2011, [Space Shuttle _Endeavour_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour") has delivered the [Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpha_Magnetic_Spectrometer "Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer") (AMS-02) to the ISS.

During Nespoli's stint with Expedition 27, his mother, Maria, died on 4 May 2011. The crew observed 1 minute of silence the following day around the time of her funeral.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paolo_A._Nespoli#cite_note-9)

Paolo Nespoli carried out an intensive programme of experiments in the Station, ranging from radiation monitoring to measurements that could improve [oil recovery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petroleum_extraction "Petroleum extraction") in petroleum reservoirs. The mission scientific programme covered different fields on human research, fluid physics, radiation, biology and technology demonstrations.

Nespoli contributed to the scientific exploitation of Europe's _Columbus_ laboratory. As an astronaut, he carried out several experiments for ESA, NASA and also the Japanese and Canadian space agencies. During the mission, Paolo participated in some educational activities: the educational programme ["Mission X: Train Like an Astronaut"](http://trainlikeanastronaut.org/) which gave children the chance to follow an international initiative built around health, well-being and nutrition. He also participated in a greenhouse activity in space. Nespoli used ESA's novel 3D camera to show images of the ISS.

As Paolo left the ISS on 23 May 2011 in the [Soyuz TMA-20](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_TMA-20 "Soyuz TMA-20") he was able to take the first pictures of a Space Shuttle docked with the ISS from the perspective of a Russian [Soyuz spacecraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_spacecraft "Soyuz spacecraft").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paolo_A._Nespoli#cite_note-10)

### Expedition 52/53 and the VITA mission

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paolo_Nespoli&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Expedition 52/53 and the VITA mission")]

Nespoli was part of Expedition 52/53, which started in 2017. He launched on [Soyuz MS-05](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_MS-05 "Soyuz MS-05") on 28 July 2017 15:41 UTC.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paolo_A._Nespoli#cite_note-sfi-20170728-11) Nespoli's mission to the ISS was called **VITA**. Vita is an acronym for Vitality, Innovation, Technology and Ability. In addition, in Italian it means life, reflecting the scientific experiments and the technologies needed for life in space. Additional activities included outreach like Mission-X: Train Like an Astronaut, the European Astro Pi Challenge (where European students run their own code on Raspberry Pi mini computers installed on the ISS).[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paolo_A._Nespoli#cite_note-VITA-12)

#### VITA mission logo

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paolo_Nespoli&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: VITA mission logo")]

The mission's logo was developed and created jointly by [ESA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESA "ESA"), [Italian Space Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_Space_Agency "Italian Space Agency"), and Nespoli. The overall circle represent the planet Earth, with the main objectives linked by a symbol which is a reformulation of the [infinity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infinity "Infinity") symbol, called "Third paradise" and designed by Michelangelo Pistoletto. Connected inside are a [DNA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNA "DNA") strand for the scientific experiments, a book for education, outreach and culture, and Earth as a symbol of humanity. The colors represent the Italian flag.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paolo_A._Nespoli#cite_note-Vita_logo-13)

#### Mission highlights

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paolo_Nespoli&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Mission highlights")]

During the VITA Mission Nespoli completed more than 60 experiments.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paolo_A._Nespoli#cite_note-landing-14) He also recorded the first content created in space specifically for use on [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia "Wikipedia").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paolo_A._Nespoli#cite_note-Mabbett-1) During his first month in orbit Nespoli acted as cinematographer for National Geographic Channel's _[One Strange Rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One\_Strange\_Rock "One Strange Rock")_, filming the sequences with astronaut [Peggy Whitson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peggy_Whitson "Peggy Whitson") which appear in episode 10 of the series.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paolo_A._Nespoli#cite_note-15)

Nespoli returned to Earth on 14 December 2017. The [Soyuz MS-05](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_MS-05 "Soyuz MS-05") landed at 8:38 UTC,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paolo_A._Nespoli#cite_note-landing-14) giving a mission duration of 138 days, 16 hours, 56 minutes and 37 seconds.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paolo_A._Nespoli#cite_note-spacefacts53-16)

**Scott Edward Parazynski** (born July 28, 1961) is an American physician and former [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")[astronaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut "Astronaut"). A veteran of five Space Shuttle flights and seven spacewalks, Parazynski's latest mission was STS-120 in October 2007 – highlighted by a dramatic, unplanned [extra-vehicular activity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extra-vehicular_activity "Extra-vehicular activity") (EVA) to repair a live solar array. In May 2016, he was inducted into the [United States Astronaut Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Astronaut_Hall_of_Fame "United States Astronaut Hall of Fame"). He retired from NASA in March 2009 to pursue entrepreneurial opportunities in the private sector, and he is currently the CEO of a technology start-up. He is the first person to have both flown in space and summited [Mount Everest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Everest "Mount Everest"), the highest point on Earth.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-1) He describes his life's experiences in his 2017 memoir _The Sky Below_.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-2)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Scott_E._Parazynski&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Parazynski is of [Polish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_people "Polish people") descent, as his great-great-grandparents migrated from [Kraków](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krak%C3%B3w "Kraków") to the US.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-se-3) He considers [Palo Alto, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palo_Alto,_California "Palo Alto, California"), and [Evergreen, Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evergreen,_Colorado "Evergreen, Colorado"), to be his hometowns. He is married to [Meenakshi Wadhwa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meenakshi_Wadhwa "Meenakshi Wadhwa"), a planetary scientist at Arizona State University. He has two children with his first wife, Gail. Scott enjoys [mountaineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountaineering "Mountaineering"), [rock climbing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_climbing "Rock climbing"), [flying](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fly "Fly") and [scuba diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scuba_diving "Scuba diving"). A commercial, multi-engine, seaplane and instrument-rated [pilot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aviator "Aviator"), Parazynski has logged over 2500 flight hours in a variety of aircraft. As a mountaineer, his [summits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topographical_summit "Topographical summit") include [Cerro Aconcagua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerro_Aconcagua "Cerro Aconcagua") (at 22,841 feet (6,962 m) above sea level, the tallest [mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountain "Mountain") in the world outside [Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asia "Asia")) and all 59 of [Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado "Colorado")'s peaks over 14,000 feet (4,300 m) in [altitude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altitude "Altitude"). He first attempted to summit [Mount Everest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Everest "Mount Everest") in May 2008, but was forced to turn back before the summit due to a severe back injury. Serving as team physician for the Discovery Channel[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-4) a year later, at 4:00 am on May 20, 2009, he successfully summited the 29,029 feet (8,848 m) mountain.

Other notable expeditions include a scientific dive into the summit caldera lake atop [Licancabur Volcano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Licancabur "Licancabur") (19,409 feet (5,916 m) on the Bolivian-Chilean border), one of the world's highest lakes, and setting the first bootprints adjacent Masaya Volcano's lava lake in Nicaragua with Sam Cossman in 2016.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-5) He also travelled aboard [OceanGate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OceanGate "OceanGate")'s submersible _Titan_ and visited the [wreck of the _Titanic_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wreck_of_the_Titanic "Wreck of the Titanic") in the North Atlantic.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-7)

## Education and early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Scott_E._Parazynski&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Education and early life")]

Parazynski attended junior high school at Dakar Academy in [Dakar, Senegal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dakar,_Senegal "Dakar, Senegal"), and [Beirut, Lebanon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beirut,_Lebanon "Beirut, Lebanon"). In March 1969 as an eight-year-old, he travelled to Florida to witness the launch of [Apollo 9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_9 "Apollo 9"), an event he argued inspired him to pursue a career in science. He attended high school at the [Community School, Tehran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Community_School,_Tehran "Community School, Tehran"), [Iran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran "Iran"), and the [American Community School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Community_Schools "American Community Schools"), [Athens, Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athens,_Greece "Athens, Greece"), graduating in 1979. He received a [Bachelor of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Science "Bachelor of Science") degree in [biology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biology "Biology") from [Stanford University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University "Stanford University") in 1983, continuing on to graduate with honors from [Stanford Medical School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_Medical_School "Stanford Medical School") in 1989. He served his medical internship at the [Brigham and Women's Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_and_Women's_Hospital "Brigham and Women's Hospital") of [Harvard Medical School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Medical_School "Harvard Medical School") (1990). He had completed 22 months of a residency program in emergency medicine in [Denver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denver "Denver"), [Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado "Colorado"), when selected for the NASA Astronaut Corps.

## Organizations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Scott_E._Parazynski&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Organizations")]

Parazynski is a Fellow of the [Aerospace Medical Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerospace_Medical_Association "Aerospace Medical Association") and [The Explorers Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Explorers_Club "The Explorers Club"). Additionally, he is a member of the American Society for Gravitational and Space Biology, the [Wilderness Medical Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilderness_Medical_Society "Wilderness Medical Society"), the [American Alpine Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Alpine_Club "American Alpine Club"), the [Association of Space Explorers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_Space_Explorers "Association of Space Explorers"), the [Experimental Aircraft Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experimental_Aircraft_Association "Experimental Aircraft Association"), and the [Aircraft Owners and Pilots Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft_Owners_and_Pilots_Association "Aircraft Owners and Pilots Association"). He is president of the board of directors of the [Challenger Center for Space Science Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_Center_for_Space_Science_Education "Challenger Center for Space Science Education"), and serves on the boards of the [Houston Museum of Natural Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston_Museum_of_Natural_Science "Houston Museum of Natural Science"), the University of Texas McDonald Observatory and [OceanGate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OceanGate "OceanGate").

In 2014, Parazynski was appointed as a professor of practice at [Arizona State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arizona_State_University "Arizona State University"), and was designated ASU's first University Explorer.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-8) He subsequently founded Fluidity Technologies[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-9) based on his intellectual property, a company aiming to manufacture and distribute novel control devices for mobility in 3-D space, for everything from drones and computer games to VR and surgical robotics.

## Medical career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Scott_E._Parazynski&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Medical career")]

While an [undergraduate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Undergraduate "Undergraduate") at [Stanford University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University "Stanford University"), Parazynski studied [antigenic shift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antigenic_shift "Antigenic shift") in [African](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa "Africa")[sleeping sickness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_trypanosomiasis "African trypanosomiasis"), using sophisticated [molecular biology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molecular_biology "Molecular biology") techniques. During [medical school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_school "Medical school"), he was awarded a NASA graduate student [fellowship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scholarship "Scholarship") and conducted [research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research "Research") at [NASA Ames Research Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_Ames_Research_Center "NASA Ames Research Center") on [fluid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluid "Fluid") shifts that occur during human [space flight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_flight "Space flight"). Additionally, he has been involved in the design of several [exercise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exercise "Exercise") devices that are being developed for long-duration [space flight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_flight "Space flight"), and has conducted research on high-[altitude acclimatization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altitude_acclimatization "Altitude acclimatization"). Parazynski has numerous publications in the field of space [physiology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physiology "Physiology"), and has a particular expertise in human [adaptation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adaptation_(biology) "Adaptation (biology)") to stressful environments.

## NASA career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Scott_E._Parazynski&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: NASA career")]

Selected as an astronaut in March 1992, Parazynski reported to the [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center") in August 1992. He completed one year of training and evaluation, and was qualified as a mission specialist. Parazynski initially served as one of the crew representatives for [extra-vehicular activity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extra-vehicular_activity "Extra-vehicular activity") (EVA) in the Astronaut Office Mission Development Branch. Following his first flight, he was assigned as a backup for the third American long-duration stay aboard Russia's [space station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_station "Space station")[Mir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mir "Mir"), and was expected to serve as a prime crew member on a subsequent mission. He spent five months in training at the [Gagarin Cosmonaut Training Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gagarin_Cosmonaut_Training_Center "Gagarin Cosmonaut Training Center"), [Star City, Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_City,_Moscow "Star City, Moscow"), Russia.

In October 1995, when sitting-height parameters raised concerns about his fitting safely in the [Soyuz spacecraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_spacecraft "Soyuz spacecraft") in the event of an emergency on board the Mir station, he was deemed too tall for the mission and was withdrawn from Mir training. He has served as the Astronaut Office Operations Planning Branch crew representative for [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle"), Space Station and Soyuz training, and also served as Deputy (Operations and Training) of the Astronaut Office [ISS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station") Branch. Most recently, he served as Chief of the Astronaut Office EVA Branch. A veteran of five space flights, [STS-66](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-66 "STS-66") (1994), [STS-86](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-86 "STS-86") (1997), [STS-95](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-95 "STS-95") (1998), [STS-100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-100 "STS-100") (2001), and STS-120 (2007), Parazynski has logged over 1,019 hours (8 weeks) in space, including 47 hours of EVA, and traveled over 17 million miles. Parazynski's most recent mission was STS-120, during which he performed four spacewalks to continue International Space Station assembly. The fourth EVA is considered one of the most challenging and dangerous ever performed: while perched on the end of a 90-foot robotic boom, further away from the safety of the airlock than anyone had previously ventured, he had to repair a fully energized solar array. He became only the second NASA astronaut to perform four spacewalks during a single shuttle mission. A photo that he took during one of the spacewalks was listed on _[Popular Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular\_Science "Popular Science")_'s photo gallery of the best [astronaut selfies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut_selfie "Astronaut selfie").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-21)

## Spaceflight experience

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Scott_E._Parazynski&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Spaceflight experience")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a7/Scott_Parazynski_space.jpg/250px-Scott_Parazynski_space.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Scott_Parazynski_space.jpg)

Scott Parazynski during a spacewalk during STS-120.

The [STS-66](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-66 "STS-66") Atmospheric [Laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laboratory "Laboratory") for Applications and Science-3 (ATLAS-3) mission was launched from [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center"), [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"), on November 3, 1994, and returned to land at [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"), on November 14, 1994. ATLAS-3 was part of an ongoing program to determine the Earth's [energy balance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_energy_budget#Earth's_energy_imbalance_(EEI) "Earth's energy budget") and [atmospheric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_atmosphere "Earth's atmosphere") change over an 11-year [solar cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_cycle "Solar cycle"), particularly with respect to humanity's impact on global-[ozone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozone "Ozone") distribution. Parazynski had responsibility for a number of on-orbit activities including operation of the ATLAS experiments and [Spacelab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacelab "Spacelab") Pallet, as well as several secondary experiments in the crew cabin. He and his crewmates also successfully evaluated the Interlimb Resistance Device, a free-floating exercise he developed to prevent [muscular atrophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muscular_atrophy "Muscular atrophy") in [microgravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microgravity "Microgravity"). [Space Shuttle _Atlantis_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis "Space Shuttle Atlantis") circled the earth 175 times and traveled over 4.5 million miles during its 262-hour and 34-minute flight.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-NASA-22)

[STS-86](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-86 "STS-86")_Atlantis_ (September 25 to October 6, 1997) was the seventh mission to rendezvous and dock with the Russian Space Station Mir. Highlights of the mission included the exchange of U.S. crew members [Michael Foale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Foale "Michael Foale") and [David Wolf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wolf_(astronaut) "David Wolf (astronaut)"), the transfer of 10,400 pounds of science and logistics, and the first Shuttle-based joint American-Russian spacewalk. Parazynski served as the flight engineer (MS2) during the flight, and was also the navigator during the Mir rendezvous. Parazynski (EV1) and Russian [cosmonaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmonaut "Cosmonaut")[Vladimir Titov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Titov_(cosmonaut) "Vladimir Titov (cosmonaut)") performed a 5-hour, 1 minute [spacewalk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacewalk "Spacewalk") during which they retrieved four experiment packages first deployed during the [STS-76](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-76 "STS-76")[Shuttle-Mir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle-Mir "Shuttle-Mir") docking mission. They also deployed the Spektr Solar Array Cap, which was designed to be used in a future Mir spacewalk to seal a leak in the Spektr module's damaged hull. Other objectives of EVA included the evaluation of common EVA tools to be used by astronauts wearing either Russian or American-made spacesuits, and a systems flight test of the Simplified Aid for EVA Rescue (SAFER). Space Shuttle _Atlantis_ circled the Earth 169 times and traveled over 4.2 million miles during its 259-hour and 21-minute flight, landing at the Kennedy Space Center.

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6a/Astronaut_Scott_Parazynski_repairs_a_damaged_ISS_solar_panel.jpg/250px-Astronaut_Scott_Parazynski_repairs_a_damaged_ISS_solar_panel.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Astronaut_Scott_Parazynski_repairs_a_damaged_ISS_solar_panel.jpg)

 Scott Parazynski during an STS-120 spacewalk to repair a damaged [solar panel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_panel "Solar panel") of the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station").

[STS-95](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-95 "STS-95")_[Discovery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Discovery "Space Shuttle Discovery")_ (October 29 to November 7, 1998) was a nine-day mission during which the crew supported a variety of research payloads, including deployment of the Spartan solar-observing spacecraft and the testing of the [Hubble Space Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_Space_Telescope "Hubble Space Telescope") Orbital Systems Test Platform. The crew also conducted investigations on the correlation between space flight and the aging process. Parazynski was the flight engineer (MS2) for the mission, as well as the navigator for the Spartan spacecraft rendezvous. During the flight, he also operated the Shuttle's robotic arm in support of the testing of several space-vision systems being considered for ISS assembly. In addition, he was responsible for monitoring several life sciences investigations, including those involving crewmate [Senator John Glenn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Glenn "John Glenn"). The mission was accomplished in 134 Earth orbits, traveling 3.6 million miles in 213 hours and 44 minutes.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-NASA-22)

[STS-100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-100 "STS-100")_[Endeavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour")_ (April 19 to May 1, 2001) was the 9th mission to the International Space Station (ISS) Alpha during which the crew successfully delivered and installed the Space Station "Canadarm2" robotic arm, to be used for all future Space Station assembly and maintenance tasks. Parazynski conducted two spacewalks with [Canadian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadians "Canadians") colleague [Chris Hadfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Hadfield "Chris Hadfield") to assemble and power the next generation robotic arm. Additionally, the pair installed a new [UHF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UHF "UHF")[radio antenna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_antenna "Radio antenna") for space-to-space communications during Space Shuttle rendezvous and ISS extravehicular activity. A critical on-orbit spare, a [direct current](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_current "Direct current") switching unit, was also transferred to Alpha during the 14 hours and 50 minutes of EVA work. Also during the flight, Parazynski operated _Endeavour_'s robotic arm to attach, and later detach, the Italian-built _Raffaello_[Multi-Purpose Logistics Module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-Purpose_Logistics_Module "Multi-Purpose Logistics Module"). Traveling 4.9 million miles in 283 hours and 30 minutes, the mission was accomplished in 186 Earth orbits.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-NASA-22)

STS-120_Discovery_ (October 23 – November 7, 2007) launched from and returned to land at the Kennedy Space Center, Florida. During the mission, the Node 2 module named _Harmony_ was delivered to the International Space Station. This element opened up the capability for future international laboratories to be added to the station. Parazynski served as EV1 (lead spacewalker) and accumulated over 27 EVA hours in 4 spacewalks. One of the major EVA mission objectives was the relocation of the P6 Solar Array from the top of the Z1 Truss to the end of the port side of the Integrated Truss Structure. During the IVA-commanded re-deploy of the solar array, several array panels snagged and were damaged, requiring an unplanned spacewalk to successfully repair the array. The mission was accomplished in 238 Earth orbits, traveling 6.2 million miles in 15 days, 2 hours, and 23 minutes.

**Scott Edward Parazynski** (born July 28, 1961) is an American physician and former [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")[astronaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut "Astronaut"). A veteran of five Space Shuttle flights and seven spacewalks, Parazynski's latest mission was STS-120 in October 2007 – highlighted by a dramatic, unplanned [extra-vehicular activity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extra-vehicular_activity "Extra-vehicular activity") (EVA) to repair a live solar array. In May 2016, he was inducted into the [United States Astronaut Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Astronaut_Hall_of_Fame "United States Astronaut Hall of Fame"). He retired from NASA in March 2009 to pursue entrepreneurial opportunities in the private sector, and he is currently the CEO of a technology start-up. He is the first person to have both flown in space and summited [Mount Everest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Everest "Mount Everest"), the highest point on Earth.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-1) He describes his life's experiences in his 2017 memoir _The Sky Below_.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-2)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Scott_E._Parazynski&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Parazynski is of [Polish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_people "Polish people") descent, as his great-great-grandparents migrated from [Kraków](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krak%C3%B3w "Kraków") to the US.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-se-3) He considers [Palo Alto, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palo_Alto,_California "Palo Alto, California"), and [Evergreen, Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evergreen,_Colorado "Evergreen, Colorado"), to be his hometowns. He is married to [Meenakshi Wadhwa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meenakshi_Wadhwa "Meenakshi Wadhwa"), a planetary scientist at Arizona State University. He has two children with his first wife, Gail. Scott enjoys [mountaineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountaineering "Mountaineering"), [rock climbing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_climbing "Rock climbing"), [flying](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fly "Fly") and [scuba diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scuba_diving "Scuba diving"). A commercial, multi-engine, seaplane and instrument-rated [pilot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aviator "Aviator"), Parazynski has logged over 2500 flight hours in a variety of aircraft. As a mountaineer, his [summits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topographical_summit "Topographical summit") include [Cerro Aconcagua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerro_Aconcagua "Cerro Aconcagua") (at 22,841 feet (6,962 m) above sea level, the tallest [mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountain "Mountain") in the world outside [Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asia "Asia")) and all 59 of [Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado "Colorado")'s peaks over 14,000 feet (4,300 m) in [altitude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altitude "Altitude"). He first attempted to summit [Mount Everest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Everest "Mount Everest") in May 2008, but was forced to turn back before the summit due to a severe back injury. Serving as team physician for the Discovery Channel[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-4) a year later, at 4:00 am on May 20, 2009, he successfully summited the 29,029 feet (8,848 m) mountain.

Other notable expeditions include a scientific dive into the summit caldera lake atop [Licancabur Volcano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Licancabur "Licancabur") (19,409 feet (5,916 m) on the Bolivian-Chilean border), one of the world's highest lakes, and setting the first bootprints adjacent Masaya Volcano's lava lake in Nicaragua with Sam Cossman in 2016.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-5) He also travelled aboard [OceanGate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OceanGate "OceanGate")'s submersible _Titan_ and visited the [wreck of the _Titanic_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wreck_of_the_Titanic "Wreck of the Titanic") in the North Atlantic.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-7)

## Education and early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Scott_E._Parazynski&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Education and early life")]

Parazynski attended junior high school at Dakar Academy in [Dakar, Senegal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dakar,_Senegal "Dakar, Senegal"), and [Beirut, Lebanon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beirut,_Lebanon "Beirut, Lebanon"). In March 1969 as an eight-year-old, he travelled to Florida to witness the launch of [Apollo 9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_9 "Apollo 9"), an event he argued inspired him to pursue a career in science. He attended high school at the [Community School, Tehran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Community_School,_Tehran "Community School, Tehran"), [Iran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran "Iran"), and the [American Community School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Community_Schools "American Community Schools"), [Athens, Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athens,_Greece "Athens, Greece"), graduating in 1979. He received a [Bachelor of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Science "Bachelor of Science") degree in [biology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biology "Biology") from [Stanford University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University "Stanford University") in 1983, continuing on to graduate with honors from [Stanford Medical School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_Medical_School "Stanford Medical School") in 1989. He served his medical internship at the [Brigham and Women's Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_and_Women's_Hospital "Brigham and Women's Hospital") of [Harvard Medical School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Medical_School "Harvard Medical School") (1990). He had completed 22 months of a residency program in emergency medicine in [Denver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denver "Denver"), [Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado "Colorado"), when selected for the NASA Astronaut Corps.

## Organizations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Scott_E._Parazynski&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Organizations")]

Parazynski is a Fellow of the [Aerospace Medical Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerospace_Medical_Association "Aerospace Medical Association") and [The Explorers Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Explorers_Club "The Explorers Club"). Additionally, he is a member of the American Society for Gravitational and Space Biology, the [Wilderness Medical Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilderness_Medical_Society "Wilderness Medical Society"), the [American Alpine Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Alpine_Club "American Alpine Club"), the [Association of Space Explorers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_Space_Explorers "Association of Space Explorers"), the [Experimental Aircraft Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experimental_Aircraft_Association "Experimental Aircraft Association"), and the [Aircraft Owners and Pilots Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft_Owners_and_Pilots_Association "Aircraft Owners and Pilots Association"). He is president of the board of directors of the [Challenger Center for Space Science Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_Center_for_Space_Science_Education "Challenger Center for Space Science Education"), and serves on the boards of the [Houston Museum of Natural Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston_Museum_of_Natural_Science "Houston Museum of Natural Science"), the University of Texas McDonald Observatory and [OceanGate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OceanGate "OceanGate").

In 2014, Parazynski was appointed as a professor of practice at [Arizona State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arizona_State_University "Arizona State University"), and was designated ASU's first University Explorer.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-8) He subsequently founded Fluidity Technologies[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-9) based on his intellectual property, a company aiming to manufacture and distribute novel control devices for mobility in 3-D space, for everything from drones and computer games to VR and surgical robotics.

## Medical career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Scott_E._Parazynski&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Medical career")]

While an [undergraduate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Undergraduate "Undergraduate") at [Stanford University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University "Stanford University"), Parazynski studied [antigenic shift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antigenic_shift "Antigenic shift") in [African](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa "Africa")[sleeping sickness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_trypanosomiasis "African trypanosomiasis"), using sophisticated [molecular biology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molecular_biology "Molecular biology") techniques. During [medical school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_school "Medical school"), he was awarded a NASA graduate student [fellowship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scholarship "Scholarship") and conducted [research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research "Research") at [NASA Ames Research Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_Ames_Research_Center "NASA Ames Research Center") on [fluid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluid "Fluid") shifts that occur during human [space flight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_flight "Space flight"). Additionally, he has been involved in the design of several [exercise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exercise "Exercise") devices that are being developed for long-duration [space flight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_flight "Space flight"), and has conducted research on high-[altitude acclimatization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altitude_acclimatization "Altitude acclimatization"). Parazynski has numerous publications in the field of space [physiology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physiology "Physiology"), and has a particular expertise in human [adaptation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adaptation_(biology) "Adaptation (biology)") to stressful environments.

## NASA career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Scott_E._Parazynski&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: NASA career")]

Selected as an astronaut in March 1992, Parazynski reported to the [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center") in August 1992. He completed one year of training and evaluation, and was qualified as a mission specialist. Parazynski initially served as one of the crew representatives for [extra-vehicular activity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extra-vehicular_activity "Extra-vehicular activity") (EVA) in the Astronaut Office Mission Development Branch. Following his first flight, he was assigned as a backup for the third American long-duration stay aboard Russia's [space station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_station "Space station")[Mir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mir "Mir"), and was expected to serve as a prime crew member on a subsequent mission. He spent five months in training at the [Gagarin Cosmonaut Training Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gagarin_Cosmonaut_Training_Center "Gagarin Cosmonaut Training Center"), [Star City, Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_City,_Moscow "Star City, Moscow"), Russia.

In October 1995, when sitting-height parameters raised concerns about his fitting safely in the [Soyuz spacecraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_spacecraft "Soyuz spacecraft") in the event of an emergency on board the Mir station, he was deemed too tall for the mission and was withdrawn from Mir training. He has served as the Astronaut Office Operations Planning Branch crew representative for [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle"), Space Station and Soyuz training, and also served as Deputy (Operations and Training) of the Astronaut Office [ISS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station") Branch. Most recently, he served as Chief of the Astronaut Office EVA Branch. A veteran of five space flights, [STS-66](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-66 "STS-66") (1994), [STS-86](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-86 "STS-86") (1997), [STS-95](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-95 "STS-95") (1998), [STS-100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-100 "STS-100") (2001), and STS-120 (2007), Parazynski has logged over 1,019 hours (8 weeks) in space, including 47 hours of EVA, and traveled over 17 million miles. Parazynski's most recent mission was STS-120, during which he performed four spacewalks to continue International Space Station assembly. The fourth EVA is considered one of the most challenging and dangerous ever performed: while perched on the end of a 90-foot robotic boom, further away from the safety of the airlock than anyone had previously ventured, he had to repair a fully energized solar array. He became only the second NASA astronaut to perform four spacewalks during a single shuttle mission. A photo that he took during one of the spacewalks was listed on _[Popular Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular\_Science "Popular Science")_'s photo gallery of the best [astronaut selfies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut_selfie "Astronaut selfie").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-21)

## Spaceflight experience

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Scott_E._Parazynski&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Spaceflight experience")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a7/Scott_Parazynski_space.jpg/250px-Scott_Parazynski_space.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Scott_Parazynski_space.jpg)

Scott Parazynski during a spacewalk during STS-120.

The [STS-66](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-66 "STS-66") Atmospheric [Laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laboratory "Laboratory") for Applications and Science-3 (ATLAS-3) mission was launched from [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center"), [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"), on November 3, 1994, and returned to land at [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"), on November 14, 1994. ATLAS-3 was part of an ongoing program to determine the Earth's [energy balance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_energy_budget#Earth's_energy_imbalance_(EEI) "Earth's energy budget") and [atmospheric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_atmosphere "Earth's atmosphere") change over an 11-year [solar cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_cycle "Solar cycle"), particularly with respect to humanity's impact on global-[ozone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozone "Ozone") distribution. Parazynski had responsibility for a number of on-orbit activities including operation of the ATLAS experiments and [Spacelab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacelab "Spacelab") Pallet, as well as several secondary experiments in the crew cabin. He and his crewmates also successfully evaluated the Interlimb Resistance Device, a free-floating exercise he developed to prevent [muscular atrophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muscular_atrophy "Muscular atrophy") in [microgravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microgravity "Microgravity"). [Space Shuttle _Atlantis_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis "Space Shuttle Atlantis") circled the earth 175 times and traveled over 4.5 million miles during its 262-hour and 34-minute flight.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-NASA-22)

[STS-86](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-86 "STS-86")_Atlantis_ (September 25 to October 6, 1997) was the seventh mission to rendezvous and dock with the Russian Space Station Mir. Highlights of the mission included the exchange of U.S. crew members [Michael Foale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Foale "Michael Foale") and [David Wolf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wolf_(astronaut) "David Wolf (astronaut)"), the transfer of 10,400 pounds of science and logistics, and the first Shuttle-based joint American-Russian spacewalk. Parazynski served as the flight engineer (MS2) during the flight, and was also the navigator during the Mir rendezvous. Parazynski (EV1) and Russian [cosmonaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmonaut "Cosmonaut")[Vladimir Titov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Titov_(cosmonaut) "Vladimir Titov (cosmonaut)") performed a 5-hour, 1 minute [spacewalk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacewalk "Spacewalk") during which they retrieved four experiment packages first deployed during the [STS-76](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-76 "STS-76")[Shuttle-Mir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle-Mir "Shuttle-Mir") docking mission. They also deployed the Spektr Solar Array Cap, which was designed to be used in a future Mir spacewalk to seal a leak in the Spektr module's damaged hull. Other objectives of EVA included the evaluation of common EVA tools to be used by astronauts wearing either Russian or American-made spacesuits, and a systems flight test of the Simplified Aid for EVA Rescue (SAFER). Space Shuttle _Atlantis_ circled the Earth 169 times and traveled over 4.2 million miles during its 259-hour and 21-minute flight, landing at the Kennedy Space Center.

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6a/Astronaut_Scott_Parazynski_repairs_a_damaged_ISS_solar_panel.jpg/250px-Astronaut_Scott_Parazynski_repairs_a_damaged_ISS_solar_panel.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Astronaut_Scott_Parazynski_repairs_a_damaged_ISS_solar_panel.jpg)

 Scott Parazynski during an STS-120 spacewalk to repair a damaged [solar panel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_panel "Solar panel") of the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station").

[STS-95](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-95 "STS-95")_[Discovery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Discovery "Space Shuttle Discovery")_ (October 29 to November 7, 1998) was a nine-day mission during which the crew supported a variety of research payloads, including deployment of the Spartan solar-observing spacecraft and the testing of the [Hubble Space Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_Space_Telescope "Hubble Space Telescope") Orbital Systems Test Platform. The crew also conducted investigations on the correlation between space flight and the aging process. Parazynski was the flight engineer (MS2) for the mission, as well as the navigator for the Spartan spacecraft rendezvous. During the flight, he also operated the Shuttle's robotic arm in support of the testing of several space-vision systems being considered for ISS assembly. In addition, he was responsible for monitoring several life sciences investigations, including those involving crewmate [Senator John Glenn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Glenn "John Glenn"). The mission was accomplished in 134 Earth orbits, traveling 3.6 million miles in 213 hours and 44 minutes.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-NASA-22)

[STS-100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-100 "STS-100")_[Endeavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour")_ (April 19 to May 1, 2001) was the 9th mission to the International Space Station (ISS) Alpha during which the crew successfully delivered and installed the Space Station "Canadarm2" robotic arm, to be used for all future Space Station assembly and maintenance tasks. Parazynski conducted two spacewalks with [Canadian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadians "Canadians") colleague [Chris Hadfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Hadfield "Chris Hadfield") to assemble and power the next generation robotic arm. Additionally, the pair installed a new [UHF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UHF "UHF")[radio antenna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_antenna "Radio antenna") for space-to-space communications during Space Shuttle rendezvous and ISS extravehicular activity. A critical on-orbit spare, a [direct current](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_current "Direct current") switching unit, was also transferred to Alpha during the 14 hours and 50 minutes of EVA work. Also during the flight, Parazynski operated _Endeavour_'s robotic arm to attach, and later detach, the Italian-built _Raffaello_[Multi-Purpose Logistics Module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-Purpose_Logistics_Module "Multi-Purpose Logistics Module"). Traveling 4.9 million miles in 283 hours and 30 minutes, the mission was accomplished in 186 Earth orbits.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-NASA-22)

STS-120_Discovery_ (October 23 – November 7, 2007) launched from and returned to land at the Kennedy Space Center, Florida. During the mission, the Node 2 module named _Harmony_ was delivered to the International Space Station. This element opened up the capability for future international laboratories to be added to the station. Parazynski served as EV1 (lead spacewalker) and accumulated over 27 EVA hours in 4 spacewalks. One of the major EVA mission objectives was the relocation of the P6 Solar Array from the top of the Z1 Truss to the end of the port side of the Integrated Truss Structure. During the IVA-commanded re-deploy of the solar array, several array panels snagged and were damaged, requiring an unplanned spacewalk to successfully repair the array. The mission was accomplished in 238 Earth orbits, traveling 6.2 million miles in 15 days, 2 hours, and 23 minutes.

## Book

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Scott_E._Parazynski&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Book")]

In 2017, Parazynski's book, _The Sky Below: A True Story of Summits, Space and Speed_,[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-23) with co-author Susy Flory, was published. [Homer Hickam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homer_Hickam "Homer Hickam") called it “a wonder, a fellow who has packed in more exploits in his lifetime than most of us can imagine.”[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-24)

**Daniel Michio Tani** (born February 1, 1961) is an American [engineer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engineer "Engineer") and retired [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")[astronaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut "Astronaut"). He was born in [Ridley Park, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ridley_Park,_Pennsylvania "Ridley Park, Pennsylvania"), but considers [Lombard, Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lombard,_Illinois "Lombard, Illinois"), to be his hometown.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_M._Tani#cite_note-NASAbio-1)

With [Peggy Whitson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peggy_Whitson "Peggy Whitson"), Tani conducted the 100th spacewalk on the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_M._Tani#cite_note-NASAbio-1)

## Education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Daniel_M._Tani&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Education")]

Tani graduated from [Glenbard East High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenbard_East_High_School "Glenbard East High School"), Lombard, Illinois, in 1979, and received a [Bachelor of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Science "Bachelor of Science") and [Master of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Science "Master of Science") degrees in mechanical engineering from [Massachusetts Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Institute_of_Technology "Massachusetts Institute of Technology") (MIT) in 1984, and 1988, respectively.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_M._Tani#cite_note-NASAbio-1) While at MIT, Tani became a brother of the Lambda Phi chapter of the [Alpha Delta Phi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpha_Delta_Phi "Alpha Delta Phi") fraternity.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_M._Tani#cite_note-ADPNotableAlumni-2)

Tani's [Space suit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_suit "Space suit") is featured prominently in the main hallway of [Glenbard East High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenbard_East_High_School "Glenbard East High School"), where he graduated from in 1979.

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Daniel_M._Tani&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

After Tani received his bachelor's degree from MIT, he worked at [Hughes Aircraft Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hughes_Aircraft_Corporation "Hughes Aircraft Corporation") in [El Segundo, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Segundo,_California "El Segundo, California") as a design engineer in the Space and Communications group.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_M._Tani#cite_note-NASAbio-1) In 1986, he returned to MIT and received his master's degree in mechanical engineering in 1988, specializing in human factors and group decision making. After graduation, Tani worked for [Bolt, Beranek and Newman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolt,_Beranek_and_Newman "Bolt, Beranek and Newman") in [Cambridge, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge,_Massachusetts "Cambridge, Massachusetts"), in the experimental psychology department. In 1988, Tani joined [Orbital Sciences Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbital_Sciences_Corporation "Orbital Sciences Corporation") (OSC) in [Dulles, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles,_Virginia "Dulles, Virginia"), initially as a senior structures engineer, and then as the mission operations manager for the Transfer Orbit Stage (TOS). In that role, he served as the TOS flight operations lead, working with NASA/[JSC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center") mission control in support of the deployment of the ACTS/TOS payload during the [STS-51](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51 "STS-51") mission in September 1993. Tani then moved to the [Pegasus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pegasus_(rocket) "Pegasus (rocket)") program at OSC as the launch operations manager. In that capacity, he served as lead for the development of procedures and constraints for the launching of the air-launched Pegasus uncrewed rocket. Tani also was responsible for defining, training, and leading the team of engineers who worked in the launch and control room.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_M._Tani#cite_note-NASAbio-1)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_M._Tani#cite_note-3)

## NASA career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Daniel_M._Tani&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: NASA career")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c4/Daniel_Tani_STS-108_EVA.jpg/250px-Daniel_Tani_STS-108_EVA.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Daniel_Tani_STS-108_EVA.jpg)

Tani during his STS-108 spacewalk

Selected as an astronaut candidate by NASA in April 1996, Tani reported to the [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center") in August 1996.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_M._Tani#cite_note-NASAbio-1) After completing two years of training and evaluation, he qualified for flight assignment as a mission specialist in 1998.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_M._Tani#cite_note-NASAbio-1) He performed technical duties in the Astronaut Office Computer Support Branch and [Extra-Vehicular Activity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extra-vehicular_activity "Extra-vehicular activity") (EVA) Branch, and served as a crew support astronaut for [Expedition 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_2 "Expedition 2").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_M._Tani#cite_note-NASAbio-1)

### STS-108

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Daniel_M._Tani&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: STS-108")]

Tani flew on [STS-108](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-108 "STS-108") in 2001, and logged over 11 days in space, including over 4 EVA hours in one spacewalk. STS-108 [_Endeavour_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour") (December 5–17, 2001) was the 12th shuttle flight to visit the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station"). During the mission, Tani served as mission specialist 2. Endeavour's crew delivered the [Expedition 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_4 "Expedition 4") crew to the station, and returned the [Expedition 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_3 "Expedition 3") crew. The crew transferred over three tons of supplies, logistics and science experiments from the _Raffaello_[Multi-Purpose Logistics Module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-Purpose_Logistics_Module "Multi-Purpose Logistics Module") to the station. Tani performed a spacewalk to wrap thermal blankets around the ISS Solar Array Gimbals. STS-108 was accomplished in 185 Earth orbits, traveling 4.8 million miles in 283 hours and 36 minutes, including an EVA of 4 hours and 12 minutes.

### NEEMO 2

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Daniel_M._Tani&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: NEEMO 2")]

In May 2002, Tani served as an [aquanaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquanaut "Aquanaut") on the [NEEMO 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NEEMO#NEEMO_2:_May_13%E2%80%9320,_2002 "NEEMO") (NASA Extreme Environment Mission Operations) crew aboard the [Aquarius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquarius_(laboratory) "Aquarius (laboratory)")[underwater laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_habitat "Underwater habitat"). Tani and his fellow crew members lived and worked for one week beneath the [Atlantic Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Ocean "Atlantic Ocean").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_M._Tani#cite_note-history-4)

### Expedition 16

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Daniel_M._Tani&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Expedition 16")]

Following his return from STS-108, Tani was assigned as the [Expedition 9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_9 "Expedition 9") backup flight engineer. Tani was eventually assigned to [Expedition 16](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_16 "Expedition 16") as flight engineer, and launched to the station aboard STS-120 on October 23, 2007. Tani completed one EVA with the crew of STS-120, and four additional spacewalks during his increment aboard the space station. Originally scheduled to return to Earth with the crew of [STS-122](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-122 "STS-122") in December, the mission was delayed due to engine cutoff sensor issues during countdown. Instead, it launched on February 7. Tani returned on [STS-122](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-122 "STS-122") on February 20, 2008.

### Retirement from NASA

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Daniel_M._Tani&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Retirement from NASA")]

Tani left NASA in August 2012 to become the vice president of mission and cargo operations in the Advanced Programs Group of Orbital Sciences Corporation in Dulles, Virginia.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_M._Tani#cite_note-retired-8)

In August 2016, Tani left Orbital Sciences Corporation (now Orbital ATK) to join the high school faculty at the [American School in Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_School_in_Japan "American School in Japan"), where he taught science, engineering and design.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_M._Tani#cite_note-9)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Daniel_M._Tani&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Tani is married to Jane Egan from Cork, Ireland, and enjoys golf, flying, running, tennis, music, and cooking.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_M._Tani#cite_note-NASAbio-1) Tani threw out the [ceremonial first pitch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceremonial_first_pitch "Ceremonial first pitch") and sang the "[Take Me Out to the Ball Game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Take_Me_Out_to_the_Ball_Game "Take Me Out to the Ball Game")" at [Wrigley Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wrigley_Field "Wrigley Field") on August 20, 2008.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_M._Tani#cite_note-10)

His parents, Rose and Henry N. Tani, are both deceased. During World War II, they and their children were relocated from their California farm to the [Tanforan Assembly Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanforan_Assembly_Center "Tanforan Assembly Center") in [San Bruno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Bruno,_California "San Bruno, California"), where they lived for several months in converted horse [stables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stable "Stable") at the [Tanforan Racetrack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanforan_Racetrack "Tanforan Racetrack"), and then [Topaz War Relocation Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topaz_War_Relocation_Center "Topaz War Relocation Center") in [Utah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utah "Utah") as part of the [Japanese American internment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_American_internment "Japanese American internment") program of the U.S. government.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_M._Tani#cite_note-11) On December 19, 2007, during Tani's stay on the International Space Station as a member of Expedition 16, he was informed by the ground team that his mother had been killed when a freight train collided with her car.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_M._Tani#cite_note-abcnews-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_M._Tani#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_M._Tani#cite_note-nytimes-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_M._Tani#cite_note-15)

**Daniel Michio Tani** (born February 1, 1961) is an American [engineer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engineer "Engineer") and retired [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")[astronaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut "Astronaut"). He was born in [Ridley Park, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ridley_Park,_Pennsylvania "Ridley Park, Pennsylvania"), but considers [Lombard, Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lombard,_Illinois "Lombard, Illinois"), to be his hometown.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_M._Tani#cite_note-NASAbio-1)

With [Peggy Whitson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peggy_Whitson "Peggy Whitson"), Tani conducted the 100th spacewalk on the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_M._Tani#cite_note-NASAbio-1)

## Education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Daniel_M._Tani&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Education")]

Tani graduated from [Glenbard East High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenbard_East_High_School "Glenbard East High School"), Lombard, Illinois, in 1979, and received a [Bachelor of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Science "Bachelor of Science") and [Master of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Science "Master of Science") degrees in mechanical engineering from [Massachusetts Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Institute_of_Technology "Massachusetts Institute of Technology") (MIT) in 1984, and 1988, respectively.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_M._Tani#cite_note-NASAbio-1) While at MIT, Tani became a brother of the Lambda Phi chapter of the [Alpha Delta Phi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpha_Delta_Phi "Alpha Delta Phi") fraternity.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_M._Tani#cite_note-ADPNotableAlumni-2)

Tani's [Space suit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_suit "Space suit") is featured prominently in the main hallway of [Glenbard East High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenbard_East_High_School "Glenbard East High School"), where he graduated from in 1979.

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Daniel_M._Tani&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

After Tani received his bachelor's degree from MIT, he worked at [Hughes Aircraft Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hughes_Aircraft_Corporation "Hughes Aircraft Corporation") in [El Segundo, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Segundo,_California "El Segundo, California") as a design engineer in the Space and Communications group.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_M._Tani#cite_note-NASAbio-1) In 1986, he returned to MIT and received his master's degree in mechanical engineering in 1988, specializing in human factors and group decision making. After graduation, Tani worked for [Bolt, Beranek and Newman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolt,_Beranek_and_Newman "Bolt, Beranek and Newman") in [Cambridge, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge,_Massachusetts "Cambridge, Massachusetts"), in the experimental psychology department. In 1988, Tani joined [Orbital Sciences Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbital_Sciences_Corporation "Orbital Sciences Corporation") (OSC) in [Dulles, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles,_Virginia "Dulles, Virginia"), initially as a senior structures engineer, and then as the mission operations manager for the Transfer Orbit Stage (TOS). In that role, he served as the TOS flight operations lead, working with NASA/[JSC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center") mission control in support of the deployment of the ACTS/TOS payload during the [STS-51](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51 "STS-51") mission in September 1993. Tani then moved to the [Pegasus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pegasus_(rocket) "Pegasus (rocket)") program at OSC as the launch operations manager. In that capacity, he served as lead for the development of procedures and constraints for the launching of the air-launched Pegasus uncrewed rocket. Tani also was responsible for defining, training, and leading the team of engineers who worked in the launch and control room.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_M._Tani#cite_note-NASAbio-1)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_M._Tani#cite_note-3)

## NASA career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Daniel_M._Tani&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: NASA career")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c4/Daniel_Tani_STS-108_EVA.jpg/250px-Daniel_Tani_STS-108_EVA.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Daniel_Tani_STS-108_EVA.jpg)

Tani during his STS-108 spacewalk

Selected as an astronaut candidate by NASA in April 1996, Tani reported to the [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center") in August 1996.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_M._Tani#cite_note-NASAbio-1) After completing two years of training and evaluation, he qualified for flight assignment as a mission specialist in 1998.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_M._Tani#cite_note-NASAbio-1) He performed technical duties in the Astronaut Office Computer Support Branch and [Extra-Vehicular Activity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extra-vehicular_activity "Extra-vehicular activity") (EVA) Branch, and served as a crew support astronaut for [Expedition 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_2 "Expedition 2").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_M._Tani#cite_note-NASAbio-1)

### STS-108

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Daniel_M._Tani&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: STS-108")]

Tani flew on [STS-108](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-108 "STS-108") in 2001, and logged over 11 days in space, including over 4 EVA hours in one spacewalk. STS-108 [_Endeavour_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour") (December 5–17, 2001) was the 12th shuttle flight to visit the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station"). During the mission, Tani served as mission specialist 2. Endeavour's crew delivered the [Expedition 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_4 "Expedition 4") crew to the station, and returned the [Expedition 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_3 "Expedition 3") crew. The crew transferred over three tons of supplies, logistics and science experiments from the _Raffaello_[Multi-Purpose Logistics Module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-Purpose_Logistics_Module "Multi-Purpose Logistics Module") to the station. Tani performed a spacewalk to wrap thermal blankets around the ISS Solar Array Gimbals. STS-108 was accomplished in 185 Earth orbits, traveling 4.8 million miles in 283 hours and 36 minutes, including an EVA of 4 hours and 12 minutes.

### NEEMO 2

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Daniel_M._Tani&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: NEEMO 2")]

In May 2002, Tani served as an [aquanaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquanaut "Aquanaut") on the [NEEMO 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NEEMO#NEEMO_2:_May_13%E2%80%9320,_2002 "NEEMO") (NASA Extreme Environment Mission Operations) crew aboard the [Aquarius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquarius_(laboratory) "Aquarius (laboratory)")[underwater laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_habitat "Underwater habitat"). Tani and his fellow crew members lived and worked for one week beneath the [Atlantic Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Ocean "Atlantic Ocean").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_M._Tani#cite_note-history-4)

### Expedition 16

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Daniel_M._Tani&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Expedition 16")]

Following his return from STS-108, Tani was assigned as the [Expedition 9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_9 "Expedition 9") backup flight engineer. Tani was eventually assigned to [Expedition 16](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_16 "Expedition 16") as flight engineer, and launched to the station aboard STS-120 on October 23, 2007. Tani completed one EVA with the crew of STS-120, and four additional spacewalks during his increment aboard the space station. Originally scheduled to return to Earth with the crew of [STS-122](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-122 "STS-122") in December, the mission was delayed due to engine cutoff sensor issues during countdown. Instead, it launched on February 7. Tani returned on [STS-122](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-122 "STS-122") on February 20, 2008.

### Retirement from NASA

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Daniel_M._Tani&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Retirement from NASA")]

Tani left NASA in August 2012 to become the vice president of mission and cargo operations in the Advanced Programs Group of Orbital Sciences Corporation in Dulles, Virginia.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_M._Tani#cite_note-retired-8)

In August 2016, Tani left Orbital Sciences Corporation (now Orbital ATK) to join the high school faculty at the [American School in Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_School_in_Japan "American School in Japan"), where he taught science, engineering and design.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_M._Tani#cite_note-9)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Daniel_M._Tani&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Tani is married to Jane Egan from Cork, Ireland, and enjoys golf, flying, running, tennis, music, and cooking.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_M._Tani#cite_note-NASAbio-1) Tani threw out the [ceremonial first pitch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceremonial_first_pitch "Ceremonial first pitch") and sang the "[Take Me Out to the Ball Game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Take_Me_Out_to_the_Ball_Game "Take Me Out to the Ball Game")" at [Wrigley Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wrigley_Field "Wrigley Field") on August 20, 2008.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_M._Tani#cite_note-10)

His parents, Rose and Henry N. Tani, are both deceased. During World War II, they and their children were relocated from their California farm to the [Tanforan Assembly Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanforan_Assembly_Center "Tanforan Assembly Center") in [San Bruno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Bruno,_California "San Bruno, California"), where they lived for several months in converted horse [stables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stable "Stable") at the [Tanforan Racetrack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanforan_Racetrack "Tanforan Racetrack"), and then [Topaz War Relocation Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topaz_War_Relocation_Center "Topaz War Relocation Center") in [Utah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utah "Utah") as part of the [Japanese American internment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_American_internment "Japanese American internment") program of the U.S. government.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_M._Tani#cite_note-11) On December 19, 2007, during Tani's stay on the International Space Station as a member of Expedition 16, he was informed by the ground team that his mother had been killed when a freight train collided with her car.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_M._Tani#cite_note-abcnews-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_M._Tani#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_M._Tani#cite_note-nytimes-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_M._Tani#cite_note-15)
