**Clayton Conrad Anderson** (born February 23, 1959) is a retired [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")[astronaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut "Astronaut"). Launched on [STS-117](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-117 "STS-117"), he replaced [Sunita Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunita_Williams "Sunita Williams") on June 10, 2007 as a member of the ISS [Expedition 15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_15 "Expedition 15") crew.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clayton_Anderson#cite_note-nasa-07-142-1) He is currently an author, a motivational speaker, and a [Professor of Practice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clinical_professor "Clinical professor") at Iowa State University in [Ames, Iowa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ames,_Iowa "Ames, Iowa"). In 2022, he became the president and CEO of the [Strategic Air Command & Aerospace Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strategic_Air_Command_&_Aerospace_Museum "Strategic Air Command & Aerospace Museum").

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Clayton_Anderson&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Anderson graduated from Ashland-Greenwood High School, [Ashland, Nebraska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashland,_Nebraska "Ashland, Nebraska"), 1977, received a Bachelor of Science degree ([cum laude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cum_laude "Cum laude")) in physics at [Hastings College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hastings_College "Hastings College"), Nebraska, in 1981 and a Master of Science degree in aerospace engineering at [Iowa State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iowa_State_University "Iowa State University") in 1983.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clayton_Anderson#cite_note-clay_bio-2)

## NASA career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Clayton_Anderson&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: NASA career")]

### Early non-astronaut duties

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Clayton_Anderson&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Early non-astronaut duties")]

Anderson joined [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center") in 1983 in the Mission Planning and Analysis Division, performing rendezvous and proximity operations trajectory designs for early [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") and [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station") missions. In 1988, he moved to the Mission Operations Directorate (MOD) as a Flight Design Manager, leading the trajectory design team for the [Galileo mission to Jupiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galileo_(spacecraft) "Galileo (spacecraft)") ([STS-34](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-34 "STS-34")) while serving as the backup for the [Magellan mission to Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magellan_(spacecraft) "Magellan (spacecraft)") ([STS-31](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-31 "STS-31")). In 1989, Anderson was chosen to be supervisor of the MOD Ascent Flight Design Section and, following reorganization, the Flight Design Engineering Office of the Flight Design and Dynamics Division. In 1993, he was named the Chief of the Flight Design Branch. From 1996 until his selection as an astronaut, Anderson held the post of Manager, Emergency Operations Center, NASA Johnson Space Center.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clayton_Anderson#cite_note-clay_bio-2)

### Astronaut duties

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Clayton_Anderson&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Astronaut duties")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b8/Clayton_Anderson_zero_g.jpg/250px-Clayton_Anderson_zero_g.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Clayton_Anderson_zero_g.jpg)

Anderson watches as a water bubble floats in front of him on the Space Shuttle _Discovery_ during the STS-131 mission.

Selected as an [astronaut candidate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut_ranks_and_positions#Ranks "Astronaut ranks and positions") by NASA in June 1998, he reported for training in August of that year. Training included orientation briefings and tours, numerous scientific and technical briefings, intensive instruction in Shuttle and International Space Station (ISS) systems, physiological training, ground school to prepare for [T-38](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T-38_Talon "T-38 Talon") flight training, as well as learning water and wilderness survival techniques.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clayton_Anderson#cite_note-clay_bio-2)

Prior to being assigned to a spaceflight, Anderson served as the lead for the Enhanced Caution and Warning (ECW) System development effort within the Space Shuttle Cockpit Avionics Upgrade (CAU) Project. Previously, he was the crew support astronaut for ISS [Expedition 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_4 "Expedition 4"), providing ground support on technical issues in addition to supporting the crew families. Anderson also served as an ISS Capsule Communicator (CAPCOM) and as the Astronaut Office crew representative for the Station's electrical power system. In November 2002, Anderson completed training in the Extravehicular Activity (EVA) Skills program. He was back-up flight engineer for [Expedition 12](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_12 "Expedition 12"), [Expedition 13](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_13 "Expedition 13") and [Expedition 14](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_14 "Expedition 14") to the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station").

Anderson served as an astronaut family escort for the [STS-107](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-107 "STS-107") mission at the request of [Rick Husband](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Husband "Rick Husband").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clayton_Anderson#cite_note-Anderson-3)

In June 2003, Anderson served as an [aquanaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquanaut "Aquanaut") during the [NEEMO 5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NEEMO#NEEMO_5:_June_16%E2%80%9329,_2003 "NEEMO") mission aboard the [Aquarius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquarius_(laboratory) "Aquarius (laboratory)")[underwater laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_habitat "Underwater habitat"), living and working underwater for fourteen days.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clayton_Anderson#cite_note-history-4) During a NEEMO 5 underwater EVA, Anderson cut his thumb with a knife. The wound was stitched up by hand surgeon and extreme medicine specialist [Kenneth Kamler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Kamler "Kenneth Kamler"), who was observing the NEEMO project and dove to Aquarius to perform the procedure.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clayton_Anderson#cite_note-Kamler-5)

He was a mission specialist on [STS-131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-131 "STS-131"), launched in April 2010. The primary payload of this mission was a Multi-Purpose Logistics Module loaded with supplies and equipment for the International Space Station.

#### International Space Station

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Clayton_Anderson&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: International Space Station")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1f/Clayton_Anderson_aboard_ISS.jpg/250px-Clayton_Anderson_aboard_ISS.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Clayton_Anderson_aboard_ISS.jpg)

Anderson in the _[Destiny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Destiny\_(ISS\_module) "Destiny (ISS module)")_ module of the International Space Station

Anderson was a member of the Expedition 15 crew and spent 152 days on board the International Space Station. He launched to the station aboard Shuttle [Atlantis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis "Space Shuttle Atlantis") as mission specialist 5 for the STS-117 mission on June 8, 2007,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clayton_Anderson#cite_note-sts-117-01-6) and remained on board as a member of the [Expedition 16](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_16 "Expedition 16") crew before returning to earth aboard _[Discovery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Discovery "Space Shuttle Discovery")_ on mission STS-120 on November 7, 2007. On return his official title was mission specialist 5.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clayton_Anderson#cite_note-sts120presskit-7) Two of the photos that he took during his July and August 2007 spacewalks were listed on [Popular Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_Science "Popular Science")'s photo gallery of the best [astronaut selfies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut_selfie "Astronaut selfie").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clayton_Anderson#cite_note-universetoday-20131003-8)

Anderson continued a tradition aboard the International Space Station, started by [Michael Lopez-Alegria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Lopez-Alegria "Michael Lopez-Alegria"), of conducting daily "trivia" contests with mission control team members on the ground.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clayton_Anderson#cite_note-malik-20070616-9) During Alegria's seven-month stay on the station he would routinely call down movie quotes and challenge the team members to determine the movie the quote was from. Towards the end of his mission, he changed to music trivia playing a portion of a song and challenging the team to complete the line. Anderson has taken this tradition and put his own personal twist on it, using the "Book of Answers: The [New York Public Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Public_Library "New York Public Library") Telephone Reference Service's Most Unusual and Entertaining Questions". Anderson often played song clips for the ground control team, or specific individuals, most notably when he played the song "(Everything I Do) I Do It for You" by [Bryan Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryan_Adams "Bryan Adams") for his wife on her birthday.

## After NASA

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Clayton_Anderson&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: After NASA")]

May 2022 - June 2025, he served as the president and CEO of the [Strategic Air Command & Aerospace Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strategic_Air_Command_&_Aerospace_Museum "Strategic Air Command & Aerospace Museum"), a museum in his hometown of Ashland.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clayton_Anderson#cite_note-wowt-20220519-10)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Clayton_Anderson&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Anderson was born in Omaha but considers [Ashland, Nebraska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashland,_Nebraska "Ashland, Nebraska") to be his hometown. Married to Susan Jane Anderson (née Harreld) of [Elkhart, Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elkhart,_Indiana "Elkhart, Indiana"). They have two children, a son and a daughter. His mother, Alice J. Anderson, died in December 2007, shortly after his return to Earth. His father, John T. Anderson, is deceased.

Like many of the other astronauts and cosmonauts, he is a licensed amateur radio operator having passed the technician class license exam in 2001 and was issued the call sign KD5PLA by the [Federal Communications Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Communications_Commission "Federal Communications Commission") on August 13, 2001.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clayton_Anderson#cite_note-fcclicense-11) During his stay on the ISS in September 2007, he used one of the two amateur radio stations on board to talk with school children.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clayton_Anderson#cite_note-ariss-12)

Anderson is the first and only astronaut from Nebraska and was widely reported in news media as the astronaut rejected fourteen times by NASA before being accepted in 1998.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clayton_Anderson#cite_note-psatranscript-13) Anderson eventually retired from NASA in January 2013 after serving fifteen years and is now in education.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clayton_Anderson#cite_note-sacmuseum-20220519-14)

**Clayton Conrad Anderson** (born February 23, 1959) is a retired [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")[astronaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut "Astronaut"). Launched on [STS-117](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-117 "STS-117"), he replaced [Sunita Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunita_Williams "Sunita Williams") on June 10, 2007 as a member of the ISS [Expedition 15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_15 "Expedition 15") crew.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clayton_Anderson#cite_note-nasa-07-142-1) He is currently an author, a motivational speaker, and a [Professor of Practice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clinical_professor "Clinical professor") at Iowa State University in [Ames, Iowa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ames,_Iowa "Ames, Iowa"). In 2022, he became the president and CEO of the [Strategic Air Command & Aerospace Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strategic_Air_Command_&_Aerospace_Museum "Strategic Air Command & Aerospace Museum").

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Clayton_Anderson&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Anderson graduated from Ashland-Greenwood High School, [Ashland, Nebraska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashland,_Nebraska "Ashland, Nebraska"), 1977, received a Bachelor of Science degree ([cum laude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cum_laude "Cum laude")) in physics at [Hastings College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hastings_College "Hastings College"), Nebraska, in 1981 and a Master of Science degree in aerospace engineering at [Iowa State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iowa_State_University "Iowa State University") in 1983.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clayton_Anderson#cite_note-clay_bio-2)

## NASA career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Clayton_Anderson&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: NASA career")]

### Early non-astronaut duties

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Clayton_Anderson&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Early non-astronaut duties")]

Anderson joined [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center") in 1983 in the Mission Planning and Analysis Division, performing rendezvous and proximity operations trajectory designs for early [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") and [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station") missions. In 1988, he moved to the Mission Operations Directorate (MOD) as a Flight Design Manager, leading the trajectory design team for the [Galileo mission to Jupiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galileo_(spacecraft) "Galileo (spacecraft)") ([STS-34](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-34 "STS-34")) while serving as the backup for the [Magellan mission to Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magellan_(spacecraft) "Magellan (spacecraft)") ([STS-31](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-31 "STS-31")). In 1989, Anderson was chosen to be supervisor of the MOD Ascent Flight Design Section and, following reorganization, the Flight Design Engineering Office of the Flight Design and Dynamics Division. In 1993, he was named the Chief of the Flight Design Branch. From 1996 until his selection as an astronaut, Anderson held the post of Manager, Emergency Operations Center, NASA Johnson Space Center.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clayton_Anderson#cite_note-clay_bio-2)

### Astronaut duties

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Clayton_Anderson&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Astronaut duties")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b8/Clayton_Anderson_zero_g.jpg/250px-Clayton_Anderson_zero_g.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Clayton_Anderson_zero_g.jpg)

Anderson watches as a water bubble floats in front of him on the Space Shuttle _Discovery_ during the STS-131 mission.

Selected as an [astronaut candidate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut_ranks_and_positions#Ranks "Astronaut ranks and positions") by NASA in June 1998, he reported for training in August of that year. Training included orientation briefings and tours, numerous scientific and technical briefings, intensive instruction in Shuttle and International Space Station (ISS) systems, physiological training, ground school to prepare for [T-38](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T-38_Talon "T-38 Talon") flight training, as well as learning water and wilderness survival techniques.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clayton_Anderson#cite_note-clay_bio-2)

Prior to being assigned to a spaceflight, Anderson served as the lead for the Enhanced Caution and Warning (ECW) System development effort within the Space Shuttle Cockpit Avionics Upgrade (CAU) Project. Previously, he was the crew support astronaut for ISS [Expedition 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_4 "Expedition 4"), providing ground support on technical issues in addition to supporting the crew families. Anderson also served as an ISS Capsule Communicator (CAPCOM) and as the Astronaut Office crew representative for the Station's electrical power system. In November 2002, Anderson completed training in the Extravehicular Activity (EVA) Skills program. He was back-up flight engineer for [Expedition 12](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_12 "Expedition 12"), [Expedition 13](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_13 "Expedition 13") and [Expedition 14](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_14 "Expedition 14") to the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station").

Anderson served as an astronaut family escort for the [STS-107](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-107 "STS-107") mission at the request of [Rick Husband](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Husband "Rick Husband").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clayton_Anderson#cite_note-Anderson-3)

In June 2003, Anderson served as an [aquanaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquanaut "Aquanaut") during the [NEEMO 5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NEEMO#NEEMO_5:_June_16%E2%80%9329,_2003 "NEEMO") mission aboard the [Aquarius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquarius_(laboratory) "Aquarius (laboratory)")[underwater laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_habitat "Underwater habitat"), living and working underwater for fourteen days.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clayton_Anderson#cite_note-history-4) During a NEEMO 5 underwater EVA, Anderson cut his thumb with a knife. The wound was stitched up by hand surgeon and extreme medicine specialist [Kenneth Kamler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Kamler "Kenneth Kamler"), who was observing the NEEMO project and dove to Aquarius to perform the procedure.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clayton_Anderson#cite_note-Kamler-5)

He was a mission specialist on [STS-131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-131 "STS-131"), launched in April 2010. The primary payload of this mission was a Multi-Purpose Logistics Module loaded with supplies and equipment for the International Space Station.

#### International Space Station

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Clayton_Anderson&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: International Space Station")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1f/Clayton_Anderson_aboard_ISS.jpg/250px-Clayton_Anderson_aboard_ISS.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Clayton_Anderson_aboard_ISS.jpg)

Anderson in the _[Destiny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Destiny\_(ISS\_module) "Destiny (ISS module)")_ module of the International Space Station

Anderson was a member of the Expedition 15 crew and spent 152 days on board the International Space Station. He launched to the station aboard Shuttle [Atlantis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis "Space Shuttle Atlantis") as mission specialist 5 for the STS-117 mission on June 8, 2007,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clayton_Anderson#cite_note-sts-117-01-6) and remained on board as a member of the [Expedition 16](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_16 "Expedition 16") crew before returning to earth aboard _[Discovery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Discovery "Space Shuttle Discovery")_ on mission STS-120 on November 7, 2007. On return his official title was mission specialist 5.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clayton_Anderson#cite_note-sts120presskit-7) Two of the photos that he took during his July and August 2007 spacewalks were listed on [Popular Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_Science "Popular Science")'s photo gallery of the best [astronaut selfies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut_selfie "Astronaut selfie").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clayton_Anderson#cite_note-universetoday-20131003-8)

Anderson continued a tradition aboard the International Space Station, started by [Michael Lopez-Alegria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Lopez-Alegria "Michael Lopez-Alegria"), of conducting daily "trivia" contests with mission control team members on the ground.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clayton_Anderson#cite_note-malik-20070616-9) During Alegria's seven-month stay on the station he would routinely call down movie quotes and challenge the team members to determine the movie the quote was from. Towards the end of his mission, he changed to music trivia playing a portion of a song and challenging the team to complete the line. Anderson has taken this tradition and put his own personal twist on it, using the "Book of Answers: The [New York Public Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Public_Library "New York Public Library") Telephone Reference Service's Most Unusual and Entertaining Questions". Anderson often played song clips for the ground control team, or specific individuals, most notably when he played the song "(Everything I Do) I Do It for You" by [Bryan Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryan_Adams "Bryan Adams") for his wife on her birthday.

## After NASA

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Clayton_Anderson&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: After NASA")]

May 2022 - June 2025, he served as the president and CEO of the [Strategic Air Command & Aerospace Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strategic_Air_Command_&_Aerospace_Museum "Strategic Air Command & Aerospace Museum"), a museum in his hometown of Ashland.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clayton_Anderson#cite_note-wowt-20220519-10)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Clayton_Anderson&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Anderson was born in Omaha but considers [Ashland, Nebraska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashland,_Nebraska "Ashland, Nebraska") to be his hometown. Married to Susan Jane Anderson (née Harreld) of [Elkhart, Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elkhart,_Indiana "Elkhart, Indiana"). They have two children, a son and a daughter. His mother, Alice J. Anderson, died in December 2007, shortly after his return to Earth. His father, John T. Anderson, is deceased.

Like many of the other astronauts and cosmonauts, he is a licensed amateur radio operator having passed the technician class license exam in 2001 and was issued the call sign KD5PLA by the [Federal Communications Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Communications_Commission "Federal Communications Commission") on August 13, 2001.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clayton_Anderson#cite_note-fcclicense-11) During his stay on the ISS in September 2007, he used one of the two amateur radio stations on board to talk with school children.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clayton_Anderson#cite_note-ariss-12)

Anderson is the first and only astronaut from Nebraska and was widely reported in news media as the astronaut rejected fourteen times by NASA before being accepted in 1998.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clayton_Anderson#cite_note-psatranscript-13) Anderson eventually retired from NASA in January 2013 after serving fifteen years and is now in education.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clayton_Anderson#cite_note-sacmuseum-20220519-14)

**STS-112** ([ISS assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISS_assembly_sequence "ISS assembly sequence") flight **9A**) was an 11-day [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") mission to the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station") (ISS) flown by [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle")[_Atlantis_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis "Space Shuttle Atlantis").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-1) Space Shuttle _Atlantis_ was launched on 7 October 2002 at 19:45 UTC from the [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center")'s launch pad 39B to deliver the 28,000 pound Starboard 1 (S1) truss segment to the Space Station.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-2) Ending a 4.5-million-mile journey, _Atlantis_ landed at 15:44 UTC on 18 October 2002 on runway 33 at the Kennedy Space Center's Shuttle Landing Facility.

During the launch, the ET bipod ramp shed a chunk of [foam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_external_tank#Thermal_protection_system "Space Shuttle external tank") that caused a dent ~4" wide and 3" deep into the metal SRB-ET Attach Ring near the bottom of the left [Space Shuttle Solid Rocket Booster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Solid_Rocket_Booster "Space Shuttle Solid Rocket Booster").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-STS-112_SRB_Foam_Damage-3) Prior to the next mission ([STS-113](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-113 "STS-113")), an upper-level decision was made at NASA to continue with launches as scheduled. The launch subsequent to that was the [Space Shuttle _Columbia_ disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster"), the ill-fated [STS-107](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-107 "STS-107").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-caib_report3-4)

Space Shuttle _Atlantis_ had been scheduled to visit the International Space Station (ISS) again on the [STS-114](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-114 "STS-114") mission in March 2003;[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-5) however, due to the [loss of _Columbia_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster"), all Space Shuttles, including _Atlantis_, were temporarily grounded. Due to rescheduling of missions, _Atlantis_ did not fly again until [STS-115](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-115 "STS-115") on 9 September 2006.

### Starboard 1 (S1) truss segment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-112&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Starboard 1 (S1) truss segment")]

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/Heat_Rejection_System_%28HRS%29_Radiator.jpg/250px-Heat_Rejection_System_%28HRS%29_Radiator.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Heat_Rejection_System_(HRS)_Radiator.jpg)

The S1 Radiator panels being manufactured at the [Michoud Assembly Facility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michoud_Assembly_Facility "Michoud Assembly Facility")

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/61/ISSafterSTS112.jpg/250px-ISSafterSTS112.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ISSafterSTS112.jpg)

Illustration of the International Space Station after STS-112.

The [S1 truss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integrated_Truss_Structure "Integrated Truss Structure") segment, which provides structural support for the Space Station radiators, was the main payload of STS-112 mission.

The [Boeing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing "Boeing") Company (along with [Lockheed Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_Martin "Lockheed Martin")) started [manufacturing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manufacturing_of_the_International_Space_Station "Manufacturing of the International Space Station") the truss in May 1998 at Michoud. The work was completed in March 1999. The S1 was shipped by aircraft to the KSC Operations and Checkout Building in October 1999 for flight processing. In June 2002, the truss was handed over to NASA for final preparations and pre-flight checks at the Space Station Processing Facility.

### Crew Equipment Translation Aid

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-112&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Crew Equipment Translation Aid")]

_Atlantis_ also delivered the Crew Equipment Translation Aid (CETA) Cart to the Space Station. The CETA cart was attached to the Mobile Transporter (launched on [STS-110](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-110 "STS-110")) to be used by assembly crews on later missions.

## Mission experiments

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-112&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Mission experiments")]

STS-112 carried several science experiments to the space station including the Plant Generic Bioprocessing Apparatus (PGBA), Commercial Generic Bioprocessing Apparatus (CGBA), the Protein Crystal Growth Single-locker Thermal Enclosure System housing the Protein Crystallization Apparatus for Microgravity (PCG-STES-PCAM) and samples for the Zeolite Crystal Growth Furnace (ZCG) experiment.

## Shuttle processing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-112&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Shuttle processing")]

| Attempt | Planned | Result | Turnaround | Reason | Decision point | Weather go (%) | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 2 Oct 2002, 2:00:00 pm | Scrubbed | — | Weather | 1 Oct 2002, 3:15 pm​(T−11:00:00 hold) | 60 | Johnson Space Center powered down due to threat of Hurricane Lili.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-6) |
| 2 | 7 Oct 2002, 3:45:51 pm | Success | 5 days 1 hour 46 minutes |  |  | 90[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-7) |  |

Launch preparations for STS-112 mission were sightly delayed due to tiny cracks found within the plumbing of _Atlantis'_ propulsion system on 17 June 2002 by an inspector. The cracks were in metal flow liners inside the main liquid hydrogen fuel lines that feed the shuttle's three main engines. Although there were no cracks in the actual fuel pipes themselves, the concern was that metal pieces from the flow liners might break off and fly into the engines. In such a worst-case scenario, the debris can potentially trigger a catastrophic engine shutdown, which in turn could lead to the loss of the crew and the shuttle.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-8) Similar cracks were found in the remaining orbiters and the space shuttle program was temporally grounded so engineers could analyze the problem.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-9) The shuttle was cleared to resume flight in September with launch originally scheduled for October 2, but due to concerns that [Hurricane Lili](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Lili "Hurricane Lili") could hit Houston, the Johnson Space Center was powered down.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-atlantis2-10)

## Mission timeline

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-112&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Mission timeline")]

### 7 October (Flight Day 1 – Launch)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-112&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: 7 October (Flight Day 1 – Launch)")]

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6a/STS-112_Launch_of_Space_Shuttle_Atlantis.jpg/250px-STS-112_Launch_of_Space_Shuttle_Atlantis.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS-112_Launch_of_Space_Shuttle_Atlantis.jpg)

_Atlantis_ launches on STS-112.

Space Shuttle _Atlantis_ lifted off from Launch Pad 39B of the [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center") at 19:45:51 GMT through mostly clear blue skies. There were no problems reported during the countdown, and the ascent conformed to the standard timeline (see [Space Shuttle – Mission Profile – Launch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle")). For the first time in Space Shuttle history, a "rocketcam" video camera mounted to the upper part of _Atlantis'_ external tank returned live video of the flight to NASA flight controllers.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-lift_off_of_Atlantis-11) The video was near perfect until the two solid rocket boosters were jettisoned. At that point, the exhaust from the separation motors fogged the camera lens and made the rest of the video difficult to see.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-Debris/Ice/TPS-12):A13

Later, NASA announced that it was looking into a problem with explosive bolts that failed to fire properly during the launch. Immediately before the twin solid rocket boosters fired into life, only one set of pyrotechnics in ten explosive bolts exploded when commanded to do so. All 10 nuts exploded as planned, but NASA was interested in finding out an explanation for the unexpected anomaly.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-13)

Arguably the most significant event from this launch was the ET bipod ramp shedding a chunk of foam, estimated to be ~4"x5"x12", that broke away and hit the lower left [SRB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Solid_Rocket_Booster "Space Shuttle Solid Rocket Booster")-ET Attach Ring near the Integrated Electronics Assembly (IEA) box causing a dent ~4" wide and 3" deep into the solid metal.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-STS-112_SRB_Foam_Damage-3) Prior to approval for the next mission, the situation was analyzed and NASA decided to press ahead under the justification that "The ET is safe to fly with no new concerns (and no added risk)"[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-Jerry_Smelser_flight_rationale_ppt-14) of further foam strikes. This fateful decision set the stage for the [STS-107 tragedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster") just two launches later. The [CAIB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Accident_Investigation_Board "Columbia Accident Investigation Board") report did not highlight the significance of video data from this being the first flight with the ET Camera.

### 8 October (Flight Day 2 – Rendezvous and docking preparations)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-112&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: 8 October (Flight Day 2 – Rendezvous and docking preparations)")]

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a4/STS-112_Sandra_Magnus_washes_her_hair_in_the_middeck_of_Atlantis.jpg/250px-STS-112_Sandra_Magnus_washes_her_hair_in_the_middeck_of_Atlantis.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS-112_Sandra_Magnus_washes_her_hair_in_the_middeck_of_Atlantis.jpg)

Sandra Magnus washes her hair in the middeck of _Atlantis_

On Flight Day 2, the STS-112 crew settled into preparations for the next day's rendezvous and docking with the International Space Station.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-15) After the wake up call went at 4:46 am CDT, the crew began its first full day on orbit. Pilot Pamela Melroy assisted Mission Specialists David Wolf and Piers Sellers in a checkout of spacewalk suits and equipment. Commander Jeff Ashby worked with the prime robotic arm operator, Mission Specialist Sandy Magnus, to verify the arm's readiness. Ashby and Magnus powered up the arm for a video survey of Atlantis' payload bay. The crew also completed the setting up of the orbiter docking system's centerline camera, extended the orbiter's spring-loaded ring that will make first contact, and checked out rendezvous tools.

During the day, the STS-112 crew successfully completed three Orbital Maneuvering System (OMS) burns to boost the shuttle into the station's orbit and refine its approach path to the station.

Astronaut Wolf also checked-out the Spatial Heterodyne Imager for Mesospheric Radicals or the SHIMMER experiment sponsored by the Naval Research Lab. The SHIMMER experiment uses an ultraviolet sensing camera to observe the Earth's atmosphere at 40–90 kilometers looking for possible ozone loss. The experiment proved balky, but with help from Mission Control the crew worked out steps to ready the gear for observations during the mission.

### 9 October (Flight Day 3 – Docking)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-112&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: 9 October (Flight Day 3 – Docking)")]

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ab/STS-112_Atlantis_carrying_S1_truss.jpg/250px-STS-112_Atlantis_carrying_S1_truss.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS-112_Atlantis_carrying_S1_truss.jpg)

_Atlantis_ during rendezvous and docking operations. The steel truss segment and radiators can be seen clearly in the payload bay

Space Shuttle _Atlantis_ docked to the Space Station at 15:17 GMT to begin a week of joint operations for the STS-112 and [Expedition 5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_5 "Expedition 5") crews. With commander [Jeffrey Ashby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeffrey_Ashby "Jeffrey Ashby") at the controls, _Atlantis'_ docking system engaged the Pressurized Mating Adapter-2 (Destiny Laboratory's forward docking port) in the front of the space station as the two spacecraft sailed 245 miles above central Asia at five miles per second.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-16) Crew members of _Atlantis_ were the first visitors for the Expedition 5 station crew who arrived at the outpost the first week of June 2002.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-17)

Following pressure checks, station science officer Peggy Whitson asked Commander Ashby if he had brought the salsa that she had asked for. When Ashby replied that he had, Whitson said "OK, we'll let you in".[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-18) The hatches between _Atlantis_ and the Space Station were opened at 16:51 GMT and astronaut Ashby floated into the Destiny Module and immediately embraced Whitson.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-19) Mission Specialist Sandra Magnus followed next, followed by the rest of _Atlantis'_ STS-112 crew members. They were greeted by the three member station crew.

After a safety briefing from station commander Valery Korzun, the combined crews split up and began preparing for a busy day of work. Astronaut Pamela Melroy, cosmonaut Korzun, and Mission Specialists Dave Wolf, Piers Sellers, and Fyodor Yurchikhin configured the spacesuits for EVA 1. Magnus and Whitson reviewed robotic arm operations for moving the new truss segment into place.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-20)

### 10 October (Flight Day 4 – EVA 1)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-112&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: 10 October (Flight Day 4 – EVA 1)")]

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3e/STS112_EVA_1_David_Wolf_anchored_to_SSRMS.jpg/250px-STS112_EVA_1_David_Wolf_anchored_to_SSRMS.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS112_EVA_1_David_Wolf_anchored_to_SSRMS.jpg)

David Wolf carries the S1 outboard nadir external camera during EVA 1.

The workday began at 3 am CDT with a musical wakeup call to _Atlantis_' crew from Mission Control, Houston. Earlier on Flight Day 4 astronauts Whitson and Magnus used the station's Canadarm2 robotic arm to grapple the S1 truss structure, remove it from _Atlantis'_ payload bay, and move it to the starboard end the S0 section. Four remotely operated motorized bolts locked the two truss segments together at 8:36 am CDT.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-21)

Simultaneously, Astronauts Dave Wolf and Piers Sellers prepared for the mission's first spacewalk. EVA 1 was the 44th spacewalk staged to support the space station assembly and maintenance. The two astronauts exited the Quest Airlock at about 11:21 am EDT. Wolf's spacesuit had solid red stripes for identification, while Sellers donned an all white spacesuit. As Wolf worked to accomplish to connect power, data and fluid lines between the S0 and the S1 trusses, Sellers, on his first spacewalk, released the locks on three folded-up radiators mounted to the S1, allowing S1's radiators to be oriented for optimal cooling.

The spacewalking astronauts worked for seven hours and one minute outside the space station, 31 minutes longer than expected due to a problem with the Canadarm2. The glitch forced Wolf to complete installation of a television camera system on the far end of the truss without the assistance of the robot arm.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-22) The only other problem of EVA 1 came near the end of the spacewalk when Wolf reported his helmet earphones appeared to be losing power.

Throughout the spacewalk, astronaut Melroy offered guidance and advice to the spacewalkers and keeping them on schedule. Shuttle Commander Jeff Ashby operated the shuttle robotic arm, providing camera views for documentation. Following a tool inventory check and cleanup activities, Wolf and Sellers re-entered Quest. The Airlock was re-pressurized at 5:22 pm CDT to end EVA 1.

### 11 October (Flight Day 5 – Off duty and transfers)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-112&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: 11 October (Flight Day 5 – Off duty and transfers)")]

[![Image 27](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/23/STS-112_and_Expedition_5_crew_share_a_meal.jpg/250px-STS-112_and_Expedition_5_crew_share_a_meal.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS-112_and_Expedition_5_crew_share_a_meal.jpg)

The STS-112 and Expedition 5 crewmembers share a meal in the Zvezda Service Module.

On Flight Day 5, the combined shuttle and space station crew took several hours of off-duty time. Then they began transfer operations between the vehicles and prepared for mission's second spacewalk. The crew moved a number of scientific experiments back and forth between the shuttle and the ISS to return completed experiments to Earth and deploy new experiments at the ISS. Transfer items included a set of liver cell tissue samples from an experiment studying the function of human liver cells in microgravity, moved from the station onto the shuttle for return to Earth.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-23)

Payload experiments such as Marshall Space Flight Center's protein crystal growth thermal enclosures for growing high-quality protein crystals in micro-gravity experiments were moved to and from the station. Seven water containers were transferred to the station. Commander Jeff Ashby initiated a [Nitrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen "Nitrogen") transfer process that moved about 15 pounds of the gas from _Atlantis_ to the station by the end of the day.

STS-112 spacewalkers David Wolf and Piers Sellers, assisted by Pilot Pamela Melroy, readied the EVA equipment They recharged water on the extravehicular mobility unit (EMU), configured their tools and prepared the Quest airlock.

The crew also participated in several live media interviews. Astronauts Magnus, Wolf and Sellers discussed about EVA 1 and the first-time experiences in space with CBS Radio Network and Cable News Network (CNN). Speaking to CBS News, Wolf told that manual work Piers and himself did at the end of EVA 1 to install the S1's outboard nadir external camera got their heart rates up to over 170 per minute.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-24) The spacewalkers were not able to use the Station's Canadarm 2 as a result of a software glitch.

Russian cosmonauts Valery Korzun, Sergei Treschev and Fyodor Yurchikhin participated in several interviews with the Russian press. Shortly before sleep, the crew reviewed procedures for EVA 2.

## Shuttlecam

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-112&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Shuttlecam")]

A camera mounted to the shuttle's external tank captured _Atlantis'_ ascent to orbit. This was the first time such footage was recorded.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-26) However, after solid rocket booster separation, the camera was fogged with the propellant, and was rendered unusable. The camera was moved downward after STS-112.

In the response to the [Space Shuttle _Columbia_ disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster") ([STS-107](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-107 "STS-107")), the camera was also used on all subsequent missions to capture images of the falling debris from the external tank.

**STS-112** ([ISS assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISS_assembly_sequence "ISS assembly sequence") flight **9A**) was an 11-day [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") mission to the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station") (ISS) flown by [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle")[_Atlantis_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis "Space Shuttle Atlantis").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-1) Space Shuttle _Atlantis_ was launched on 7 October 2002 at 19:45 UTC from the [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center")'s launch pad 39B to deliver the 28,000 pound Starboard 1 (S1) truss segment to the Space Station.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-2) Ending a 4.5-million-mile journey, _Atlantis_ landed at 15:44 UTC on 18 October 2002 on runway 33 at the Kennedy Space Center's Shuttle Landing Facility.

During the launch, the ET bipod ramp shed a chunk of [foam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_external_tank#Thermal_protection_system "Space Shuttle external tank") that caused a dent ~4" wide and 3" deep into the metal SRB-ET Attach Ring near the bottom of the left [Space Shuttle Solid Rocket Booster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Solid_Rocket_Booster "Space Shuttle Solid Rocket Booster").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-STS-112_SRB_Foam_Damage-3) Prior to the next mission ([STS-113](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-113 "STS-113")), an upper-level decision was made at NASA to continue with launches as scheduled. The launch subsequent to that was the [Space Shuttle _Columbia_ disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster"), the ill-fated [STS-107](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-107 "STS-107").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-caib_report3-4)

Space Shuttle _Atlantis_ had been scheduled to visit the International Space Station (ISS) again on the [STS-114](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-114 "STS-114") mission in March 2003;[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-5) however, due to the [loss of _Columbia_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster"), all Space Shuttles, including _Atlantis_, were temporarily grounded. Due to rescheduling of missions, _Atlantis_ did not fly again until [STS-115](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-115 "STS-115") on 9 September 2006.

### Starboard 1 (S1) truss segment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-112&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Starboard 1 (S1) truss segment")]

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/Heat_Rejection_System_%28HRS%29_Radiator.jpg/250px-Heat_Rejection_System_%28HRS%29_Radiator.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Heat_Rejection_System_(HRS)_Radiator.jpg)

The S1 Radiator panels being manufactured at the [Michoud Assembly Facility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michoud_Assembly_Facility "Michoud Assembly Facility")

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/61/ISSafterSTS112.jpg/250px-ISSafterSTS112.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ISSafterSTS112.jpg)

Illustration of the International Space Station after STS-112.

The [S1 truss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integrated_Truss_Structure "Integrated Truss Structure") segment, which provides structural support for the Space Station radiators, was the main payload of STS-112 mission.

The [Boeing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing "Boeing") Company (along with [Lockheed Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_Martin "Lockheed Martin")) started [manufacturing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manufacturing_of_the_International_Space_Station "Manufacturing of the International Space Station") the truss in May 1998 at Michoud. The work was completed in March 1999. The S1 was shipped by aircraft to the KSC Operations and Checkout Building in October 1999 for flight processing. In June 2002, the truss was handed over to NASA for final preparations and pre-flight checks at the Space Station Processing Facility.

### Crew Equipment Translation Aid

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-112&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Crew Equipment Translation Aid")]

_Atlantis_ also delivered the Crew Equipment Translation Aid (CETA) Cart to the Space Station. The CETA cart was attached to the Mobile Transporter (launched on [STS-110](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-110 "STS-110")) to be used by assembly crews on later missions.

## Mission experiments

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-112&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Mission experiments")]

STS-112 carried several science experiments to the space station including the Plant Generic Bioprocessing Apparatus (PGBA), Commercial Generic Bioprocessing Apparatus (CGBA), the Protein Crystal Growth Single-locker Thermal Enclosure System housing the Protein Crystallization Apparatus for Microgravity (PCG-STES-PCAM) and samples for the Zeolite Crystal Growth Furnace (ZCG) experiment.

## Shuttle processing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-112&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Shuttle processing")]

| Attempt | Planned | Result | Turnaround | Reason | Decision point | Weather go (%) | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 2 Oct 2002, 2:00:00 pm | Scrubbed | — | Weather | 1 Oct 2002, 3:15 pm​(T−11:00:00 hold) | 60 | Johnson Space Center powered down due to threat of Hurricane Lili.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-6) |
| 2 | 7 Oct 2002, 3:45:51 pm | Success | 5 days 1 hour 46 minutes |  |  | 90[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-7) |  |

Launch preparations for STS-112 mission were sightly delayed due to tiny cracks found within the plumbing of _Atlantis'_ propulsion system on 17 June 2002 by an inspector. The cracks were in metal flow liners inside the main liquid hydrogen fuel lines that feed the shuttle's three main engines. Although there were no cracks in the actual fuel pipes themselves, the concern was that metal pieces from the flow liners might break off and fly into the engines. In such a worst-case scenario, the debris can potentially trigger a catastrophic engine shutdown, which in turn could lead to the loss of the crew and the shuttle.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-8) Similar cracks were found in the remaining orbiters and the space shuttle program was temporally grounded so engineers could analyze the problem.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-9) The shuttle was cleared to resume flight in September with launch originally scheduled for October 2, but due to concerns that [Hurricane Lili](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Lili "Hurricane Lili") could hit Houston, the Johnson Space Center was powered down.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-atlantis2-10)

## Mission timeline

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-112&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Mission timeline")]

### 7 October (Flight Day 1 – Launch)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-112&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: 7 October (Flight Day 1 – Launch)")]

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6a/STS-112_Launch_of_Space_Shuttle_Atlantis.jpg/250px-STS-112_Launch_of_Space_Shuttle_Atlantis.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS-112_Launch_of_Space_Shuttle_Atlantis.jpg)

_Atlantis_ launches on STS-112.

Space Shuttle _Atlantis_ lifted off from Launch Pad 39B of the [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center") at 19:45:51 GMT through mostly clear blue skies. There were no problems reported during the countdown, and the ascent conformed to the standard timeline (see [Space Shuttle – Mission Profile – Launch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle")). For the first time in Space Shuttle history, a "rocketcam" video camera mounted to the upper part of _Atlantis'_ external tank returned live video of the flight to NASA flight controllers.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-lift_off_of_Atlantis-11) The video was near perfect until the two solid rocket boosters were jettisoned. At that point, the exhaust from the separation motors fogged the camera lens and made the rest of the video difficult to see.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-Debris/Ice/TPS-12):A13

Later, NASA announced that it was looking into a problem with explosive bolts that failed to fire properly during the launch. Immediately before the twin solid rocket boosters fired into life, only one set of pyrotechnics in ten explosive bolts exploded when commanded to do so. All 10 nuts exploded as planned, but NASA was interested in finding out an explanation for the unexpected anomaly.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-13)

Arguably the most significant event from this launch was the ET bipod ramp shedding a chunk of foam, estimated to be ~4"x5"x12", that broke away and hit the lower left [SRB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Solid_Rocket_Booster "Space Shuttle Solid Rocket Booster")-ET Attach Ring near the Integrated Electronics Assembly (IEA) box causing a dent ~4" wide and 3" deep into the solid metal.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-STS-112_SRB_Foam_Damage-3) Prior to approval for the next mission, the situation was analyzed and NASA decided to press ahead under the justification that "The ET is safe to fly with no new concerns (and no added risk)"[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-Jerry_Smelser_flight_rationale_ppt-14) of further foam strikes. This fateful decision set the stage for the [STS-107 tragedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster") just two launches later. The [CAIB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Accident_Investigation_Board "Columbia Accident Investigation Board") report did not highlight the significance of video data from this being the first flight with the ET Camera.

### 8 October (Flight Day 2 – Rendezvous and docking preparations)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-112&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: 8 October (Flight Day 2 – Rendezvous and docking preparations)")]

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a4/STS-112_Sandra_Magnus_washes_her_hair_in_the_middeck_of_Atlantis.jpg/250px-STS-112_Sandra_Magnus_washes_her_hair_in_the_middeck_of_Atlantis.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS-112_Sandra_Magnus_washes_her_hair_in_the_middeck_of_Atlantis.jpg)

Sandra Magnus washes her hair in the middeck of _Atlantis_

On Flight Day 2, the STS-112 crew settled into preparations for the next day's rendezvous and docking with the International Space Station.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-15) After the wake up call went at 4:46 am CDT, the crew began its first full day on orbit. Pilot Pamela Melroy assisted Mission Specialists David Wolf and Piers Sellers in a checkout of spacewalk suits and equipment. Commander Jeff Ashby worked with the prime robotic arm operator, Mission Specialist Sandy Magnus, to verify the arm's readiness. Ashby and Magnus powered up the arm for a video survey of Atlantis' payload bay. The crew also completed the setting up of the orbiter docking system's centerline camera, extended the orbiter's spring-loaded ring that will make first contact, and checked out rendezvous tools.

During the day, the STS-112 crew successfully completed three Orbital Maneuvering System (OMS) burns to boost the shuttle into the station's orbit and refine its approach path to the station.

Astronaut Wolf also checked-out the Spatial Heterodyne Imager for Mesospheric Radicals or the SHIMMER experiment sponsored by the Naval Research Lab. The SHIMMER experiment uses an ultraviolet sensing camera to observe the Earth's atmosphere at 40–90 kilometers looking for possible ozone loss. The experiment proved balky, but with help from Mission Control the crew worked out steps to ready the gear for observations during the mission.

### 9 October (Flight Day 3 – Docking)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-112&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: 9 October (Flight Day 3 – Docking)")]

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ab/STS-112_Atlantis_carrying_S1_truss.jpg/250px-STS-112_Atlantis_carrying_S1_truss.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS-112_Atlantis_carrying_S1_truss.jpg)

_Atlantis_ during rendezvous and docking operations. The steel truss segment and radiators can be seen clearly in the payload bay

Space Shuttle _Atlantis_ docked to the Space Station at 15:17 GMT to begin a week of joint operations for the STS-112 and [Expedition 5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_5 "Expedition 5") crews. With commander [Jeffrey Ashby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeffrey_Ashby "Jeffrey Ashby") at the controls, _Atlantis'_ docking system engaged the Pressurized Mating Adapter-2 (Destiny Laboratory's forward docking port) in the front of the space station as the two spacecraft sailed 245 miles above central Asia at five miles per second.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-16) Crew members of _Atlantis_ were the first visitors for the Expedition 5 station crew who arrived at the outpost the first week of June 2002.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-17)

Following pressure checks, station science officer Peggy Whitson asked Commander Ashby if he had brought the salsa that she had asked for. When Ashby replied that he had, Whitson said "OK, we'll let you in".[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-18) The hatches between _Atlantis_ and the Space Station were opened at 16:51 GMT and astronaut Ashby floated into the Destiny Module and immediately embraced Whitson.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-19) Mission Specialist Sandra Magnus followed next, followed by the rest of _Atlantis'_ STS-112 crew members. They were greeted by the three member station crew.

After a safety briefing from station commander Valery Korzun, the combined crews split up and began preparing for a busy day of work. Astronaut Pamela Melroy, cosmonaut Korzun, and Mission Specialists Dave Wolf, Piers Sellers, and Fyodor Yurchikhin configured the spacesuits for EVA 1. Magnus and Whitson reviewed robotic arm operations for moving the new truss segment into place.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-20)

### 10 October (Flight Day 4 – EVA 1)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-112&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: 10 October (Flight Day 4 – EVA 1)")]

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3e/STS112_EVA_1_David_Wolf_anchored_to_SSRMS.jpg/250px-STS112_EVA_1_David_Wolf_anchored_to_SSRMS.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS112_EVA_1_David_Wolf_anchored_to_SSRMS.jpg)

David Wolf carries the S1 outboard nadir external camera during EVA 1.

The workday began at 3 am CDT with a musical wakeup call to _Atlantis_' crew from Mission Control, Houston. Earlier on Flight Day 4 astronauts Whitson and Magnus used the station's Canadarm2 robotic arm to grapple the S1 truss structure, remove it from _Atlantis'_ payload bay, and move it to the starboard end the S0 section. Four remotely operated motorized bolts locked the two truss segments together at 8:36 am CDT.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-21)

Simultaneously, Astronauts Dave Wolf and Piers Sellers prepared for the mission's first spacewalk. EVA 1 was the 44th spacewalk staged to support the space station assembly and maintenance. The two astronauts exited the Quest Airlock at about 11:21 am EDT. Wolf's spacesuit had solid red stripes for identification, while Sellers donned an all white spacesuit. As Wolf worked to accomplish to connect power, data and fluid lines between the S0 and the S1 trusses, Sellers, on his first spacewalk, released the locks on three folded-up radiators mounted to the S1, allowing S1's radiators to be oriented for optimal cooling.

The spacewalking astronauts worked for seven hours and one minute outside the space station, 31 minutes longer than expected due to a problem with the Canadarm2. The glitch forced Wolf to complete installation of a television camera system on the far end of the truss without the assistance of the robot arm.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-22) The only other problem of EVA 1 came near the end of the spacewalk when Wolf reported his helmet earphones appeared to be losing power.

Throughout the spacewalk, astronaut Melroy offered guidance and advice to the spacewalkers and keeping them on schedule. Shuttle Commander Jeff Ashby operated the shuttle robotic arm, providing camera views for documentation. Following a tool inventory check and cleanup activities, Wolf and Sellers re-entered Quest. The Airlock was re-pressurized at 5:22 pm CDT to end EVA 1.

### 11 October (Flight Day 5 – Off duty and transfers)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-112&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: 11 October (Flight Day 5 – Off duty and transfers)")]

[![Image 27](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/23/STS-112_and_Expedition_5_crew_share_a_meal.jpg/250px-STS-112_and_Expedition_5_crew_share_a_meal.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS-112_and_Expedition_5_crew_share_a_meal.jpg)

The STS-112 and Expedition 5 crewmembers share a meal in the Zvezda Service Module.

On Flight Day 5, the combined shuttle and space station crew took several hours of off-duty time. Then they began transfer operations between the vehicles and prepared for mission's second spacewalk. The crew moved a number of scientific experiments back and forth between the shuttle and the ISS to return completed experiments to Earth and deploy new experiments at the ISS. Transfer items included a set of liver cell tissue samples from an experiment studying the function of human liver cells in microgravity, moved from the station onto the shuttle for return to Earth.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-23)

Payload experiments such as Marshall Space Flight Center's protein crystal growth thermal enclosures for growing high-quality protein crystals in micro-gravity experiments were moved to and from the station. Seven water containers were transferred to the station. Commander Jeff Ashby initiated a [Nitrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen "Nitrogen") transfer process that moved about 15 pounds of the gas from _Atlantis_ to the station by the end of the day.

STS-112 spacewalkers David Wolf and Piers Sellers, assisted by Pilot Pamela Melroy, readied the EVA equipment They recharged water on the extravehicular mobility unit (EMU), configured their tools and prepared the Quest airlock.

The crew also participated in several live media interviews. Astronauts Magnus, Wolf and Sellers discussed about EVA 1 and the first-time experiences in space with CBS Radio Network and Cable News Network (CNN). Speaking to CBS News, Wolf told that manual work Piers and himself did at the end of EVA 1 to install the S1's outboard nadir external camera got their heart rates up to over 170 per minute.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-24) The spacewalkers were not able to use the Station's Canadarm 2 as a result of a software glitch.

Russian cosmonauts Valery Korzun, Sergei Treschev and Fyodor Yurchikhin participated in several interviews with the Russian press. Shortly before sleep, the crew reviewed procedures for EVA 2.

## Shuttlecam

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-112&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Shuttlecam")]

A camera mounted to the shuttle's external tank captured _Atlantis'_ ascent to orbit. This was the first time such footage was recorded.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-112#cite_note-26) However, after solid rocket booster separation, the camera was fogged with the propellant, and was rendered unusable. The camera was moved downward after STS-112.

In the response to the [Space Shuttle _Columbia_ disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster") ([STS-107](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-107 "STS-107")), the camera was also used on all subsequent missions to capture images of the falling debris from the external tank.
