**Glenn Anton** "**Doc**" **Rivers** (born October 13, 1961) is an American former professional [basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball "Basketball") player and coach in the [National Basketball Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Basketball_Association "National Basketball Association") (NBA). An NBA player for 14 seasons, he was an [NBA All-Star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_All-Star "NBA All-Star") and was named one of the [15 Greatest Coaches in NBA History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/15_Greatest_Coaches_in_NBA_History "15 Greatest Coaches in NBA History").

Rivers played [college basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_basketball "College basketball") for the [Marquette Golden Eagles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marquette_Golden_Eagles_men's_basketball "Marquette Golden Eagles men's basketball") and was selected by the [Atlanta Hawks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta_Hawks "Atlanta Hawks") in the second round of the [1983 NBA draft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1983_NBA_draft "1983 NBA draft"). He played [point guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_guard "Point guard") for the Hawks from 1983 to 1991 and was later a member of the [Los Angeles Clippers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Clippers "Los Angeles Clippers"), [New York Knicks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Knicks "New York Knicks"), and [San Antonio Spurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Antonio_Spurs "San Antonio Spurs"). Rivers was an All-Star with the Hawks in [1988](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1988_NBA_All-Star_Game "1988 NBA All-Star Game").

After retiring as a player in 1996, Rivers called games for the [NBA on TNT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_on_TNT "NBA on TNT"). Rivers began his NBA coaching career in 1999. He was the head coach of the [Orlando Magic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orlando_Magic "Orlando Magic") from 1999 to 2003, the [Boston Celtics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Celtics "Boston Celtics") from 2004 to 2013, the [Los Angeles Clippers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Clippers "Los Angeles Clippers") from 2013 to 2020, the [Philadelphia 76ers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia_76ers "Philadelphia 76ers") from 2020 to 2023, and the [Milwaukee Bucks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milwaukee_Bucks "Milwaukee Bucks") from 2024 to 2026. Rivers was named the 2000 [NBA Coach of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_Coach_of_the_Year_Award "NBA Coach of the Year Award") in his first season with the Magic and won an [NBA championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_NBA_champions "List of NBA champions") with the Celtics in [2008](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_NBA_Finals "2008 NBA Finals"). He was also an analyst for [ESPN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_on_ESPN "NBA on ESPN").

In April 2026, he was announced as a [coaching inductee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_coaches_in_the_Naismith_Memorial_Basketball_Hall_of_Fame "List of coaches in the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame") to the [Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naismith_Basketball_Hall_of_Fame "Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame"), and will formally enter the Hall that August.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-2)

## Playing career

### High school and college career

Rivers was a [McDonald's All-American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McDonald's_All-American_Game "McDonald's All-American Game") for [Proviso East High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proviso_East_High_School "Proviso East High School") in the [Chicago metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_metropolitan_area "Chicago metropolitan area").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-3) He was given his nickname while attending a [summer basketball camp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer_camp "Summer camp") at [Marquette University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marquette_University "Marquette University") while wearing a "Dr. J" t-shirt of [Philadelphia 76ers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia_76ers "Philadelphia 76ers") player [Julius Erving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Erving "Julius Erving").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-4) Rivers has alternated on whether the nickname originated from [Golden Eagles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marquette_Golden_Eagles_men's_basketball "Marquette Golden Eagles men's basketball") head coach [Al McGuire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_McGuire "Al McGuire") or assistant [Rick Majerus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Majerus "Rick Majerus").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-7)

Rivers later played college ball for Marquette. After his third season at Marquette, Rivers was drafted in the second round (31st overall)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-coachfile-8) of the [1983 NBA draft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1983_NBA_draft "1983 NBA draft") by the [Atlanta Hawks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta_Hawks "Atlanta Hawks"). He graduated from Marquette by completing course work while he was an active NBA player.

### Professional career

After three seasons at Marquette, Rivers entered the NBA draft and was a second-round choice of the Atlanta Hawks. Rivers played point guard for the Atlanta Hawks from 1983 to 1991,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-9) assisting star [Dominique Wilkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominique_Wilkins "Dominique Wilkins") as the team found great regular season success.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Rivers' first NBA start was against [Julius Erving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Erving "Julius Erving") (Dr. J), who referred to Rivers as "Doc" and "made [him] feel like a million bucks".[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-lowe16-10)

On March 4, 1986, Rivers recorded a career-high 21 assists in a game against the [Philadelphia 76ers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia_76ers "Philadelphia 76ers").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-11) He averaged a [double-double](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double-double "Double-double") for the [1986–87 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1986-87_NBA_season "1986-87 NBA season") with 12.8 points and 10.0 assists per game.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-12) In 1988, Rivers played in the [NBA All-Star Game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_All-Star_Game "NBA All-Star Game").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-13) He received the [J. Walter Kennedy Citizenship Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._Walter_Kennedy_Citizenship_Award "J. Walter Kennedy Citizenship Award") in 1990.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-14) After eight seasons with the Hawks, Rivers remains their all-time leader in assists with 3,866.

Rivers later spent one year as a starter for the [Los Angeles Clippers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Clippers "Los Angeles Clippers") (1991–1992), two years playing for the [New York Knicks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Knicks "New York Knicks") (1992–1994), and two years playing for the [San Antonio Spurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Antonio_Spurs "San Antonio Spurs") (1994–1996). Rivers retired after the 1996 season. During his professional career, Rivers would go on to play 864 regular-season games in which he averaged 10.9 points, 5.7 assists, and 3 rebounds per game.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-15)

### National team career

Rivers played for the [United States national team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_men's_national_basketball_team "United States men's national basketball team") during the [1982 FIBA World Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1982_FIBA_World_Championship "1982 FIBA World Championship") in [Colombia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colombia "Colombia"). He was named the [tournaments MVP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIBA_Basketball_World_Cup_Most_Valuable_Player "FIBA Basketball World Cup Most Valuable Player") after leading the United States to the gold medal game where they lost against the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union_men's_national_basketball_team "Soviet Union men's national basketball team"), 94–95, after Rivers' eight-foot jumper at the buzzer rimmed out.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-17)

## Coaching career

### Orlando Magic (1999–2003)

Rivers began his coaching career with the [Orlando Magic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orlando_Magic "Orlando Magic") in 1999,[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-18) where he coached for more than four [NBA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Basketball_Association "National Basketball Association") seasons.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-auto-19) Rivers won the [Coach of the Year award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_Coach_of_the_Year_Award "NBA Coach of the Year Award") in [2000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999%E2%80%932000_NBA_season "1999–2000 NBA season") after his first year with the Magic.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-20) Despite having been picked to finish last in that year's standings, Rivers led the Magic close to a playoff berth.

During the Magic's free agency spending spree in the summer of 2000, Rivers tried to assemble a "Big Three" team in the NBA. The Magic were courting free agent [Tim Duncan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Duncan "Tim Duncan"), who came close to signing with the Magic and teaming up with fellow stars [Grant Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grant_Hill "Grant Hill") and [Tracy McGrady](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tracy_McGrady "Tracy McGrady"). However, Duncan re-signed with the San Antonio Spurs due to Rivers' strict policy of family members not being allowed to travel on the team's plane.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-21)

The Magic made the postseason in Rivers's next three years as head coach, but he was fired in 2003 after a 1–10 start to the season.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-auto-19)

### Boston Celtics (2004–2013)

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6d/Doc_Rivers.jpg/250px-Doc_Rivers.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Doc_Rivers.jpg)

Rivers in 2011

After spending a year working as a commentator for the _[NBA on ABC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA\_on\_ABC "NBA on ABC")_ (calling the [2004 Finals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_NBA_Finals "2004 NBA Finals") with [Al Michaels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Michaels "Al Michaels")), he was hired by the [Boston Celtics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Celtics "Boston Celtics") as their head coach in 2004. During his first years with the Celtics, he was criticized by many in the media for his coaching style, most vociferously by [Bill Simmons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Simmons "Bill Simmons"), who in 2006 publicly called for Rivers to be fired in his columns.

As a result of the Celtics' 109–93 victory over the [New York Knicks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Knicks "New York Knicks") on January 21, 2008, Rivers, as the coach of the team with the best winning percentage in the [Eastern Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Conference_(NBA) "Eastern Conference (NBA)"), earned the honor to coach the East for the [2008 NBA All-Star Game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_NBA_All-Star_Game "2008 NBA All-Star Game") in [New Orleans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans_Hornets "New Orleans Hornets").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-22)

On June 17, 2008, Rivers won his first and sole [NBA Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_Finals "NBA Finals") as a head coach after defeating the [Los Angeles Lakers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Lakers "Los Angeles Lakers") in six games.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-23) The Celtics needed an NBA record 26 postseason games to win it. Rivers played for the team that held the previous record for most games played in a single postseason when the New York Knicks played in 25 postseason games during 1994.

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/ba/Members_of_the_2008_NBA_Champion_Boston_Celtics_at_the_White_House.jpg/250px-Members_of_the_2008_NBA_Champion_Boston_Celtics_at_the_White_House.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Members_of_the_2008_NBA_Champion_Boston_Celtics_at_the_White_House.jpg)

Rivers and the [2008 NBA champion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_NBA_Finals "2008 NBA Finals") Boston Celtics with President George W. Bush at the White House

Rivers led the Celtics to the [2010 NBA Finals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_NBA_Finals "2010 NBA Finals"), where they once again faced the Los Angeles Lakers, this time losing the series in seven games. After deliberating between staying on the job or returning to Orlando in order to spend more time with his family, Rivers finally decided that he would honor the last year of his contract and return for the 2010–11 season.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-24)

On May 13, 2011, after months of rumors that he would retire, ESPN reported that the Celtics and Rivers had agreed upon a 5-year contract extension worth $35 million.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-26) On February 6, 2013, Rivers notched his 400th win with the Celtics in a 99–95 victory over the [Toronto Raptors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto_Raptors "Toronto Raptors").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-27)

### Los Angeles Clippers (2013–2020)

On June 25, 2013, the [Los Angeles Clippers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Clippers "Los Angeles Clippers") acquired Rivers from the Celtics for an unprotected 2015 NBA first-round draft pick. He also became the senior vice president of basketball operations on the team.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-28) In his first season as their head coach, Rivers led the Clippers to a franchise-record 57 wins, garnering the 3rd seed in the Western conference. The [2014 NBA playoffs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_NBA_playoffs "2014 NBA playoffs") first round playoff series against the [Golden State Warriors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_State_Warriors "Golden State Warriors") was marred when [TMZ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TMZ "TMZ") released an audiotape containing racially insensitive remarks made by the then-Clippers owner [Donald Sterling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Sterling "Donald Sterling").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-29) Though there was a possibility of the Clippers boycotting the series, [[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-30) they instead played on, instead holding a silent protest by leaving their shooting jerseys at center court and obscuring the Clippers logo on their warm-up shirts.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-31) Rivers himself stated that he would not return to the Clippers if Sterling remained as owner the following season.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-32) NBA commissioner [Adam Silver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_Silver "Adam Silver") responded to the controversy by banning Sterling from the NBA for life and compelling him to sell the team.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-33) The team was sold to [Microsoft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft "Microsoft") CEO [Steve Ballmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Ballmer "Steve Ballmer") for $2 billion on August 12, 2014,[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-34) and Rivers remained with the Clippers.

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b9/Doc_Rivers_2013_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Doc_Rivers_2013_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Doc_Rivers_2013_(cropped).jpg)

Rivers in 2013

On June 16, 2014, the Clippers promoted Rivers to president of basketball operations in conjunction with his continuing head coaching duties. Although [Dave Wohl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Wohl "Dave Wohl") was hired as general manager, Rivers had the final say in basketball matters.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-35) On August 27, 2014, he signed a new five-year contract with the Clippers.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-36)

On January 16, 2015, Rivers became the first NBA coach to coach his own son, [Austin Rivers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_Rivers "Austin Rivers"),[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-37) until June 26, 2018, when Austin Rivers was traded to the [Washington Wizards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Wizards "Washington Wizards") for [Marcin Gortat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcin_Gortat "Marcin Gortat").

On August 4, 2017, Rivers gave up his post as president of basketball operations. However, he continued to split responsibility for basketball matters with executive vice president of basketball operations [Lawrence Frank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_Frank "Lawrence Frank").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-38) On May 23, 2018, Rivers and the Clippers agreed to a contract extension.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-39)

On May 31, 2019, Rivers made comments on [Kawhi Leonard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kawhi_Leonard "Kawhi Leonard") during an appearance on ESPN, stating that "He is the most like [Michael] [Jordan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Jordan "Michael Jordan") that we've seen", while Leonard was still under contract to the [Toronto Raptors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto_Raptors "Toronto Raptors").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-40) The Clippers were fined $50,000 due to Rivers' comments in violation of the league's anti-tampering rule.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-41) The Clippers signed Leonard to a three-year contract on July 10, 2019.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-42)

In the [2019–20 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019%E2%80%9320_Los_Angeles_Clippers_season "2019–20 Los Angeles Clippers season"), Rivers earned his 900th win as a head coach after the Clippers won at home against the [Portland Trail Blazers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_Trail_Blazers "Portland Trail Blazers") on November 8, 2019.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-43) In the Western Conference semifinals, the Clippers jumped to a 3 games to 1 lead before losing the last three of the best-of-seven series to the [Denver Nuggets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denver_Nuggets "Denver Nuggets"). Rivers became the first coach in NBA history to have three teams fail to advance from a best-of-seven series after taking a 3 games to 1 lead.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-Urbina-44) He had previously been the only coach in NBA history whose teams had twice failed to advance from a best of seven series after taking a 3–1 lead.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-Urbina-44)

On September 28, 2020, Rivers stepped down following the Clippers' defeat to the Nuggets in the [conference semifinals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_NBA_playoffs "2020 NBA playoffs"). His record through seven seasons with the team was 356–208, but he was ultimately unable to lead the Clippers to their first conference finals appearance in franchise history.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-45)

### Philadelphia 76ers (2020–2023)

On October 3, 2020, the [Philadelphia 76ers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia_76ers "Philadelphia 76ers") announced that they had hired Rivers as their head coach.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-46) The 76ers won their first two games of the 2020–21 season, which earned Rivers his 945th career win, passing Hall of Famer [Bill Fitch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Fitch "Bill Fitch") for 10th on the all-time coaching regular season wins list.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-47) The 76ers went on to secure the first seed in the Eastern Conference,[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-48) and defeated the [Washington Wizards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Wizards "Washington Wizards") in five games in the first round of the playoffs,[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-49) but lost in the semifinals to the [Atlanta Hawks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta_Hawks "Atlanta Hawks") in seven games.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-50) On May 14, 2023, the 76ers lost the conference semifinals series to the Celtics;[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-51) two days later, Rivers was fired, ending his three-year tenure as head coach of the 76ers.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-52)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-53)

### Milwaukee Bucks (2023–2026)

Beginning in December 2023, Rivers began serving as an informal consultant to [Milwaukee Bucks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milwaukee_Bucks "Milwaukee Bucks") first-year coach [Adrian Griffin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrian_Griffin "Adrian Griffin") at the team's request.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-charania_01242024-54) On January 26, 2024, after firing Griffin after 43 games,[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-charania_01242024-54) the Bucks announced that Rivers was hired as their head coach.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-55) Rivers' first game as the Bucks' head coach was a loss to the [reigning champion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_NBA_Finals "2023 NBA Finals")[Denver Nuggets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denver_Nuggets "Denver Nuggets") on January 29, 2024.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-56)

On December 17, 2024, under the leadership of head coach Doc Rivers, the Milwaukee Bucks won the [NBA Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_Cup "NBA Cup") final against the [Oklahoma City Thunder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma_City_Thunder "Oklahoma City Thunder") with a score of 97–81. This victory marked the Bucks as the second champions of this mid-season tournament, which was held in [Las Vegas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Las_Vegas "Las Vegas"). [Giannis Antetokounmpo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giannis_Antetokounmpo "Giannis Antetokounmpo") delivered an impressive performance, recording a triple-double with 26 points, 19 rebounds, and 10 assists, earning him the title of Most Valuable Player for the event. [Damian Lillard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damian_Lillard "Damian Lillard") contributed significantly to the win with 23 points. The Bucks' triumph represented a turnaround in their season, as they had secured victories in 13 of their last 16 games during this period after a slow start.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-57)

On April 13, 2026, he resigned from his position as head coach.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-58)[Myles Turner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myles_Turner "Myles Turner"), center for the Bucks, stated on the Game Recognize Game podcast that under Doc Rivers there was a culture of disorganization. Players arrived late to practices, meetings, and even trips without facing punishment. Rivers was accused of failing to enforce discipline and allowing players to ignore schedules and commitments. The situation created a chaotic environment, with reports of low-intensity practices and internal conflict between the coach and the roster during the season.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-59)

## Broadcasting career

Following his retirement as a player, Rivers called games for the [NBA on TNT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_on_TNT "NBA on TNT") before joining the Orlando Magic as head coach in 1999. With TNT Rivers was normally paired with [Verne Lundquist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verne_Lundquist "Verne Lundquist") and later with [Kevin Harlan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Harlan "Kevin Harlan").[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-60)

After being fired by the Orlando Magic in 2003, Rivers joined [ESPN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_on_ESPN "NBA on ESPN")/[ABC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_on_ABC "NBA on ABC")'s NBA coverage, calling regular season games and the [2004 NBA Finals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_NBA_Finals "2004 NBA Finals"). Rivers worked on the top broadcast team with [Brad Nessler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brad_Nessler "Brad Nessler") on ESPN and [Al Michaels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Michaels "Al Michaels") on ABC. After the Finals, he left the broadcast booth to become the head coach of the Boston Celtics. In the summer of 2023, he was added to the lead broadcasting team for ESPN/ABC, joining [Mike Breen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Breen "Mike Breen") and [Doris Burke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doris_Burke "Doris Burke").[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-61)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-62)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-63) During the [semifinals of the 2023 NBA In-Season Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_NBA_In-Season_Tournament#Semifinals "2023 NBA In-Season Tournament"), Rivers worked with TNT commentators Kevin Harlan and [Candace Parker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candace_Parker "Candace Parker") during one game, as part of a collaboration between ESPN/ABC and TNT.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-64)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-65) In January 2024, Rivers left ESPN mid-season to become Milwaukee's head coach.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-charania_01242024-54)

## Personal life

Rivers is the nephew of former NBA player [Jim Brewer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Brewer_(basketball) "Jim Brewer (basketball)").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-coachfile-8)

Rivers married wife Kristen in 1986, with whom he had four children, three sons and one daughter. Their oldest son, [Jeremiah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremiah_Rivers "Jeremiah Rivers"), played basketball at [Georgetown University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgetown_Hoyas_men's_basketball "Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball") and [Indiana University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana_Hoosiers_men's_basketball "Indiana Hoosiers men's basketball"),[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-66) and has played in the [NBA D-League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_D-League "NBA D-League") for the [Maine Red Claws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maine_Red_Claws "Maine Red Claws"). His daughter Callie played [volleyball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida_Gators_women's_volleyball "Florida Gators women's volleyball") for the [University of Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Florida "University of Florida")[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-67) and is married to NBA player [Seth Curry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seth_Curry "Seth Curry").[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-68)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-69) Rivers's son [Austin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_Rivers "Austin Rivers") is an NBA player who last played for the [Minnesota Timberwolves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota_Timberwolves "Minnesota Timberwolves") in 2023.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-70) His youngest son, Spencer, is a guard who played for [Winter Park High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winter_Park_High_School "Winter Park High School") and for [UC Irvine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UC_Irvine_Anteaters_men's_basketball "UC Irvine Anteaters men's basketball").[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-71) Rivers and Kristen divorced in 2019.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-72)

Rivers became good friends with [Major League Baseball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_League_Baseball "Major League Baseball") (MLB) [Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Baseball_Hall_of_Fame_and_Museum "National Baseball Hall of Fame and Museum") pitcher [John Smoltz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Smoltz "John Smoltz") of the [Atlanta Braves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta_Braves "Atlanta Braves") during Rivers's tenure with the Atlanta Hawks. In 2009, Rivers was credited with helping lure Smoltz into signing with the [Boston Red Sox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Red_Sox "Boston Red Sox") while Rivers was the head coach of the Boston Celtics.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-73)

Rivers is featured in a Netflix documentary series, "The Playbook". In the first episode, Rivers details his experiences with family, the Celtics championship run and the Donald Sterling situation.

Rivers is a cousin of former NBA guard [Byron Irvin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byron_Irvin "Byron Irvin") and former MLB outfielder [Ken Singleton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Singleton "Ken Singleton").[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-74)

Rivers has [attention deficit hyperactivity disorder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attention_deficit_hyperactivity_disorder "Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder").[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers#cite_note-75)

**Stephanie Diana Wilson** (born September 27, 1966)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-womenastronauts-1) is an American [engineer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engineer "Engineer") and a [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")[astronaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut "Astronaut"). She flew to space onboard three [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") missions and is the second [African American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_American "African American") woman to go into space after [Mae Jemison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mae_Jemison "Mae Jemison"). As of 2026,[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephanie_Wilson&action=edit) her almost 43 days in space are the second most of any female African American astronaut, having been surpassed by [Jessica Watkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessica_Watkins "Jessica Watkins") in 2022.

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephanie_Wilson&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Wilson was born in [Boston, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston,_Massachusetts "Boston, Massachusetts") on September 27, 1966. About a year later, her parents, Eugene and Barbara Wilson,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-:0-2) decided to move to [Pittsfield, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsfield,_Massachusetts "Pittsfield, Massachusetts").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-3) Eugene, a native of [Nesmith, South Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nesmith,_South_Carolina "Nesmith, South Carolina"), used his electronics training from his time in the Navy to get himself a degree from [Northeastern University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northeastern_University "Northeastern University") and a long career in electrical engineering for [Raytheon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raytheon "Raytheon"), [Sprague Electric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_C._Sprague "Robert C. Sprague"), and [Lockheed Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_Martin "Lockheed Martin"),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-:0-2)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-4) while Barbara, from [Talbot County, Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_County,_Georgia "Talbot County, Georgia"),[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-5) worked as a production assistant for Lockheed Martin.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-:0-2)

After attending Stearns Elementary School, she attended Crosby Junior High School.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-iberkshires.com-6) For a career awareness class in middle school, Wilson was assigned to interview someone in a field that interested her. Since she liked to look up at the sky,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-7) she interviewed [Williams College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Williams_College "Williams College") astronomer [Jay Pasachoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jay_Pasachoff "Jay Pasachoff"),[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-iberkshires.com-6) clarifying her potential career interest in space. In high school, Eugene encouraged Stephanie to go into engineering,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-:0-2) so she decided to become an aerospace engineer.

Wilson graduated from Taconic High School, Pittsfield, Massachusetts, in 1984. She attended [Harvard University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University"), receiving a [Bachelor of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Science "Bachelor of Science") degree in engineering science in 1988. Wilson earned a [Master of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Science "Master of Science") degree in aerospace engineering from the [University of Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Austin "University of Texas at Austin") in 1992.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-womenastronauts-1) Wilson has returned to Harvard as a member of the [Harvard Board of Overseers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Board_of_Overseers "Harvard Board of Overseers").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-8) She was the Chief Marshal for the 362nd Harvard Commencement on May 30, 2013.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-9)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephanie_Wilson&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

### Engineering

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephanie_Wilson&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Engineering")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2c/STS120_Day_7_Harmony_Model.jpg/250px-STS120_Day_7_Harmony_Model.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS120_Day_7_Harmony_Model.jpg)

Wilson during STS-120, with a model of Node 2 "STS-120") floating in front of her

Wilson worked for two years for the former [Martin Marietta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Marietta "Martin Marietta") Astronautics Group in Denver, Colorado. As a Loads and Dynamics engineer for the [Titan IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titan_IV "Titan IV") rocket, Wilson was responsible for performing coupled loads analyses for the launch vehicle and payloads during flight events. Wilson left Martin Marietta in 1990 to attend graduate school at the University of Texas. Her research focused on the control and modeling of large, flexible space structures.

Following the completion of her graduate work, Wilson began working for the [Jet Propulsion Laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jet_Propulsion_Laboratory "Jet Propulsion Laboratory") in [Pasadena, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pasadena,_California "Pasadena, California"), in 1992. As a member of the Attitude and Articulation Control Subsystem for the [Galileo spacecraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galileo_spacecraft "Galileo spacecraft"), Wilson was responsible for assessing attitude controller performance, science platform pointing accuracy, antenna pointing accuracy, and spin rate accuracy. She worked in the areas of sequence development and testing as well. While at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Wilson also supported the Interferometery Technology Program as a member of the Integrated Modeling Team, which was responsible for finite element modeling, controller design, and software development.

## NASA

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephanie_Wilson&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: NASA")]

Selected by [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA") as an astronaut candidate in April 1996, Wilson reported to the [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center") in August 1996. Having completed two years of training and evaluation, she is qualified for flight assignment as a mission specialist. She was initially assigned technical duties in the Astronaut Office Space Station Operations Branch to work with Space Station payload displays and procedures. She then served in the Astronaut Office [CAPCOM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flight_controller#Spacecraft_communicator_(CAPCOM) "Flight controller") Branch, working in Mission Control as a prime communicator with on-orbit crews. Following her work in Mission Control, Wilson was assigned technical duties in the Astronaut Office Shuttle Operations Branch involving the Space Shuttle Main Engines, External Tank and Solid Rocket Boosters.

Wilson has flown on three shuttle missions. On [STS-121](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-121 "STS-121"), Wilson flew aboard as a mission specialist. She also flew on the STS-120 mission that delivered the [Harmony connecting module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmony_Module "Harmony Module") to the International Space Station.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-NASAbio-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-12) In April 2010, Wilson flew as a mission specialist on [STS-131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-131 "STS-131").

On October 18, 2019, Wilson was ground controller at [Houston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center") for the first all woman spacewalk by [Christina Koch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christina_Koch "Christina Koch") and [Jessica Meir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessica_Meir "Jessica Meir").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-13)

On December 9, 2020, NASA announced that Stephanie Wilson was among the candidates for the [Artemis program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artemis_program "Artemis program"), and if selected, she could be both the first woman and the first African-American on the Moon.

On January 31, 2024, NASA announced that Wilson would fly as mission specialist on the [SpaceX Crew-9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpaceX_Crew-9 "SpaceX Crew-9") mission to the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-14) However, when NASA decided to return the [Boeing Starliner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_Starliner "Boeing Starliner") capsule on the [Boeing Crew Flight Test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_Crew_Flight_Test "Boeing Crew Flight Test") uncrewed, Wilson was removed from Crew-9, along with commander and fellow astronaut [Zena Cardman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zena_Cardman "Zena Cardman"), to make room on the return journey for the Starliner astronauts, [Barry E. Wilmore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barry_E._Wilmore "Barry E. Wilmore") and [Sunita Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunita_Williams "Sunita Williams").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-15) On September 28, 2024, she made a brief appearance during NASA's coverage of the Crew-9 launch, which was co-hosted by Cardman and NASA communicator Derrol Nail. Cardman had commented during the nearly five-hour broadcast at length on the experience that [Nick Hague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Hague "Nick Hague") and [Roscosmos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roscosmos "Roscosmos") cosmonaut [Aleksandr Gorbunov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aleksandr_Gorbunov "Aleksandr Gorbunov") were going through as they successfully launched from [Cape Canaveral Space Force Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Canaveral_Space_Force_Station "Cape Canaveral Space Force Station") in Florida.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-16)

### Spaceflight experience

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephanie_Wilson&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Spaceflight experience")]

#### STS-121

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephanie_Wilson&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: STS-121")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/18/Jsc2009e207942Wilson.jpg/250px-Jsc2009e207942Wilson.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jsc2009e207942Wilson.jpg)

Wilson participates in a training session in the Space Vehicle Mock-up Facility at NASA's [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center")

[STS-121](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-121 "STS-121") (July 4–17, 2006), was a return-to-flight test mission and assembly flight to the International Space Station. During the 13-day flight, the crew of Space Shuttle Discovery tested new equipment and procedures that increase the safety of space shuttles, repaired a rail car on the International Space Station and produced never-before-seen, high-resolution images of the Shuttle during and after its July 4 launch. Wilson supported robotic arm operations for vehicle inspection, [Multi-Purpose Logistics Module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-Purpose_Logistics_Module "Multi-Purpose Logistics Module") installation and EVAs and was responsible for transferring more than 28,000 pounds of supplies and equipment to the ISS. The crew also performed maintenance on the space station and delivered a new [Expedition 13](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_13 "Expedition 13") crew member to the station. The mission was accomplished in 306 hours, 37 minutes, and 54 seconds.

#### STS-120

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephanie_Wilson&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: STS-120")]

STS-120 (October 23 – November 7, 2007) was a 6.25 million mile [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") mission to the International Space Station.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-main-17) It delivered the _[Harmony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmony\_Module "Harmony Module")_ module, and reconfigured the [P6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integrated_Truss_Structure#P6,_S6_trusses "Integrated Truss Structure") truss in preparation for future assembly missions.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-presskit-18) STS-120 carried a new [Expedition 16](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_16 "Expedition 16") crew member, [Daniel Tani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Tani "Daniel Tani"), and returned [Expedition 15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_15 "Expedition 15") and Expedition 16 crewmember Clayton Anderson. The crew conducted four [spacewalks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extra-vehicular_activity "Extra-vehicular activity") and performed a previously untested repair method on the station's solar array. The mission was accomplished in 15 days, 2 hours, 23 minutes, during 238 orbits.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-finalsr-19)

#### STS-131

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephanie_Wilson&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: STS-131")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b2/STS-131_ISS-23_Four_Astronauts.jpg/330px-STS-131_ISS-23_Four_Astronauts.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS-131_ISS-23_Four_Astronauts.jpg)

The four astronauts of [STS-131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-131 "STS-131") and [Expedition 23](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_23 "Expedition 23") (Wilson to the bottom right), the first time four women being at the same time in space.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-20)

[STS-131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-131 "STS-131") (April 5–20, 2010) was a resupply mission to the International Space Station. Space Shuttle Discovery was launched pre-dawn from Kennedy Space Center. Once docked to the space station, the crew delivered more than 27,000 pounds of hardware, supplies, experiments and equipment, including a tank full of ammonia coolant that required three spacewalks and robotics to install, new crew sleeping quarters, a window observation facility and a freezer for experiments.

During the mission, Wilson was responsible for robotics for spacewalking support using the space station robotic arm and for robotic removal of the "Leonardo" Multi-Purpose Logistics Module from the payload bay of Discovery. For the return to Earth, Wilson robotically installed Leonardo, which was packed with more than 6,000 pounds of hardware, science results and used supplies, inside Discovery's payload bay. The STS-131 mission was accomplished in 15 days, 2 hours, 47 minutes, and 10 seconds and traveled 6,232,235 statute miles in 238 orbits.

#### Artemis

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephanie_Wilson&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Artemis")]

[Artemis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artemis_program "Artemis program") (2017–present) is the mission NASA announced in 2020 to return to the Moon.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-21) Wilson has been selected as one of 18 astronauts comprising the Artemis team.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-23)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephanie_Wilson&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Wilson is a Christian.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-24) She is a member of [Alpha Kappa Alpha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpha_Kappa_Alpha "Alpha Kappa Alpha") sorority.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-25) Her hobbies include skiing and stamp collecting.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-26) She married Julius "BJ" McCurdy, a television producer, in June 1999.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-30) The couple divorced in 2003.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-31)

## Awards and honors

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephanie_Wilson&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Awards and honors")]

*   [NASA Distinguished Service Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_Distinguished_Service_Medal "NASA Distinguished Service Medal") (2009, 2011)
*   [NASA Space Flight Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_Space_Flight_Medal "NASA Space Flight Medal") (2006, 2007, 2010)
*   Honorary Doctorate of Science from Williams College (2011)
*   Harvard College Women's Professional Achievement Award (2008)
*   Harvard Foundation Scientist of the Year Award (2008)
*   Young Outstanding Texas Exes Award (2005)
*   Johnson Space Center Innovation Group Achievement Award (2013)
*   Johnson Space Center Director Commendation Award (2013)
*   Salem Trailblazer Award (2019)

**Stephanie Diana Wilson** (born September 27, 1966)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-womenastronauts-1) is an American [engineer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engineer "Engineer") and a [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")[astronaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut "Astronaut"). She flew to space onboard three [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") missions and is the second [African American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_American "African American") woman to go into space after [Mae Jemison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mae_Jemison "Mae Jemison"). As of 2026,[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephanie_Wilson&action=edit) her almost 43 days in space are the second most of any female African American astronaut, having been surpassed by [Jessica Watkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessica_Watkins "Jessica Watkins") in 2022.

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephanie_Wilson&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Wilson was born in [Boston, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston,_Massachusetts "Boston, Massachusetts") on September 27, 1966. About a year later, her parents, Eugene and Barbara Wilson,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-:0-2) decided to move to [Pittsfield, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsfield,_Massachusetts "Pittsfield, Massachusetts").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-3) Eugene, a native of [Nesmith, South Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nesmith,_South_Carolina "Nesmith, South Carolina"), used his electronics training from his time in the Navy to get himself a degree from [Northeastern University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northeastern_University "Northeastern University") and a long career in electrical engineering for [Raytheon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raytheon "Raytheon"), [Sprague Electric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_C._Sprague "Robert C. Sprague"), and [Lockheed Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_Martin "Lockheed Martin"),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-:0-2)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-4) while Barbara, from [Talbot County, Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_County,_Georgia "Talbot County, Georgia"),[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-5) worked as a production assistant for Lockheed Martin.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-:0-2)

After attending Stearns Elementary School, she attended Crosby Junior High School.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-iberkshires.com-6) For a career awareness class in middle school, Wilson was assigned to interview someone in a field that interested her. Since she liked to look up at the sky,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-7) she interviewed [Williams College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Williams_College "Williams College") astronomer [Jay Pasachoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jay_Pasachoff "Jay Pasachoff"),[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-iberkshires.com-6) clarifying her potential career interest in space. In high school, Eugene encouraged Stephanie to go into engineering,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-:0-2) so she decided to become an aerospace engineer.

Wilson graduated from Taconic High School, Pittsfield, Massachusetts, in 1984. She attended [Harvard University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University"), receiving a [Bachelor of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Science "Bachelor of Science") degree in engineering science in 1988. Wilson earned a [Master of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Science "Master of Science") degree in aerospace engineering from the [University of Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Austin "University of Texas at Austin") in 1992.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-womenastronauts-1) Wilson has returned to Harvard as a member of the [Harvard Board of Overseers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Board_of_Overseers "Harvard Board of Overseers").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-8) She was the Chief Marshal for the 362nd Harvard Commencement on May 30, 2013.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-9)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephanie_Wilson&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

### Engineering

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephanie_Wilson&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Engineering")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2c/STS120_Day_7_Harmony_Model.jpg/250px-STS120_Day_7_Harmony_Model.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS120_Day_7_Harmony_Model.jpg)

Wilson during STS-120, with a model of Node 2 "STS-120") floating in front of her

Wilson worked for two years for the former [Martin Marietta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Marietta "Martin Marietta") Astronautics Group in Denver, Colorado. As a Loads and Dynamics engineer for the [Titan IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titan_IV "Titan IV") rocket, Wilson was responsible for performing coupled loads analyses for the launch vehicle and payloads during flight events. Wilson left Martin Marietta in 1990 to attend graduate school at the University of Texas. Her research focused on the control and modeling of large, flexible space structures.

Following the completion of her graduate work, Wilson began working for the [Jet Propulsion Laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jet_Propulsion_Laboratory "Jet Propulsion Laboratory") in [Pasadena, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pasadena,_California "Pasadena, California"), in 1992. As a member of the Attitude and Articulation Control Subsystem for the [Galileo spacecraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galileo_spacecraft "Galileo spacecraft"), Wilson was responsible for assessing attitude controller performance, science platform pointing accuracy, antenna pointing accuracy, and spin rate accuracy. She worked in the areas of sequence development and testing as well. While at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Wilson also supported the Interferometery Technology Program as a member of the Integrated Modeling Team, which was responsible for finite element modeling, controller design, and software development.

## NASA

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephanie_Wilson&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: NASA")]

Selected by [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA") as an astronaut candidate in April 1996, Wilson reported to the [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center") in August 1996. Having completed two years of training and evaluation, she is qualified for flight assignment as a mission specialist. She was initially assigned technical duties in the Astronaut Office Space Station Operations Branch to work with Space Station payload displays and procedures. She then served in the Astronaut Office [CAPCOM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flight_controller#Spacecraft_communicator_(CAPCOM) "Flight controller") Branch, working in Mission Control as a prime communicator with on-orbit crews. Following her work in Mission Control, Wilson was assigned technical duties in the Astronaut Office Shuttle Operations Branch involving the Space Shuttle Main Engines, External Tank and Solid Rocket Boosters.

Wilson has flown on three shuttle missions. On [STS-121](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-121 "STS-121"), Wilson flew aboard as a mission specialist. She also flew on the STS-120 mission that delivered the [Harmony connecting module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmony_Module "Harmony Module") to the International Space Station.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-NASAbio-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-12) In April 2010, Wilson flew as a mission specialist on [STS-131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-131 "STS-131").

On October 18, 2019, Wilson was ground controller at [Houston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center") for the first all woman spacewalk by [Christina Koch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christina_Koch "Christina Koch") and [Jessica Meir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessica_Meir "Jessica Meir").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-13)

On December 9, 2020, NASA announced that Stephanie Wilson was among the candidates for the [Artemis program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artemis_program "Artemis program"), and if selected, she could be both the first woman and the first African-American on the Moon.

On January 31, 2024, NASA announced that Wilson would fly as mission specialist on the [SpaceX Crew-9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpaceX_Crew-9 "SpaceX Crew-9") mission to the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-14) However, when NASA decided to return the [Boeing Starliner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_Starliner "Boeing Starliner") capsule on the [Boeing Crew Flight Test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_Crew_Flight_Test "Boeing Crew Flight Test") uncrewed, Wilson was removed from Crew-9, along with commander and fellow astronaut [Zena Cardman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zena_Cardman "Zena Cardman"), to make room on the return journey for the Starliner astronauts, [Barry E. Wilmore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barry_E._Wilmore "Barry E. Wilmore") and [Sunita Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunita_Williams "Sunita Williams").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-15) On September 28, 2024, she made a brief appearance during NASA's coverage of the Crew-9 launch, which was co-hosted by Cardman and NASA communicator Derrol Nail. Cardman had commented during the nearly five-hour broadcast at length on the experience that [Nick Hague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Hague "Nick Hague") and [Roscosmos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roscosmos "Roscosmos") cosmonaut [Aleksandr Gorbunov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aleksandr_Gorbunov "Aleksandr Gorbunov") were going through as they successfully launched from [Cape Canaveral Space Force Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Canaveral_Space_Force_Station "Cape Canaveral Space Force Station") in Florida.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-16)

### Spaceflight experience

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephanie_Wilson&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Spaceflight experience")]

#### STS-121

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephanie_Wilson&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: STS-121")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/18/Jsc2009e207942Wilson.jpg/250px-Jsc2009e207942Wilson.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jsc2009e207942Wilson.jpg)

Wilson participates in a training session in the Space Vehicle Mock-up Facility at NASA's [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center")

[STS-121](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-121 "STS-121") (July 4–17, 2006), was a return-to-flight test mission and assembly flight to the International Space Station. During the 13-day flight, the crew of Space Shuttle Discovery tested new equipment and procedures that increase the safety of space shuttles, repaired a rail car on the International Space Station and produced never-before-seen, high-resolution images of the Shuttle during and after its July 4 launch. Wilson supported robotic arm operations for vehicle inspection, [Multi-Purpose Logistics Module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-Purpose_Logistics_Module "Multi-Purpose Logistics Module") installation and EVAs and was responsible for transferring more than 28,000 pounds of supplies and equipment to the ISS. The crew also performed maintenance on the space station and delivered a new [Expedition 13](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_13 "Expedition 13") crew member to the station. The mission was accomplished in 306 hours, 37 minutes, and 54 seconds.

#### STS-120

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephanie_Wilson&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: STS-120")]

STS-120 (October 23 – November 7, 2007) was a 6.25 million mile [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") mission to the International Space Station.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-main-17) It delivered the _[Harmony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmony\_Module "Harmony Module")_ module, and reconfigured the [P6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integrated_Truss_Structure#P6,_S6_trusses "Integrated Truss Structure") truss in preparation for future assembly missions.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-presskit-18) STS-120 carried a new [Expedition 16](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_16 "Expedition 16") crew member, [Daniel Tani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Tani "Daniel Tani"), and returned [Expedition 15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_15 "Expedition 15") and Expedition 16 crewmember Clayton Anderson. The crew conducted four [spacewalks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extra-vehicular_activity "Extra-vehicular activity") and performed a previously untested repair method on the station's solar array. The mission was accomplished in 15 days, 2 hours, 23 minutes, during 238 orbits.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-finalsr-19)

#### STS-131

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephanie_Wilson&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: STS-131")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b2/STS-131_ISS-23_Four_Astronauts.jpg/330px-STS-131_ISS-23_Four_Astronauts.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS-131_ISS-23_Four_Astronauts.jpg)

The four astronauts of [STS-131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-131 "STS-131") and [Expedition 23](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_23 "Expedition 23") (Wilson to the bottom right), the first time four women being at the same time in space.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-20)

[STS-131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-131 "STS-131") (April 5–20, 2010) was a resupply mission to the International Space Station. Space Shuttle Discovery was launched pre-dawn from Kennedy Space Center. Once docked to the space station, the crew delivered more than 27,000 pounds of hardware, supplies, experiments and equipment, including a tank full of ammonia coolant that required three spacewalks and robotics to install, new crew sleeping quarters, a window observation facility and a freezer for experiments.

During the mission, Wilson was responsible for robotics for spacewalking support using the space station robotic arm and for robotic removal of the "Leonardo" Multi-Purpose Logistics Module from the payload bay of Discovery. For the return to Earth, Wilson robotically installed Leonardo, which was packed with more than 6,000 pounds of hardware, science results and used supplies, inside Discovery's payload bay. The STS-131 mission was accomplished in 15 days, 2 hours, 47 minutes, and 10 seconds and traveled 6,232,235 statute miles in 238 orbits.

#### Artemis

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephanie_Wilson&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Artemis")]

[Artemis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artemis_program "Artemis program") (2017–present) is the mission NASA announced in 2020 to return to the Moon.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-21) Wilson has been selected as one of 18 astronauts comprising the Artemis team.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-23)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephanie_Wilson&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Wilson is a Christian.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-24) She is a member of [Alpha Kappa Alpha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpha_Kappa_Alpha "Alpha Kappa Alpha") sorority.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-25) Her hobbies include skiing and stamp collecting.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-26) She married Julius "BJ" McCurdy, a television producer, in June 1999.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-30) The couple divorced in 2003.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-31)

**Steven Gerald Clifford** (born September 17, 1961) is an American professional [basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball "Basketball") coach and executive who serves as a coaching advisor for the [Washington Wizards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Wizards "Washington Wizards") of the [National Basketball Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Basketball_Association "National Basketball Association") (NBA). He has previously served as the head coach of the [Charlotte Hornets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlotte_Hornets "Charlotte Hornets") and [Orlando Magic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orlando_Magic "Orlando Magic").

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Steve_Clifford&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Born in [Island Falls, Maine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Island_Falls,_Maine "Island Falls, Maine"), Clifford grew up in [Mattawamkeag, Maine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mattawamkeag,_Maine "Mattawamkeag, Maine"), until the third grade, when he moved to [Vermont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vermont "Vermont").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-1) He played varsity basketball under Gerald Clifford, his father and head coach at [North Country Union High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Country_Union_High_School "North Country Union High School") in [Newport, Vermont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newport_(city),_Vermont "Newport (city), Vermont").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-maine_native-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-3)

Clifford attended the [University of Maine at Farmington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Maine_at_Farmington "University of Maine at Farmington"), where he played [college basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_basketball "College basketball") for four years. In his final two seasons, he was team captain and was named Best Defensive Player. He graduated with a degree in [special education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_education "Special education").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-4)

## Coaching career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Steve_Clifford&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Coaching career")]

After graduating from college, Clifford became a teacher at [Woodland High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodland_High_School_(Maine) "Woodland High School (Maine)") in Maine. He also gained his first coaching experience at the school, serving as their [head coach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_coach "Head coach") for two seasons while leading them to two tournaments.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-maine_native-2)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-nba_profile-5) He then served as an assistant coach at [St. Anselm College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Anselm_College "St. Anselm College"), [Fairfield University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairfield_University "Fairfield University"), [Boston University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_University "Boston University") and [Siena College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siena_College "Siena College"). In 1995, he assumed the head coaching duties at [Adelphi University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adelphi_University "Adelphi University") and coached for four seasons leading his team to four appearances in the NCAA Division II Tournament, an 86–36 (.705) record and four consecutive 20-win seasons. He was the first coach in the school's history with back-to-back 20-plus-win seasons.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-nba_profile-5)

Clifford became an NBA assistant coach with the [New York Knicks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Knicks "New York Knicks") and [Houston Rockets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston_Rockets "Houston Rockets") under [Jeff Van Gundy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Van_Gundy "Jeff Van Gundy") and quickly developed a reputation as a defensive expert. He then was an assistant for [Stan Van Gundy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy "Stan Van Gundy") with the [Orlando Magic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orlando_Magic "Orlando Magic").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-maine_native-2) He considers both the Van Gundy brothers as mentors.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-6) He reached the NBA playoffs in each of his five seasons with Orlando, appearing in the NBA Finals in 2009.

Clifford then joined the [Los Angeles Lakers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Lakers "Los Angeles Lakers") in [2012–13](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012%E2%80%9313_Los_Angeles_Lakers_season "2012–13 Los Angeles Lakers season") as an assistant.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-7)

### Charlotte Bobcats/Hornets

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Steve_Clifford&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Charlotte Bobcats/Hornets")]

On May 29, 2013, Clifford was hired by the [Charlotte Bobcats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlotte_Bobcats "Charlotte Bobcats") to be their head coach.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-nba_05292013-8)

Clifford implemented a defensive mentality in Charlotte during his first year as head coach turning the [Charlotte Bobcats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlotte_Bobcats "Charlotte Bobcats") into a top five defensive team when in the years prior to his tenure they ranked near the bottom of the NBA in that category. He led the Bobcats to the [2014 NBA playoffs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_NBA_playoffs "2014 NBA playoffs") in his first year as head coach, during which he coached the Bobcats to a 43–39 record. The two years prior to him joining the Bobcats only had a combined total of 28 wins. He was named Eastern Conference Coach of the Month for April 2014 after he led the Bobcats to a 7–1 record leading to the playoffs. He finished fourth in Coach of the Year voting in his first year. On December 6, 2017, it was announced that Clifford would not coach indefinitely to deal with his health issue.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-10) On January 11, 2018, the Hornets announced that Clifford was medically cleared to return to coaching[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-11) after a 21-game absence after dealing with [sleep deprivation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleep_deprivation "Sleep deprivation").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-12) After the [2017–18 regular season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017%E2%80%9318_NBA_season "2017–18 NBA season"), he was fired as head coach on April 13, 2018, after five seasons coaching the team to a 196–214 record total.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-13)

### Orlando Magic

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Steve_Clifford&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Orlando Magic")]

On May 30, 2018, Clifford was named the head coach of the [Orlando Magic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orlando_Magic "Orlando Magic").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-14)

The Magic started the 2018–19 season by splitting their first 24 games before falling 11 games under .500 after a 126–117 loss to the [Oklahoma City Thunder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma_City_Thunder "Oklahoma City Thunder").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-15) Despite the dismal start, Clifford led the Magic on a dramatic turnaround. On April 7, 2019, Orlando defeated the [Boston Celtics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Celtics "Boston Celtics") 116–108 to clinch their first playoff berth since the [2011–12 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011%E2%80%9312_Orlando_Magic_season "2011–12 Orlando Magic season").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-16) The win also clinched the Magic's first [Southeast Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_Division_(NBA) "Southeast Division (NBA)") title since the [2009–10 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009%E2%80%9310_Orlando_Magic_season "2009–10 Orlando Magic season"). This was the Magic's first playoff appearance since trading [Dwight Howard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dwight_Howard "Dwight Howard") to the [Los Angeles Lakers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Lakers "Los Angeles Lakers") in 2012,[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-17) ending the longest playoff drought in franchise history.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-18)

On June 5, 2021, Clifford and the Magic decided to part ways.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-19)

### Charlotte Hornets (second stint)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Steve_Clifford&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Charlotte Hornets (second stint)")]

After the [2021–22 NBA season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%9322_NBA_season "2021–22 NBA season") concluded, the Hornets re-hired Clifford as their head coach on June 24, 2022.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-20)

On April 3, 2024, the Hornets announced that Clifford would step down as head coach at the end of the [2023–24 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023%E2%80%9324_NBA_season "2023–24 NBA season") and move into a front-office advisory role.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-21)

### Phoenix Suns

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Steve_Clifford&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Phoenix Suns")]

On August 13, 2025, the [Phoenix Suns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix_Suns "Phoenix Suns") hired Clifford to serve as a coaching advisor under head coach [Jordan Ott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan_Ott "Jordan Ott").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-22)

### Washington Wizards

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Steve_Clifford&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Washington Wizards")]

On July 6, 2026, the [Washington Wizards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Wizards "Washington Wizards") hired Clifford to serve as an advisor under head coach [Brian Keefe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Keefe "Brian Keefe").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-23)
